frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: diagnosis and management: Blood cultures first: […].
backHtml: Blood cultures first: at least 3 sets from separate venipunctures before antibiotics.

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: diagnosis and management: Go on to […] when TTE is negative but suspicion stays high, when the patient has a prosthetic valve or device, when S. aureus bacteremia is present, or when a complication (abscess, perforation) is suspected.
backHtml: Go on to transesophageal echo (TEE) when TTE is negative but suspicion stays high, when the patient has a prosthetic valve or device, when S. aureus bacteremia is present, or when a complication (abscess, perforation) is suspected.

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: diagnosis and management: S. gallolyticus → […]. Enterococcus → look for a GU or GI source.
backHtml: S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy. Enterococcus → look for a GU or GI source.

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: diagnosis and management: The usual regimen is […] 30–60 minutes before the procedure; alternatives for penicillin allergy include cephalexin (if the reaction was not anaphylaxis), azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline.
backHtml: The usual regimen is a single oral dose of amoxicillin 30–60 minutes before the procedure; alternatives for penicillin allergy include cephalexin (if the reaction was not anaphylaxis), azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline.

frontHtml: Myocarditis, Lyme carditis, Chagas disease and syphilitic aortitis in practice: Tests: ECG (sinus tachycardia, ST changes, arrhythmia), troponin, echocardiogram (global or regional dysfunction). […] is the best noninvasive test (myocardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary pattern).
backHtml: Tests: ECG (sinus tachycardia, ST changes, arrhythmia), troponin, echocardiogram (global or regional dysfunction). Cardiac MRI is the best noninvasive test (myocardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary pattern).

frontHtml: Myocarditis, Lyme carditis, Chagas disease and syphilitic aortitis in practice: Admit and monitor patients who are symptomatic or who have […], second- or third-degree block.
backHtml: Admit and monitor patients who are symptomatic or who have a PR interval of 300 ms or more, second- or third-degree block.

frontHtml: Myocarditis, Lyme carditis, Chagas disease and syphilitic aortitis in practice: Diagnosis in the chronic phase is serologic ([…]); blood smears help only in the acute phase.
backHtml: Diagnosis in the chronic phase is serologic (two different IgG assays); blood smears help only in the acute phase.

frontHtml: Myocarditis, Lyme carditis, Chagas disease and syphilitic aortitis in practice: Treat tertiary (non-neurologic) syphilis with […] IM weekly for 3 weeks; neurosyphilis needs IV aqueous penicillin G.
backHtml: Treat tertiary (non-neurologic) syphilis with benzathine penicillin G IM weekly for 3 weeks; neurosyphilis needs IV aqueous penicillin G.

frontHtml: Rheumatic fever: diagnosis, treatment and prevention: […] (the most sensitive evidence when cultures are negative); throat culture or rapid antigen test.
backHtml: Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers (the most sensitive evidence when cultures are negative); throat culture or rapid antigen test.

frontHtml: Rheumatic fever: diagnosis, treatment and prevention: Secondary prevention after a diagnosis of ARF: […] (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings).
backHtml: Secondary prevention after a diagnosis of ARF: IM benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings).

frontHtml: Rheumatic fever: diagnosis, treatment and prevention: Atrial fibrillation with rheumatic mitral stenosis needs a […]; direct oral anticoagulants are not used for moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis because warfarin was superior in a trial of this population.
backHtml: Atrial fibrillation with rheumatic mitral stenosis needs a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin); direct oral anticoagulants are not used for moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis because warfarin was superior in a trial of this population.

frontHtml: Rheumatic fever: diagnosis, treatment and prevention: Pregnancy raises heart rate and plasma volume and can precipitate pulmonary edema; first-line treatment is a […] (such as metoprolol) to lengthen diastolic filling, plus a diuretic for congestion; balloon commissurotomy is an option for refractory symptoms.
backHtml: Pregnancy raises heart rate and plasma volume and can precipitate pulmonary edema; first-line treatment is a β-blocker (such as metoprolol) to lengthen diastolic filling, plus a diuretic for congestion; balloon commissurotomy is an option for refractory symptoms.

frontHtml: Kawasaki disease: Complete Kawasaki disease : […]:
backHtml: Complete Kawasaki disease : fever for at least 5 days plus at least 4 of these 5 findings:

frontHtml: Kawasaki disease: IVIG […], ideally within the first 10 days of fever (and later if fever or inflammation persists), plus aspirin (moderate or high dose while febrile, then low dose until follow-up echo is normal, typically 6–8 weeks).
backHtml: IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion, ideally within the first 10 days of fever (and later if fever or inflammation persists), plus aspirin (moderate or high dose while febrile, then low dose until follow-up echo is normal, typically 6–8 weeks).

frontHtml: Kawasaki disease: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) should be delayed about […], because passively transferred antibody blunts the response.
backHtml: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) should be delayed about 11 months after IVIG, because passively transferred antibody blunts the response.

frontHtml: Kawasaki disease: Children on aspirin need yearly inactivated influenza vaccine (not the live intranasal vaccine), because influenza or varicella during aspirin therapy raises the risk of […].
backHtml: Children on aspirin need yearly inactivated influenza vaccine (not the live intranasal vaccine), because influenza or varicella during aspirin therapy raises the risk of Reye syndrome.

frontHtml: Sterile endocarditis, carcinoid heart disease and large-vessel vasculitis in practice: Patients with APS and thrombosis or embolism need long-term anticoagulation with a […]; direct oral anticoagulants performed worse in high-risk (especially triple-positive) APS and are avoided there.
backHtml: Patients with APS and thrombosis or embolism need long-term anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin); direct oral anticoagulants performed worse in high-risk (especially triple-positive) APS and are avoided there.

frontHtml: Sterile endocarditis, carcinoid heart disease and large-vessel vasculitis in practice: Treat with […] (unfractionated or low-molecular-weight), which works better than warfarin in cancer-associated hypercoagulability, and treat the cancer.
backHtml: Treat with therapeutic heparin (unfractionated or low-molecular-weight), which works better than warfarin in cancer-associated hypercoagulability, and treat the cancer.

frontHtml: Sterile endocarditis, carcinoid heart disease and large-vessel vasculitis in practice: Best initial test: […] (or plasma 5-HIAA); avoid serotonin-rich foods (bananas, walnuts, avocado, pineapple) and some drugs before testing.
backHtml: Best initial test: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA (or plasma 5-HIAA); avoid serotonin-rich foods (bananas, walnuts, avocado, pineapple) and some drugs before testing.

frontHtml: Sterile endocarditis, carcinoid heart disease and large-vessel vasculitis in practice: New headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms in someone over 50 with a high ESR or CRP: start […] (IV methylprednisolone if vision is threatened) and arrange temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound within the next 1–2 weeks.
backHtml: New headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms in someone over 50 with a high ESR or CRP: start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately (IV methylprednisolone if vision is threatened) and arrange temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound within the next 1–2 weeks.

frontHtml: Sterile endocarditis, carcinoid heart disease and large-vessel vasculitis in practice: Diagnosis: […] (long smooth stenoses, wall thickening); ESR and CRP may be normal despite active disease.
backHtml: Diagnosis: MR or CT angiography of the aorta and branches (long smooth stenoses, wall thickening); ESR and CRP may be normal despite active disease.

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: organisms and pathology: Virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus can attach to normal valves directly, using surface adhesins that bind fibronectin and fibrinogen ([…]).
backHtml: Virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus can attach to normal valves directly, using surface adhesins that bind fibronectin and fibrinogen (clumping factor).

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: organisms and pathology: […]: spread by body lice; people experiencing homelessness or alcohol use disorder. Bartonella henselae comes from cats.
backHtml: Bartonella quintana: spread by body lice; people experiencing homelessness or alcohol use disorder. Bartonella henselae comes from cats.

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: organisms and pathology: Persistent antigenemia drives circulating immune complexes ([…], positive rheumatoid factor).
backHtml: Persistent antigenemia drives circulating immune complexes (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, positive rheumatoid factor).

frontHtml: Infective endocarditis: organisms and pathology: Injection drug use shifts infection to the […] valve, which presents with fever, a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that rises with inspiration, and multiple cavitating lung nodules.
backHtml: Injection drug use shifts infection to the tricuspid valve, which presents with fever, a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that rises with inspiration, and multiple cavitating lung nodules.

frontHtml: Other infections of the heart and aorta: Agents: enteroviruses (classically […]), adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, influenza and SARS-CoV-2.
backHtml: Agents: enteroviruses (classically coxsackievirus B), adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, influenza and SARS-CoV-2.

frontHtml: Other infections of the heart and aorta: Histology: a […] next to the lymphocytes.
backHtml: Histology: a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis next to the lymphocytes.

frontHtml: Other infections of the heart and aorta: Heart: dilated cardiomyopathy , left ventricular apical aneurysm with mural thrombus, […], ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death.
backHtml: Heart: dilated cardiomyopathy , left ventricular apical aneurysm with mural thrombus, right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death.

frontHtml: Other infections of the heart and aorta: Mechanism: obliterative endarteritis of the […] of the ascending aorta → ischemic loss of medial smooth muscle and elastic fibers → scarring that wrinkles the intima ("tree-bark" appearance).
backHtml: Mechanism: obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta → ischemic loss of medial smooth muscle and elastic fibers → scarring that wrinkles the intima ("tree-bark" appearance).

frontHtml: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease: This is a […] reaction, with a T-cell component in the valve.
backHtml: This is a type II hypersensitivity reaction, with a T-cell component in the valve.

frontHtml: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease: Skin infection (impetigo) can cause […] but not rheumatic fever.
backHtml: Skin infection (impetigo) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.

frontHtml: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease: Aschoff bodies : foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells and plump macrophages called […], whose nuclei hold a central wavy ribbon of chromatin ("caterpillar" nuclei).
backHtml: Aschoff bodies : foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells and plump macrophages called Anitschkow cells, whose nuclei hold a central wavy ribbon of chromatin ("caterpillar" nuclei).

frontHtml: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease: […] is the signature lesion ("fish-mouth" orifice), often with regurgitation; the aortic valve is next; tricuspid involvement nearly always accompanies mitral disease; the pulmonic valve is rarely affected.
backHtml: Mitral stenosis is the signature lesion ("fish-mouth" orifice), often with regurgitation; the aortic valve is next; tricuspid involvement nearly always accompanies mitral disease; the pulmonic valve is rarely affected.

frontHtml: Noninfective vegetations and carcinoid heart disease: Strongly associated with […] (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I).
backHtml: Strongly associated with antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I).

frontHtml: Noninfective vegetations and carcinoid heart disease: The classic setting is a […] (pancreas, lung, stomach, ovary), where mucin and tissue factor activate coagulation (the same process causes migratory thrombophlebitis).
backHtml: The classic setting is a mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma (pancreas, lung, stomach, ovary), where mucin and tissue factor activate coagulation (the same process causes migratory thrombophlebitis).

frontHtml: Noninfective vegetations and carcinoid heart disease: The left heart is spared because […] degrades serotonin.
backHtml: The left heart is spared because monoamine oxidase in the lung degrades serotonin.

frontHtml: Noninfective vegetations and carcinoid heart disease: Serotonin is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid ([…]), which is measured in the urine.
backHtml: Serotonin is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which is measured in the urine.

frontHtml: Vasculitis of the heart and aorta: Untreated, about a quarter of children develop […]; prompt intravenous immunoglobulin lowers that risk to a few per cent.
backHtml: Untreated, about a quarter of children develop coronary aneurysms; prompt intravenous immunoglobulin lowers that risk to a few per cent.

frontHtml: Vasculitis of the heart and aorta: Aortic root dilation can cause aortic regurgitation; […].
backHtml: Aortic root dilation can cause aortic regurgitation; renal artery stenosis causes hypertension.

frontHtml: Vasculitis of the heart and aorta: The cytokine IL-6 drives the systemic inflammation; […], a monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor, spares glucocorticoids.
backHtml: The cytokine IL-6 drives the systemic inflammation; tocilizumab, a monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor, spares glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Cardiac masses: evaluation and management: Myxoma: […], because of the risk of embolism and sudden obstruction.
backHtml: Myxoma: surgical excision soon after diagnosis, because of the risk of embolism and sudden obstruction.

frontHtml: Cardiac masses: evaluation and management: The stalk and a cuff of the septum are removed to reduce recurrence. […].
backHtml: The stalk and a cuff of the septum are removed to reduce recurrence. Anticoagulation does not treat the tumor.

frontHtml: Cardiac masses: evaluation and management: Rhabdomyoma (child): usually […] because most regress.
backHtml: Rhabdomyoma (child): usually observation with serial echocardiography because most regress.

frontHtml: Cardiac masses: evaluation and management: Malignant effusions often recur, so definitive options include extended catheter drainage, a […], or intrapericardial sclerosis in selected patients, together with systemic cancer treatment.
backHtml: Malignant effusions often recur, so definitive options include extended catheter drainage, a surgical pericardial window, or intrapericardial sclerosis in selected patients, together with systemic cancer treatment.

frontHtml: Primary and metastatic cardiac tumors: Where and what. About three quarters arise in the […], typically on a stalk attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis; most of the rest are in the right atrium.
backHtml: Where and what. About three quarters arise in the left atrium, typically on a stalk attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis; most of the rest are in the right atrium.

frontHtml: Primary and metastatic cardiac tumors: Microscopically, scattered stellate and spindle-shaped "myxoma cells", single or in cords and ring-like clusters around small vessels, sit in an abundant […], often with hemorrhage and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
backHtml: Microscopically, scattered stellate and spindle-shaped "myxoma cells", single or in cords and ring-like clusters around small vessels, sit in an abundant mucopolysaccharide (myxoid) ground substance, often with hemorrhage and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

frontHtml: Primary and metastatic cardiac tumors: Constitutional effects. Myxomas secrete […], which drives fever, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia, anemia, raised ESR and CRP and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.
backHtml: Constitutional effects. Myxomas secrete interleukin-6, which drives fever, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia, anemia, raised ESR and CRP and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.

frontHtml: Primary and metastatic cardiac tumors: Familial disease. About 5–10% of myxomas are familial, most within Carney complex : autosomal dominant, usually from loss-of-function variants in […], which encodes the type 1A regulatory subunit of protein kinase A (so cAMP signalling is unrestrained).
backHtml: Familial disease. About 5–10% of myxomas are familial, most within Carney complex : autosomal dominant, usually from loss-of-function variants in PRKAR1A, which encodes the type 1A regulatory subunit of protein kinase A (so cAMP signalling is unrestrained).

frontHtml: Primary and metastatic cardiac tumors: Usually multiple, within the ventricular walls or septum, and strongly associated with […] ( TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin; loss of either removes inhibition of mTOR signalling).
backHtml: Usually multiple, within the ventricular walls or septum, and strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis complex ( TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin; loss of either removes inhibition of mTOR signalling).

frontHtml: Tachyarrhythmias: recognition and management: Any unstable tachycardia with a pulse is treated with […], whatever the rhythm, after sedation if time allows.
backHtml: Any unstable tachycardia with a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion, whatever the rhythm, after sedation if time allows.

frontHtml: Tachyarrhythmias: recognition and management: Steps: vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva, carotid sinus massage if no bruit or cerebrovascular disease) → […] (rapid push, then a flush; a larger second dose if needed) → IV diltiazem/verapamil or a β-blocker → synchronized cardioversion if all fail or the patient becomes unstable.
backHtml: Steps: vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva, carotid sinus massage if no bruit or cerebrovascular disease) → IV adenosine (rapid push, then a flush; a larger second dose if needed) → IV diltiazem/verapamil or a β-blocker → synchronized cardioversion if all fail or the patient becomes unstable.

frontHtml: Tachyarrhythmias: recognition and management: A direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) is preferred over warfarin, except with a mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis , where […].
backHtml: A direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) is preferred over warfarin, except with a mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis , where warfarin is required.

frontHtml: Tachyarrhythmias: recognition and management: Stable → […].
backHtml: Stable → IV procainamide or ibutilide.

frontHtml: Tachyarrhythmias: recognition and management: Give […]; stop all QT-prolonging drugs; correct potassium and magnesium.
backHtml: Give IV magnesium sulfate; stop all QT-prolonging drugs; correct potassium and magnesium.

frontHtml: Bradyarrhythmias, conduction disease and pacemakers: If there are signs of poor perfusion: […] IV, repeated as needed up to the maximum dose.
backHtml: If there are signs of poor perfusion: atropine IV, repeated as needed up to the maximum dose.

frontHtml: Bradyarrhythmias, conduction disease and pacemakers: If atropine fails: […] or an infusion of dopamine or epinephrine , then expert consultation for transvenous pacing.
backHtml: If atropine fails: transcutaneous pacing or an infusion of dopamine or epinephrine , then expert consultation for transvenous pacing.

frontHtml: Bradyarrhythmias, conduction disease and pacemakers: Recurrent syncope from the cardioinhibitory type is treated with […].
backHtml: Recurrent syncope from the cardioinhibitory type is treated with dual-chamber pacing.

frontHtml: Bradyarrhythmias, conduction disease and pacemakers: LBBB with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction is the main indication for […].
backHtml: LBBB with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction is the main indication for cardiac resynchronization therapy.

frontHtml: Cardiac arrest, sudden cardiac death and the inherited arrhythmias: Recognize arrest (unresponsive, not breathing normally, no definite pulse within 10 seconds), call for help and a defibrillator, and start high-quality chest compressions: […], full recoil, minimal interruptions, and a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed.
backHtml: Recognize arrest (unresponsive, not breathing normally, no definite pulse within 10 seconds), call for help and a defibrillator, and start high-quality chest compressions: a rate of 100–120/min, a depth of at least 5 cm, full recoil, minimal interruptions, and a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed.

frontHtml: Cardiac arrest, sudden cardiac death and the inherited arrhythmias: ST elevation → […].
backHtml: ST elevation → emergent coronary angiography.

frontHtml: Cardiac arrest, sudden cardiac death and the inherited arrhythmias: Primary prevention : an ICD for […] with NYHA class II–III symptoms despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy (and at least 40 days after a myocardial infarction), with reasonable expected survival.
backHtml: Primary prevention : an ICD for left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 35% with NYHA class II–III symptoms despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy (and at least 40 days after a myocardial infarction), with reasonable expected survival.

frontHtml: Cardiac arrest, sudden cardiac death and the inherited arrhythmias: Management: avoid QT-prolonging drugs, keep potassium and magnesium normal, give a β-blocker (nonselective agents such as […] are preferred), screen first-degree relatives with ECGs and genetic testing, and place an ICD after cardiac arrest or with recurrent events despite therapy.
backHtml: Management: avoid QT-prolonging drugs, keep potassium and magnesium normal, give a β-blocker (nonselective agents such as nadolol or propranolol are preferred), screen first-degree relatives with ECGs and genetic testing, and place an ICD after cardiac arrest or with recurrent events despite therapy.

frontHtml: Cardiac electrophysiology and the conduction system: Conduction is fastest in Purkinje fibers, slower in atrial and ventricular muscle and […].
backHtml: Conduction is fastest in Purkinje fibers, slower in atrial and ventricular muscle and slowest in the AV node.

frontHtml: Cardiac electrophysiology and the conduction system: A stimulus in the […], which overlaps the downslope of the T wave, can; this is the vulnerable window in which an early impulse ("R on T") can start ventricular fibrillation.
backHtml: A stimulus in the relative refractory period, which overlaps the downslope of the T wave, can; this is the vulnerable window in which an early impulse ("R on T") can start ventricular fibrillation.

frontHtml: Cardiac electrophysiology and the conduction system: The SA node is usually supplied by the […] and the AV node by the artery that gives off the posterior descending artery, most often the right coronary artery.
backHtml: The SA node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery (about 60% of people) and the AV node by the artery that gives off the posterior descending artery, most often the right coronary artery.

frontHtml: Antiarrhythmic drugs by mechanism: Its toxicity comes from iodine content, lipophilicity and a very long half-life: […], hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, raised transaminases, corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy, photosensitivity and blue-gray skin, and bradycardia.
backHtml: Its toxicity comes from iodine content, lipophilicity and a very long half-life: pulmonary fibrosis or pneumonitis, hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, raised transaminases, corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy, photosensitivity and blue-gray skin, and bradycardia.

frontHtml: Antiarrhythmic drugs by mechanism: Adenosine acts on A 1 receptors in the AV node, increasing K + conductance and reducing Ca 2+ current, which causes a […].
backHtml: Adenosine acts on A 1 receptors in the AV node, increasing K + conductance and reducing Ca 2+ current, which causes a transient (seconds-long) AV block.

frontHtml: Antiarrhythmic drugs by mechanism: Expected effects: flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnea and a brief pause. […] block adenosine receptors and blunt its effect; dipyridamole blocks its uptake and enhances it.
backHtml: Expected effects: flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnea and a brief pause. Methylxanthines (theophylline, caffeine) block adenosine receptors and blunt its effect; dipyridamole blocks its uptake and enhances it.

frontHtml: Antiarrhythmic drugs by mechanism: It can cause luminous visual phenomena ([…]) because related HCN channels exist in the retina.
backHtml: It can cause luminous visual phenomena (phosphenes) because related HCN channels exist in the retina.

frontHtml: Mechanisms behind common rhythms: block, re-entry and channelopathies: The block is usually in the […], often with a wide QRS, and can progress suddenly to complete block.
backHtml: The block is usually in the His–Purkinje system, often with a wide QRS, and can progress suddenly to complete block.

frontHtml: Mechanisms behind common rhythms: block, re-entry and channelopathies: Atrial fibrillation is different: it is driven mostly by rapid firing from muscle sleeves in the […] plus many wandering wavelets in remodelled, fibrosed and dilated atria.
backHtml: Atrial fibrillation is different: it is driven mostly by rapid firing from muscle sleeves in the pulmonary veins plus many wandering wavelets in remodelled, fibrosed and dilated atria.

frontHtml: Mechanisms behind common rhythms: block, re-entry and channelopathies: Part of the ventricle is therefore activated early through the pathway, giving the triad of a short PR interval , a slurred initial QRS upstroke ([…]) and a slightly wide QRS , often with secondary ST–T changes. "WPW syndrome" means the pattern plus tachyarrhythmias.
backHtml: Part of the ventricle is therefore activated early through the pathway, giving the triad of a short PR interval , a slurred initial QRS upstroke (delta wave) and a slightly wide QRS , often with secondary ST–T changes. "WPW syndrome" means the pattern plus tachyarrhythmias.

frontHtml: Mechanisms behind common rhythms: block, re-entry and channelopathies: The autosomal recessive form with congenital sensorineural deafness ([…]) involves the I Ks channel subunits, which are also needed for endolymph production in the inner ear.
backHtml: The autosomal recessive form with congenital sensorineural deafness (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome) involves the I Ks channel subunits, which are also needed for endolymph production in the inner ear.

frontHtml: Mechanisms behind common rhythms: block, re-entry and channelopathies: Brugada syndrome , often from loss of function of the same Na + channel gene, shows a […] and causes polymorphic VT, typically at rest or with fever; it is more often diagnosed in men and in people of East and Southeast Asian ancestry.
backHtml: Brugada syndrome , often from loss of function of the same Na + channel gene, shows a coved ST elevation in V1–V2 and causes polymorphic VT, typically at rest or with fever; it is more often diagnosed in men and in people of East and Southeast Asian ancestry.

frontHtml: Chronic heart failure: diagnosis and guideline-directed therapy: Best initial test once HF is suspected : […].
backHtml: Best initial test once HF is suspected : transthoracic echocardiography.

frontHtml: Chronic heart failure: diagnosis and guideline-directed therapy: Sacubitril raises BNP (it blocks its breakdown), so […] in patients taking an ARNI.
backHtml: Sacubitril raises BNP (it blocks its breakdown), so follow NT-proBNP in patients taking an ARNI.

frontHtml: Chronic heart failure: diagnosis and guideline-directed therapy: Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate : […] with NYHA III–IV symptoms despite optimal therapy (mortality benefit), or anyone who cannot take any renin–angiotensin blocker.
backHtml: Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate : patients who self-identify as Black with NYHA III–IV symptoms despite optimal therapy (mortality benefit), or anyone who cannot take any renin–angiotensin blocker.

frontHtml: Chronic heart failure: diagnosis and guideline-directed therapy: Cardiac resynchronization therapy : EF ≤ 35%, sinus rhythm, […], symptoms despite guideline therapy.
backHtml: Cardiac resynchronization therapy : EF ≤ 35%, sinus rhythm, left bundle branch block with QRS ≥ 150 ms, symptoms despite guideline therapy.

frontHtml: Chronic heart failure: diagnosis and guideline-directed therapy: When a patient with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation is on diltiazem, […].
backHtml: When a patient with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation is on diltiazem, replace it with a beta-blocker.

frontHtml: Acute decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic shock: […] (CPAP or BiPAP) when there is respiratory distress or hypoxemia despite oxygen in a patient who is awake and protecting the airway.
backHtml: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) when there is respiratory distress or hypoxemia despite oxygen in a patient who is awake and protecting the airway.

frontHtml: Acute decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic shock: Avoid with hypotension, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use or […].
backHtml: Avoid with hypotension, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use or right ventricular infarction.

frontHtml: Acute decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic shock: […] is the usual first vasopressor; add an inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) for low output.
backHtml: Norepinephrine is the usual first vasopressor; add an inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) for low output.

frontHtml: Acute decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic shock: Stabilize with afterload reduction ([…]) if blood pressure allows, and an intra-aortic balloon pump; definitive treatment is urgent surgery.
backHtml: Stabilize with afterload reduction (nitroprusside) if blood pressure allows, and an intra-aortic balloon pump; definitive treatment is urgent surgery.

frontHtml: Heart failure: physiology and pathophysiology: They are degraded by […].
backHtml: They are degraded by neprilysin.

frontHtml: Heart failure: physiology and pathophysiology: The key mechanism is […], which raises pulmonary vascular resistance and loads the thin-walled right ventricle.
backHtml: The key mechanism is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which raises pulmonary vascular resistance and loads the thin-walled right ventricle.

frontHtml: Heart failure: physiology and pathophysiology: Causes: thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia, large arteriovenous fistula (including dialysis access), Paget disease of bone, pregnancy, sepsis and liver cirrhosis, and […] (thiamine deficiency: thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase).
backHtml: Causes: thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia, large arteriovenous fistula (including dialysis access), Paget disease of bone, pregnancy, sepsis and liver cirrhosis, and wet beriberi (thiamine deficiency: thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase).

frontHtml: Heart failure: physiology and pathophysiology: Left atrial pressure rises abruptly, producing […] on the wedge tracing and flash pulmonary edema.
backHtml: Left atrial pressure rises abruptly, producing giant v waves on the wedge tracing and flash pulmonary edema.

frontHtml: Heart failure: physiology and pathophysiology: An S3 is normal in children, young adults and pregnancy; after about age 40 it suggests volume overload or systolic dysfunction. […] at any age.
backHtml: An S3 is normal in children, young adults and pregnancy; after about age 40 it suggests volume overload or systolic dysfunction. An S4 is never normal at any age.

frontHtml: Stable angina and chronic coronary disease: Resting ECG […] for ischemia (ST depression ≥ 1 mm, LVH with repolarization changes, digoxin, pre-excitation)
backHtml: Resting ECG uninterpretable for ischemia (ST depression ≥ 1 mm, LVH with repolarization changes, digoxin, pre-excitation)

frontHtml: Stable angina and chronic coronary disease: Avoid vasodilator agents in active bronchospasm and second- or third-degree AV block; […] beforehand because they block adenosine receptors.
backHtml: Avoid vasodilator agents in active bronchospasm and second- or third-degree AV block; hold caffeine and theophylline beforehand because they block adenosine receptors.

frontHtml: Stable angina and chronic coronary disease: First-line daily drug: […].
backHtml: First-line daily drug: a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker.

frontHtml: Stable angina and chronic coronary disease: Surgery is favored for significant left main disease, […], and multivessel disease with reduced ejection fraction, where it can improve survival.
backHtml: Surgery is favored for significant left main disease, multivessel disease with diabetes, and multivessel disease with reduced ejection fraction, where it can improve survival.

frontHtml: Stable angina and chronic coronary disease: Treat with a calcium channel blocker (first line) plus a nitrate, stop smoking and remove triggers (cocaine, amphetamines, triptans). […], which leave α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed.
backHtml: Treat with a calcium channel blocker (first line) plus a nitrate, stop smoking and remove triggers (cocaine, amphetamines, triptans). Avoid non-selective beta-blockers, which leave α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed.

frontHtml: Acute coronary syndromes: diagnosis and management: Primary PCI is preferred when it can be done promptly: […] at a PCI-capable hospital, or within 120 minutes when the patient must be transferred.
backHtml: Primary PCI is preferred when it can be done promptly: within 90 minutes of first medical contact at a PCI-capable hospital, or within 120 minutes when the patient must be transferred.

frontHtml: Acute coronary syndromes: diagnosis and management: Fibrinolysis […] when timely PCI is not possible and symptoms began less than 12 hours earlier, with no contraindication.
backHtml: Fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of arrival when timely PCI is not possible and symptoms began less than 12 hours earlier, with no contraindication.

frontHtml: Acute coronary syndromes: diagnosis and management: The right ventricle depends on preload: […], and reperfuse quickly.
backHtml: The right ventricle depends on preload: give IV fluid, avoid nitrates and diuretics, and reperfuse quickly.

frontHtml: Acute coronary syndromes: diagnosis and management: […]: it gives no benefit without complete occlusion and adds bleeding.
backHtml: Fibrinolysis is not used: it gives no benefit without complete occlusion and adds bleeding.

frontHtml: Coronary ischemia: plaque, ECG territories and the infarct timeline: Coronary angiography may be normal; provocative testing with […] confirms it.
backHtml: Coronary angiography may be normal; provocative testing with intracoronary acetylcholine confirms it.

frontHtml: Coronary ischemia: plaque, ECG territories and the infarct timeline: That pattern favors a […].
backHtml: That pattern favors a right coronary artery occlusion.

frontHtml: Coronary ischemia: plaque, ECG territories and the infarct timeline: Myocytes stop contracting within about a minute of ischemia; irreversible injury starts after roughly 20–40 minutes, beginning in the […] and spreading outward as a 'wavefront'.
backHtml: Myocytes stop contracting within about a minute of ischemia; irreversible injury starts after roughly 20–40 minutes, beginning in the subendocardium and spreading outward as a 'wavefront'.

frontHtml: Coronary ischemia: plaque, ECG territories and the infarct timeline: When flow is restored after cells are already lethally injured, calcium floods in and causes […]; reperfusion also brings free radicals (reperfusion injury) and hemorrhage into the infarct.
backHtml: When flow is restored after cells are already lethally injured, calcium floods in and causes contraction band necrosis; reperfusion also brings free radicals (reperfusion injury) and hemorrhage into the infarct.

frontHtml: Coronary ischemia: plaque, ECG territories and the infarct timeline: The infarct is weakest while macrophages remove dead muscle and before collagen is laid down, […].
backHtml: The infarct is weakest while macrophages remove dead muscle and before collagen is laid down, roughly days 3–14.

frontHtml: Anti-ischemic and antithrombotic pharmacology: P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockers : clopidogrel and prasugrel are prodrugs that bind irreversibly; clopidogrel needs activation by […], so poor metabolizers get less effect.
backHtml: P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockers : clopidogrel and prasugrel are prodrugs that bind irreversibly; clopidogrel needs activation by CYP2C19, so poor metabolizers get less effect.

frontHtml: Anti-ischemic and antithrombotic pharmacology: Alteplase, reteplase and tenecteplase convert […], which digests fibrin in the clot.
backHtml: Alteplase, reteplase and tenecteplase convert plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin in the clot.

frontHtml: Anti-ischemic and antithrombotic pharmacology: Arterioles beyond a severe stenosis are […], so flow is diverted toward normal territory and the stenotic region shows relatively reduced perfusion on imaging.
backHtml: Arterioles beyond a severe stenosis are already maximally dilated, so flow is diverted toward normal territory and the stenotic region shows relatively reduced perfusion on imaging.

frontHtml: Anti-ischemic and antithrombotic pharmacology: Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol uptake ([…]); PCSK9 inhibitors prevent LDL receptor degradation.
backHtml: Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol uptake (NPC1L1); PCSK9 inhibitors prevent LDL receptor degradation.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathy: diagnosis and management: Alcohol : […] can produce substantial recovery of ejection fraction.
backHtml: Alcohol : complete abstinence can produce substantial recovery of ejection fraction.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathy: diagnosis and management: Symptomatic obstruction, first line : […] titrated to effect; if not tolerated or ineffective, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem) in patients without severe obstruction or low blood pressure.
backHtml: Symptomatic obstruction, first line : a non-vasodilating β-blocker titrated to effect; if not tolerated or ineffective, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem) in patients without severe obstruction or low blood pressure.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathy: diagnosis and management: Treat hypotension in obstructive HCM with […], not inotropes.
backHtml: Treat hypotension in obstructive HCM with intravenous fluids and phenylephrine, not inotropes.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathy: diagnosis and management: Atrial fibrillation in HCM: […] regardless of the CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score.
backHtml: Atrial fibrillation in HCM: anticoagulate regardless of the CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathy: diagnosis and management: First exclude AL amyloidosis : […].
backHtml: First exclude AL amyloidosis : serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation.

frontHtml: Post-infarction mechanical complications and myocarditis: management: Any sudden hemodynamic deterioration or new murmur after infarction : perform […] first.
backHtml: Any sudden hemodynamic deterioration or new murmur after infarction : perform urgent bedside echocardiography first.

frontHtml: Post-infarction mechanical complications and myocarditis: management: Ventricular septal rupture : confirm with echocardiography (color flow across the septum); a right heart catheter shows an […].
backHtml: Ventricular septal rupture : confirm with echocardiography (color flow across the septum); a right heart catheter shows an oxygen saturation step-up in the right ventricle.

frontHtml: Post-infarction mechanical complications and myocarditis: management: Free wall rupture : tamponade with pulseless electrical activity or profound shock; pericardiocentesis only as a temporizing bridge to […].
backHtml: Free wall rupture : tamponade with pulseless electrical activity or profound shock; pericardiocentesis only as a temporizing bridge to emergency surgical repair.

frontHtml: Post-infarction mechanical complications and myocarditis: management: Suspect it in every inferior STEMI: record right-sided leads ([…]).
backHtml: Suspect it in every inferior STEMI: record right-sided leads (ST elevation in V4R).

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive: The mechanism is a […] that stuns the apical myocardium.
backHtml: The mechanism is a catecholamine surge that stuns the apical myocardium.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive: Variants are in […], most often MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (cardiac myosin-binding protein C).
backHtml: Variants are in sarcomere genes, most often MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (cardiac myosin-binding protein C).

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive: In the obstructive form, the septum narrows the left ventricular outflow tract and the anterior mitral leaflet is drawn toward it in systole ([…]), producing a dynamic obstruction and often mitral regurgitation.
backHtml: In the obstructive form, the septum narrows the left ventricular outflow tract and the anterior mitral leaflet is drawn toward it in systole (systolic anterior motion), producing a dynamic obstruction and often mitral regurgitation.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive: Congo red staining shows […] under polarized light.
backHtml: Congo red staining shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

frontHtml: Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive: Chronic pressure overload makes myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel : […] with a thick wall and normal or small cavity.
backHtml: Chronic pressure overload makes myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel : concentric hypertrophy with a thick wall and normal or small cavity.

frontHtml: Myocarditis and complications of myocardial infarction: Cardiac MRI shows edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary pattern ([…] rather than subendocardial).
backHtml: Cardiac MRI shows edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary pattern (subepicardial or mid-wall rather than subendocardial).

frontHtml: Myocarditis and complications of myocardial infarction: Giant cell myocarditis shows […] and has a poor prognosis without immunosuppression.
backHtml: Giant cell myocarditis shows multinucleated giant cells with eosinophils and has a poor prognosis without immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Myocarditis and complications of myocardial infarction: The necrotic wall is softest about […] after infarction, when macrophages have removed dead myocytes but collagen has not yet been laid down.
backHtml: The necrotic wall is softest about 3–14 days after infarction, when macrophages have removed dead myocytes but collagen has not yet been laid down.

frontHtml: Myocarditis and complications of myocardial infarction: Why the posteromedial papillary muscle? It usually has a single blood supply from the […] (from the right coronary artery in right-dominant circulations), whereas the anterolateral muscle receives blood from both the left anterior descending and the circumflex arteries.
backHtml: Why the posteromedial papillary muscle? It usually has a single blood supply from the posterior descending artery (from the right coronary artery in right-dominant circulations), whereas the anterolateral muscle receives blood from both the left anterior descending and the circumflex arteries.

frontHtml: Pericardial disease: diagnosis and management: First line : a high-dose NSAID (ibuprofen) or aspirin, tapered once symptoms and CRP settle, […] for about 3 months (about 6 months for recurrent disease), which halves the risk of recurrence.
backHtml: First line : a high-dose NSAID (ibuprofen) or aspirin, tapered once symptoms and CRP settle, plus colchicine for about 3 months (about 6 months for recurrent disease), which halves the risk of recurrence.

frontHtml: Pericardial disease: diagnosis and management: […] is the test of choice: effusion size, right atrial systolic collapse , right ventricular diastolic collapse , a plethoric inferior vena cava, and exaggerated respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow.
backHtml: Echocardiography is the test of choice: effusion size, right atrial systolic collapse , right ventricular diastolic collapse , a plethoric inferior vena cava, and exaggerated respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow.

frontHtml: Pericardial disease: diagnosis and management: Treat with urgent […] (echocardiography-guided) or surgical drainage.
backHtml: Treat with urgent pericardiocentesis (echocardiography-guided) or surgical drainage.

frontHtml: Pericardial disease: diagnosis and management: Chronic constriction: diuretics relieve congestion temporarily; the definitive treatment is […], best done before severe functional decline.
backHtml: Chronic constriction: diuretics relieve congestion temporarily; the definitive treatment is surgical pericardiectomy, best done before severe functional decline.

frontHtml: Pericarditis, effusion, tamponade and constriction: Causes: most cases in high-income countries are idiopathic or viral (enteroviruses such as […], echovirus).
backHtml: Causes: most cases in high-income countries are idiopathic or viral (enteroviruses such as coxsackie B, echovirus).

frontHtml: Pericarditis, effusion, tamponade and constriction: ECG: inflammation of the epicardium injures the subepicardial myocardium, producing […] in most limb and precordial leads, with PR depression (atrial injury).
backHtml: ECG: inflammation of the epicardium injures the subepicardial myocardium, producing diffuse concave ST elevation in most limb and precordial leads, with PR depression (atrial injury).

frontHtml: Pericarditis, effusion, tamponade and constriction: […] matters more than how much.
backHtml: How fast fluid accumulates matters more than how much.

frontHtml: Pericarditis, effusion, tamponade and constriction: Beck triad : […].
backHtml: Beck triad : hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds.

frontHtml: Pericarditis, effusion, tamponade and constriction: Findings: chronic right-sided congestion out of proportion to other signs (raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema), […] (jugular venous pressure rises or fails to fall on inspiration), a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound earlier and higher-pitched than an S3, caused by the abrupt halt of ventricular filling), a prominent, steep y descent , and a "dip-and-plateau" (square-root) ventricular diastolic pressure tracing.
backHtml: Findings: chronic right-sided congestion out of proportion to other signs (raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema), Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises or fails to fall on inspiration), a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound earlier and higher-pitched than an S3, caused by the abrupt halt of ventricular filling), a prominent, steep y descent , and a "dip-and-plateau" (square-root) ventricular diastolic pressure tracing.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: evaluation, intervention and anticoagulation: Severity on echocardiography for aortic stenosis: severe when […], mean gradient 40 mm Hg or more, or valve area 1.0 cm 2 or less.
backHtml: Severity on echocardiography for aortic stenosis: severe when peak velocity is 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mm Hg or more, or valve area 1.0 cm 2 or less.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: evaluation, intervention and anticoagulation: Acute severe regurgitation (endocarditis, type A dissection): urgent surgery . […] (inflation in diastole worsens regurgitation). β-Blockers are used cautiously because the tachycardia shortens diastole and limits the regurgitant volume.
backHtml: Acute severe regurgitation (endocarditis, type A dissection): urgent surgery . An intra-aortic balloon pump is contraindicated (inflation in diastole worsens regurgitation). β-Blockers are used cautiously because the tachycardia shortens diastole and limits the regurgitant volume.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: evaluation, intervention and anticoagulation: Anticoagulation : rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation, prior embolism or left atrial thrombus requires a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) ; […].
backHtml: Anticoagulation : rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation, prior embolism or left atrial thrombus requires a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) ; DOACs are not used in moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: evaluation, intervention and anticoagulation: Secondary prevention of rheumatic fever: long-term intramuscular […].
backHtml: Secondary prevention of rheumatic fever: long-term intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 3–4 weeks.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: evaluation, intervention and anticoagulation: Mechanical valve : lifelong warfarin (higher INR targets for mitral position or added risk factors). […]: they caused more valve thrombosis and bleeding than warfarin in a trial of mechanical valves.
backHtml: Mechanical valve : lifelong warfarin (higher INR targets for mitral position or added risk factors). DOACs are contraindicated: they caused more valve thrombosis and bleeding than warfarin in a trial of mechanical valves.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: murmurs, mechanisms and causes: […] of a trileaflet valve is the most common cause in older adults.
backHtml: Age-related calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve is the most common cause in older adults.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: murmurs, mechanisms and causes: High shear across the valve unfolds […], which is then cleaved by ADAMTS13, leaving too few high-molecular-weight multimers.
backHtml: High shear across the valve unfolds von Willebrand factor, which is then cleaved by ADAMTS13, leaving too few high-molecular-weight multimers.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: murmurs, mechanisms and causes: […] remains the leading cause of mitral stenosis and a major cause of heart failure in low- and middle-income countries.
backHtml: Rheumatic heart disease remains the leading cause of mitral stenosis and a major cause of heart failure in low- and middle-income countries.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: murmurs, mechanisms and causes: The higher the left atrial pressure, the sooner the valve snaps open after S2: a […] means more severe stenosis.
backHtml: The higher the left atrial pressure, the sooner the valve snaps open after S2: a shorter S2–opening snap interval means more severe stenosis.

frontHtml: Valvular heart disease: murmurs, mechanisms and causes: Complications: valve thrombosis, thromboembolism, prosthetic valve endocarditis, paravalvular leak and […] (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin) from shear across a leak or a mechanical valve.
backHtml: Complications: valve thrombosis, thromboembolism, prosthetic valve endocarditis, paravalvular leak and intravascular hemolysis (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin) from shear across a leak or a mechanical valve.

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: evaluation and management: Stand the patient and record both […].
backHtml: Stand the patient and record both at 1 and 3 minutes.

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: evaluation and management: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is different: a sustained heart-rate rise of […] (≥ 40/min at age 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing, with symptoms, without OH; typically a young woman.
backHtml: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is different: a sustained heart-rate rise of ≥ 30/min (≥ 40/min at age 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing, with symptoms, without OH; typically a young woman.

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: evaluation and management: Drugs when symptoms persist: […] (dosed during upright daytime hours), droxidopa (approved for neurogenic OH), or fludrocortisone (avoid in heart failure, hypokalemia or significant supine hypertension).
backHtml: Drugs when symptoms persist: midodrine (dosed during upright daytime hours), droxidopa (approved for neurogenic OH), or fludrocortisone (avoid in heart failure, hypokalemia or significant supine hypertension).

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: evaluation and management: The best first intervention for an older patient with new OH is almost always to […], not to add a pressor.
backHtml: The best first intervention for an older patient with new OH is almost always to stop or reduce the culprit drug, not to add a pressor.

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension: baroreflex physiology and causes: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a sustained fall in systolic pressure of […], or in diastolic pressure of at least 10 mm Hg, within 3 minutes of standing (or of head-up tilt to at least 60°).
backHtml: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a sustained fall in systolic pressure of at least 20 mm Hg, or in diastolic pressure of at least 10 mm Hg, within 3 minutes of standing (or of head-up tilt to at least 60°).

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension: baroreflex physiology and causes: Less stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch lowers afferent firing (carotid sinus → […]; aortic arch → vagus, CN X).
backHtml: Less stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch lowers afferent firing (carotid sinus → glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX; aortic arch → vagus, CN X).

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension: baroreflex physiology and causes: α 1 antagonists (terazosin, doxazosin, prazosin; less so tamsulosin): venous and arteriolar dilation; worst with the first dose (“[…]”).
backHtml: α 1 antagonists (terazosin, doxazosin, prazosin; less so tamsulosin): venous and arteriolar dilation; worst with the first dose (“first-dose effect”).

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension: baroreflex physiology and causes: Parkinson disease and pure autonomic failure : […] in neurons , including postganglionic sympathetic neurons (cardiac sympathetic denervation on imaging).
backHtml: Parkinson disease and pure autonomic failure : α-synuclein Lewy pathology in neurons , including postganglionic sympathetic neurons (cardiac sympathetic denervation on imaging).

frontHtml: Orthostatic hypotension: baroreflex physiology and causes: Multiple system atrophy : α-synuclein […]; the lesion is mostly central (preganglionic), with early severe autonomic failure (OH, urinary dysfunction, erectile dysfunction), parkinsonism that responds poorly to levodopa and/or cerebellar ataxia.
backHtml: Multiple system atrophy : α-synuclein glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes; the lesion is mostly central (preganglionic), with early severe autonomic failure (OH, urinary dysfunction, erectile dysfunction), parkinsonism that responds poorly to levodopa and/or cerebellar ataxia.

frontHtml: Hypertension: diagnosis and long-term treatment: […]: normal office readings, high out-of-office readings; carries risk similar to sustained hypertension.
backHtml: Masked hypertension: normal office readings, high out-of-office readings; carries risk similar to sustained hypertension.

frontHtml: Hypertension: diagnosis and long-term treatment: Less sodium (aim well under 2,300 mg/day, ideally […]) and more potassium from food (unless CKD or a potassium-raising drug makes this unsafe); potassium-enriched salt substitutes help many patients.
backHtml: Less sodium (aim well under 2,300 mg/day, ideally about 1,500 mg) and more potassium from food (unless CKD or a potassium-raising drug makes this unsafe); potassium-enriched salt substitutes help many patients.

frontHtml: Hypertension: diagnosis and long-term treatment: Target : […] for most adults, including older adults living in the community, if tolerated.
backHtml: Target : below 130/80 mm Hg for most adults, including older adults living in the community, if tolerated.

frontHtml: Hypertension: diagnosis and long-term treatment: A creatinine rise of […] is expected with RAAS blockade; a larger rise suggests renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
backHtml: A creatinine rise of up to about 30% is expected with RAAS blockade; a larger rise suggests renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.

frontHtml: Secondary hypertension and hypertensive emergencies: The difference is […], not the number.
backHtml: The difference is acute target-organ damage, not the number.

frontHtml: Secondary hypertension and hypertensive emergencies: Most emergencies: lower pressure by […], then toward 160/100–110 mm Hg over the next 2–6 hours, then to normal over 24–48 hours.
backHtml: Most emergencies: lower pressure by no more than about 25% within the first hour, then toward 160/100–110 mm Hg over the next 2–6 hours, then to normal over 24–48 hours.

frontHtml: Secondary hypertension and hypertensive emergencies: Aortic dissection : […] with an IV β blocker (esmolol or labetalol), then systolic pressure to about 120 mm Hg or lower within the first hour.
backHtml: Aortic dissection : lower heart rate first with an IV β blocker (esmolol or labetalol), then systolic pressure to about 120 mm Hg or lower within the first hour.

frontHtml: Secondary hypertension and hypertensive emergencies: Sublingual or rapid-release oral […] causes unpredictable precipitous falls in pressure, stroke and MI.
backHtml: Sublingual or rapid-release oral nifedipine causes unpredictable precipitous falls in pressure, stroke and MI.

frontHtml: Hypertension: regulation, pathology and drug mechanisms: Renin is released by […] in response to low renal perfusion pressure, β 1 sympathetic stimulation, and low NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa.
backHtml: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole in response to low renal perfusion pressure, β 1 sympathetic stimulation, and low NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa.

frontHtml: Hypertension: regulation, pathology and drug mechanisms: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (liver) to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme ([…]) makes angiotensin II and also degrades bradykinin .
backHtml: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (liver) to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (mostly pulmonary endothelium) makes angiotensin II and also degrades bradykinin .

frontHtml: Hypertension: regulation, pathology and drug mechanisms: Angiotensin II (AT 1 receptor): arteriolar vasoconstriction, efferent arteriolar constriction (preserves GFR when renal perfusion falls), aldosterone release from the […], proximal tubule Na + /H + exchange, ADH release and thirst, and cardiac and vascular remodelling.
backHtml: Angiotensin II (AT 1 receptor): arteriolar vasoconstriction, efferent arteriolar constriction (preserves GFR when renal perfusion falls), aldosterone release from the zona glomerulosa, proximal tubule Na + /H + exchange, ADH release and thirst, and cardiac and vascular remodelling.

frontHtml: Hypertension: regulation, pathology and drug mechanisms: Brain : lacunar infarcts; […] of lenticulostriate arteries → intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.
backHtml: Brain : lacunar infarcts; Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriate arteries → intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.

frontHtml: Dyslipidemia: screening, statin therapy and hypertriglyceridemia: Exclude secondary causes before labelling dyslipidemia primary: […] (high LDL); uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, alcohol, CKD, estrogen therapy, glucocorticoids, retinoids, antiretrovirals, atypical antipsychotics, thiazides and β blockers (high triglyceride).
backHtml: Exclude secondary causes before labelling dyslipidemia primary: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease (high LDL); uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, alcohol, CKD, estrogen therapy, glucocorticoids, retinoids, antiretrovirals, atypical antipsychotics, thiazides and β blockers (high triglyceride).

frontHtml: Dyslipidemia: screening, statin therapy and hypertriglyceridemia: Rare statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy ([…]) persists after stopping the drug and needs immunosuppression.
backHtml: Rare statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (anti-HMG-CoA reductase antibodies) persists after stopping the drug and needs immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Dyslipidemia: screening, statin therapy and hypertriglyceridemia: Moderate hypertriglyceridemia in a patient with ASCVD (or diabetes plus risk factors) already on a statin: […] (purified EPA) reduces cardiovascular events; mixed EPA/DHA supplements have not.
backHtml: Moderate hypertriglyceridemia in a patient with ASCVD (or diabetes plus risk factors) already on a statin: icosapent ethyl (purified EPA) reduces cardiovascular events; mixed EPA/DHA supplements have not.

frontHtml: Dyslipidemia: screening, statin therapy and hypertriglyceridemia: LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL is treated with a […].
backHtml: LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL is treated with a high-intensity statin regardless of calculated risk.

frontHtml: Lipoprotein metabolism and inherited dyslipidemias: It needs […] as its activator; insulin increases LPL in adipose tissue.
backHtml: It needs apoC-II as its activator; insulin increases LPL in adipose tissue.

frontHtml: Lipoprotein metabolism and inherited dyslipidemias: Hepatocytes adjust receptor number through the sterol-sensing […] pathway: low intracellular cholesterol → more HMG-CoA reductase and more LDL receptors. PCSK9 binds the receptor and sends it for lysosomal degradation instead of recycling.
backHtml: Hepatocytes adjust receptor number through the sterol-sensing SREBP-2 pathway: low intracellular cholesterol → more HMG-CoA reductase and more LDL receptors. PCSK9 binds the receptor and sends it for lysosomal degradation instead of recycling.

frontHtml: Lipoprotein metabolism and inherited dyslipidemias: Atherosclerosis begins when LDL enters the intima, is oxidized, and is ingested by macrophages through […] (which, unlike the LDL receptor, are not down-regulated).
backHtml: Atherosclerosis begins when LDL enters the intima, is oxidized, and is ingested by macrophages through scavenger receptors (which, unlike the LDL receptor, are not down-regulated).

frontHtml: Lipoprotein metabolism and inherited dyslipidemias: Bile acid sequestrants are a poor choice when triglycerides are high: they […].
backHtml: Bile acid sequestrants are a poor choice when triglycerides are high: they increase hepatic VLDL production.

frontHtml: Acute aortic syndromes, aneurysm screening and repair: Unstable, or cannot go to the scanner: […] at the bedside or in the operating room.
backHtml: Unstable, or cannot go to the scanner: transesophageal echocardiography at the bedside or in the operating room.

frontHtml: Acute aortic syndromes, aneurysm screening and repair: An […] (esmolol, labetalol or metoprolol) to lower heart rate (target about 60/min or less) and the force of ejection.
backHtml: An intravenous beta-blocker first (esmolol, labetalol or metoprolol) to lower heart rate (target about 60/min or less) and the force of ejection.

frontHtml: Acute aortic syndromes, aneurysm screening and repair: A one-time abdominal ultrasound is recommended for […] (USPSTF).
backHtml: A one-time abdominal ultrasound is recommended for men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked (USPSTF).

frontHtml: Acute aortic syndromes, aneurysm screening and repair: Meanwhile: […] (the single most effective way to slow growth), treat blood pressure, and give a statin and antiplatelet therapy for the accompanying atherosclerotic risk.
backHtml: Meanwhile: stop smoking (the single most effective way to slow growth), treat blood pressure, and give a statin and antiplatelet therapy for the accompanying atherosclerotic risk.

frontHtml: Peripheral artery disease, limb ischemia and carotid disease: Resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the first test: […] diagnoses PAD, 0.91–0.99 is borderline, 1.00–1.40 is normal, and > 1.40 means noncompressible (calcified) arteries.
backHtml: Resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the first test: ≤ 0.90 diagnoses PAD, 0.91–0.99 is borderline, 1.00–1.40 is normal, and > 1.40 means noncompressible (calcified) arteries.

frontHtml: Peripheral artery disease, limb ischemia and carotid disease: ABI > 1.40 (common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease) → […] (digital arteries are rarely calcified) or other physiological testing.
backHtml: ABI > 1.40 (common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease) → toe-brachial index (digital arteries are rarely calcified) or other physiological testing.

frontHtml: Peripheral artery disease, limb ischemia and carotid disease: Claudication: a […] (walking to moderate pain, rest, repeat; about three sessions a week for at least 12 weeks) is first-line and improves walking distance more than most drugs. Cilostazol can be added if symptoms still limit life, but never in heart failure.
backHtml: Claudication: a supervised exercise program (walking to moderate pain, rest, repeat; about three sessions a week for at least 12 weeks) is first-line and improves walking distance more than most drugs. Cilostazol can be added if symptoms still limit life, but never in heart failure.

frontHtml: Peripheral artery disease, limb ischemia and carotid disease: Give an […] to stop clot propagation, unless contraindicated.
backHtml: Give an intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion immediately to stop clot propagation, unless contraindicated.

frontHtml: Peripheral artery disease, limb ischemia and carotid disease: After reperfusion watch for compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch, tense calf; treat with […]), hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria and acidosis.
backHtml: After reperfusion watch for compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch, tense calf; treat with fasciotomy), hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria and acidosis.

frontHtml: Deep vein thrombosis, HIT and chronic venous disease: DVT unlikely (low pretest probability): […].
backHtml: DVT unlikely (low pretest probability): high-sensitivity D-dimer.

frontHtml: Deep vein thrombosis, HIT and chronic venous disease: Positive → […].
backHtml: Positive → compression ultrasound.

frontHtml: Deep vein thrombosis, HIT and chronic venous disease: Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple positive) and mechanical heart valves: […].
backHtml: Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple positive) and mechanical heart valves: warfarin, not a DOAC.

frontHtml: Deep vein thrombosis, HIT and chronic venous disease: Massive iliofemoral DVT can obstruct nearly all venous outflow: a swollen, painful, cyanotic leg ( […] ) that can progress to venous gangrene and compromise arterial inflow.
backHtml: Massive iliofemoral DVT can obstruct nearly all venous outflow: a swollen, painful, cyanotic leg ( phlegmasia cerulea dolens ) that can progress to venous gangrene and compromise arterial inflow.

frontHtml: Deep vein thrombosis, HIT and chronic venous disease: Estimate probability with the […] (degree of thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes).
backHtml: Estimate probability with the 4Ts score (degree of thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes).

frontHtml: Aortic dissection, aneurysms and the great veins: By the […], wall tension rises with pressure × radius and falls with wall thickness.
backHtml: By the law of Laplace, wall tension rises with pressure × radius and falls with wall thickness.

frontHtml: Aortic dissection, aneurysms and the great veins: Inferior ST elevation plus severe back pain: think of a type A dissection occluding the […] before reaching for fibrinolysis or heparin.
backHtml: Inferior ST elevation plus severe back pain: think of a type A dissection occluding the right coronary ostium before reaching for fibrinolysis or heparin.

frontHtml: Aortic dissection, aneurysms and the great veins: The characteristic lesion is fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers with pools of basophilic, mucoid ground substance in the media and loss of smooth muscle cells (older term: […], although there is no true necrosis).
backHtml: The characteristic lesion is fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers with pools of basophilic, mucoid ground substance in the media and loss of smooth muscle cells (older term: cystic medial necrosis, although there is no true necrosis).

frontHtml: Aortic dissection, aneurysms and the great veins: Tertiary syphilis (now rare) inflames the vasa vasorum: an […] with plasma cells starves the outer media, which scars and weakens.
backHtml: Tertiary syphilis (now rare) inflames the vasa vasorum: an obliterative endarteritis with plasma cells starves the outer media, which scars and weakens.

frontHtml: Aortic dissection, aneurysms and the great veins: They are linked to atherosclerosis, but the defining process is chronic transmural inflammation with […] from macrophages degrading elastin and collagen in the media.
backHtml: They are linked to atherosclerosis, but the defining process is chronic transmural inflammation with matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages degrading elastin and collagen in the media.

frontHtml: Atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis and limb arterial disease: Age over 50, diabetes, chronic kidney disease; "pipe-stem" arteries on radiographs, […] ankle pressures
backHtml: Age over 50, diabetes, chronic kidney disease; "pipe-stem" arteries on radiographs, falsely high ankle pressures

frontHtml: Atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis and limb arterial disease: Collections of foam cells form the […], the earliest visible lesion (present even in adolescents).
backHtml: Collections of foam cells form the fatty streak, the earliest visible lesion (present even in adolescents).

frontHtml: Atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis and limb arterial disease: Smooth muscle migration and proliferation: growth factors such as […] from platelets, macrophages and endothelium draw smooth muscle cells from the media into the intima, where they make collagen and form the fibrous cap .
backHtml: Smooth muscle migration and proliferation: growth factors such as PDGF from platelets, macrophages and endothelium draw smooth muscle cells from the media into the intima, where they make collagen and form the fibrous cap .

frontHtml: Atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis and limb arterial disease: Resistance in a tube rises with the […] of the falling radius (Poiseuille), so a stenosis that is trivial at rest becomes limiting when exercise lowers downstream resistance and flow should rise.
backHtml: Resistance in a tube rises with the fourth power of the falling radius (Poiseuille), so a stenosis that is trivial at rest becomes limiting when exercise lowers downstream resistance and flow should rise.

frontHtml: Venous thrombosis, thrombophilia and anticoagulant pharmacology: Deep vein thrombi usually start in the […], where flow is slow, and may propagate into the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins.
backHtml: Deep vein thrombi usually start in the valve pockets of the calf veins, where flow is slow, and may propagate into the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins.

frontHtml: Venous thrombosis, thrombophilia and anticoagulant pharmacology: Factor VII and […] have the shortest half-lives, so the INR rises early while protein C falls before the long-lived prothrombin.
backHtml: Factor VII and protein C have the shortest half-lives, so the INR rises early while protein C falls before the long-lived prothrombin.

frontHtml: Venous thrombosis, thrombophilia and anticoagulant pharmacology: An immune reaction: IgG antibodies bind complexes of heparin and […] (PF4) on platelets; the Fc parts cross-link platelet FcγRIIa receptors, activating platelets, releasing procoagulant microparticles and removing platelets.
backHtml: An immune reaction: IgG antibodies bind complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4 (PF4) on platelets; the Fc parts cross-link platelet FcγRIIa receptors, activating platelets, releasing procoagulant microparticles and removing platelets.

frontHtml: Venous thrombosis, thrombophilia and anticoagulant pharmacology: Chronic venous hypertension pushes red cells and fluid into tissue: edema, brown hemosiderin pigmentation, stasis dermatitis, fibrosis of fat (lipodermatosclerosis) and finally ulcers, typically above the […].
backHtml: Chronic venous hypertension pushes red cells and fluid into tissue: edema, brown hemosiderin pigmentation, stasis dermatitis, fibrosis of fat (lipodermatosclerosis) and finally ulcers, typically above the medial malleolus.

frontHtml: Traumatic cardiac and aortic injury: evaluation and management: Unstable, pericardial blood on ultrasound : […] (median sternotomy or anterolateral thoracotomy) to relieve tamponade and repair the wound.
backHtml: Unstable, pericardial blood on ultrasound : immediate operation (median sternotomy or anterolateral thoracotomy) to relieve tamponade and repair the wound.

frontHtml: Traumatic cardiac and aortic injury: evaluation and management: […]: for a patient with penetrating chest trauma who loses pulses shortly before or after arrival (signs of life recently present).
backHtml: Resuscitative (emergency department) thoracotomy: for a patient with penetrating chest trauma who loses pulses shortly before or after arrival (signs of life recently present).

frontHtml: Traumatic cardiac and aortic injury: evaluation and management: Diagnosis : […] (fast, sensitive, shows other injuries).
backHtml: Diagnosis : CT angiography of the chest (fast, sensitive, shows other injuries).

frontHtml: Traumatic cardiac and aortic injury: evaluation and management: Repair : […] (TEVAR) is preferred over open repair for suitable anatomy.
backHtml: Repair : thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is preferred over open repair for suitable anatomy.

frontHtml: Traumatic cardiac and aortic injury: evaluation and management: Collapse right after a blow to the chest during sport: start CPR and attach an […] immediately.
backHtml: Collapse right after a blow to the chest during sport: start CPR and attach an automated external defibrillator immediately.

frontHtml: Cardiac and aortic injury: anatomy and mechanisms: The […] forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart and lies directly behind the sternum and the left parasternal intercostal spaces, so it is the chamber most often hit by anterior stab wounds and squeezed in blunt trauma.
backHtml: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart and lies directly behind the sternum and the left parasternal intercostal spaces, so it is the chamber most often hit by anterior stab wounds and squeezed in blunt trauma.

frontHtml: Cardiac and aortic injury: anatomy and mechanisms: Rising pericardial pressure is transmitted to all chambers, so diastolic pressures in the right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery and left atrium (wedge) […].
backHtml: Rising pericardial pressure is transmitted to all chambers, so diastolic pressures in the right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery and left atrium (wedge) equalize.

frontHtml: Cardiac and aortic injury: anatomy and mechanisms: A low-energy blow to the precordium (a baseball, hockey puck or fist) without structural damage can trigger ventricular fibrillation if it lands during a narrow window on the […] , when repolarization is heterogeneous.
backHtml: A low-energy blow to the precordium (a baseball, hockey puck or fist) without structural damage can trigger ventricular fibrillation if it lands during a narrow window on the upstroke of the T wave , when repolarization is heterogeneous.

frontHtml: Cardiac and aortic injury: anatomy and mechanisms: Rapid deceleration (high-speed crash, fall from height) lets the mobile ascending aorta and arch keep moving while the descending aorta is held by the […], the intercostal arteries and the pleura.
backHtml: Rapid deceleration (high-speed crash, fall from height) lets the mobile ascending aorta and arch keep moving while the descending aorta is held by the ligamentum arteriosum, the intercostal arteries and the pleura.

frontHtml: Cardiac and aortic injury: anatomy and mechanisms: Kussmaul sign (a rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration) is typical of constrictive pericarditis, not acute tamponade; […].
backHtml: Kussmaul sign (a rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration) is typical of constrictive pericarditis, not acute tamponade; pulsus paradoxus is the classic tamponade sign.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in the newborn and child: Newborn pulse-oximetry screening ([…], after 24 hours of age) detects many critical lesions before discharge; a low saturation or a hand–foot difference prompts echocardiography.
backHtml: Newborn pulse-oximetry screening (right hand and a foot, after 24 hours of age) detects many critical lesions before discharge; a low saturation or a hand–foot difference prompts echocardiography.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in the newborn and child: For either, start […] as soon as a duct-dependent lesion is suspected; do not wait for echocardiography.
backHtml: For either, start prostaglandin E 1 (alprostadil) as soon as a duct-dependent lesion is suspected; do not wait for echocardiography.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in the newborn and child: Small VSD (loud murmur, normal growth, normal chamber sizes and pulmonary pressures): reassurance and follow-up; many close […].
backHtml: Small VSD (loud murmur, normal growth, normal chamber sizes and pulmonary pressures): reassurance and follow-up; many close spontaneously.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in the newborn and child: AV septal defect ([…]): surgical repair at 3–6 months.
backHtml: AV septal defect (Down syndrome): surgical repair at 3–6 months.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in adults: Close an ASD that causes right atrial or ventricular enlargement (a significant shunt, often […]) when pulmonary vascular resistance is not prohibitively high.
backHtml: Close an ASD that causes right atrial or ventricular enlargement (a significant shunt, often Qp:Qs ≥ 1.5:1) when pulmonary vascular resistance is not prohibitively high.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in adults: Closure is not done when pulmonary vascular disease is severe and the shunt has reversed ([…]); closing it removes the right ventricle's "pop-off" valve.
