backHtml: Closure is not done when pulmonary vascular disease is severe and the shunt has reversed (Eisenmenger physiology); closing it removes the right ventricle's "pop-off" valve.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in adults: A PFO is present in […] and is usually harmless.
backHtml: A PFO is present in about a quarter of adults and is usually harmless.

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in adults: Tetralogy of Fallot after repair: chronic […] leads to RV dilation; ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death are late risks (QRS duration is a marker).
backHtml: Tetralogy of Fallot after repair: chronic pulmonary regurgitation leads to RV dilation; ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death are late risks (QRS duration is a marker).

frontHtml: Congenital heart disease in adults: After the arterial switch, watch for […] and coronary problems.
backHtml: After the arterial switch, watch for neo-aortic root dilation and coronary problems.

frontHtml: Heart development, fetal circulation and shunts: Atria. The septum primum grows toward the […], leaving the ostium primum; perforations in its upper part form the ostium secundum.
backHtml: Atria. The septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions, leaving the ostium primum; perforations in its upper part form the ostium secundum.

frontHtml: Heart development, fetal circulation and shunts: Outflow. […] migrate into the truncal and bulbar ridges, which fuse in a spiral to form the aorticopulmonary septum.
backHtml: Outflow. Neural crest cells migrate into the truncal and bulbar ridges, which fuse in a spiral to form the aorticopulmonary septum.

frontHtml: Heart development, fetal circulation and shunts: Oxygenated blood returns from the placenta in the umbilical vein (the most saturated fetal blood), partly bypasses the liver through the […], and enters the right atrium, where the crista directs it across the foramen ovale to the left heart and the head and arms.
backHtml: Oxygenated blood returns from the placenta in the umbilical vein (the most saturated fetal blood), partly bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus, and enters the right atrium, where the crista directs it across the foramen ovale to the left heart and the head and arms.

frontHtml: Heart development, fetal circulation and shunts: Chronic high pulmonary flow and pressure remodel the small pulmonary arteries (medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, […]).
backHtml: Chronic high pulmonary flow and pressure remodel the small pulmonary arteries (medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions).

frontHtml: Congenital heart lesions: Tetralogy of Fallot : […] causes (1) right ventricular outflow obstruction, (2) a large malaligned VSD, (3) an aorta overriding the VSD and (4) right ventricular hypertrophy.
backHtml: Tetralogy of Fallot : anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum causes (1) right ventricular outflow obstruction, (2) a large malaligned VSD, (3) an aorta overriding the VSD and (4) right ventricular hypertrophy.

frontHtml: Congenital heart lesions: Transposition of the great arteries : the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, giving […].
backHtml: Transposition of the great arteries : the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, giving two parallel circuits.

frontHtml: Congenital heart lesions: Persistent truncus arteriosus : one vessel overriding a VSD supplies systemic, pulmonary and coronary circulations; linked to […].
backHtml: Persistent truncus arteriosus : one vessel overriding a VSD supplies systemic, pulmonary and coronary circulations; linked to 22q11.2 deletion.

frontHtml: Congenital heart lesions: Associated with […], although the absolute risk is small.
backHtml: Associated with maternal lithium exposure, although the absolute risk is small.

frontHtml: Congenital heart lesions: When the left coronary artery arises from the […], it is perfused well enough in fetal life, when pulmonary pressure is high.
backHtml: When the left coronary artery arises from the pulmonary trunk, it is perfused well enough in fetal life, when pulmonary pressure is high.

frontHtml: Recognizing and managing cardiovascular drug toxicity: Before an anthracycline or trastuzumab, assess cardiovascular risk and obtain a […] (left ventricular ejection fraction).
backHtml: Before an anthracycline or trastuzumab, assess cardiovascular risk and obtain a baseline echocardiogram (left ventricular ejection fraction).

frontHtml: Recognizing and managing cardiovascular drug toxicity: New heart block, arrhythmia or troponin rise on an immune checkpoint inhibitor: suspect myocarditis; hold the drug and give […] promptly.
backHtml: New heart block, arrhythmia or troponin rise on an immune checkpoint inhibitor: suspect myocarditis; hold the drug and give high-dose glucocorticoids promptly.

frontHtml: Recognizing and managing cardiovascular drug toxicity: […] first for agitation, tachycardia and hypertension: they reduce central sympathetic outflow.
backHtml: Benzodiazepines first for agitation, tachycardia and hypertension: they reduce central sympathetic outflow.

frontHtml: Recognizing and managing cardiovascular drug toxicity: Avoid β-blockers during acute intoxication ([…]).
backHtml: Avoid β-blockers during acute intoxication (unopposed α-stimulation).

frontHtml: Recognizing and managing cardiovascular drug toxicity: Amlodipine edema : lower the dose, or […]; diuretics are largely ineffective.
backHtml: Amlodipine edema : lower the dose, or add an ACE inhibitor or ARB; diuretics are largely ineffective.

frontHtml: Cardiotoxic drugs: mechanisms and recognition: Cocaine blocks […] of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin.
backHtml: Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin.

frontHtml: Cardiotoxic drugs: mechanisms and recognition: Amphetamines and methamphetamine release catecholamines from nerve terminals; chronic use causes a […].
backHtml: Amphetamines and methamphetamine release catecholamines from nerve terminals; chronic use causes a dilated cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.

frontHtml: Cardiotoxic drugs: mechanisms and recognition: Phencyclidine (PCP) is an […] that also has sympathomimetic effects: hypertension and tachycardia with violent agitation, vertical or rotatory nystagmus and analgesia.
backHtml: Phencyclidine (PCP) is an NMDA receptor antagonist that also has sympathomimetic effects: hypertension and tachycardia with violent agitation, vertical or rotatory nystagmus and analgesia.

frontHtml: Cardiotoxic drugs: mechanisms and recognition: Most culprit drugs block the […] (I Kr ): class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, citalopram and tricyclic antidepressants.
backHtml: Most culprit drugs block the hERG channel (I Kr ): class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, citalopram and tricyclic antidepressants.

frontHtml: Sore throat: who to test, how to treat, and deep neck abscesses: Care is supportive. […] for at least 3–4 weeks from onset, longer while the spleen is enlarged, because of splenic rupture.
backHtml: Care is supportive. Avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for at least 3–4 weeks from onset, longer while the spleen is enlarged, because of splenic rupture.

frontHtml: Sore throat: who to test, how to treat, and deep neck abscesses: Peritonsillar cellulitis (no pus collection) may settle with antibiotics alone; an abscess needs […] (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) plus antibiotics covering streptococci and oral anaerobes (for example ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin).
backHtml: Peritonsillar cellulitis (no pus collection) may settle with antibiotics alone; an abscess needs drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) plus antibiotics covering streptococci and oral anaerobes (for example ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin).

frontHtml: Sore throat: who to test, how to treat, and deep neck abscesses: Lateral neck film: widened prevertebral soft tissue. […] of the neck defines an abscess.
backHtml: Lateral neck film: widened prevertebral soft tissue. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck defines an abscess.

frontHtml: Sore throat: who to test, how to treat, and deep neck abscesses: In an unvaccinated or under-vaccinated patient (often after travel) with a gray adherent pharyngeal membrane and bull neck, treat on suspicion: isolate, obtain diphtheria […] through public health, start erythromycin or penicillin, monitor the ECG for myocarditis, notify public health and give contacts prophylaxis and vaccination.
backHtml: In an unvaccinated or under-vaccinated patient (often after travel) with a gray adherent pharyngeal membrane and bull neck, treat on suspicion: isolate, obtain diphtheria antitoxin through public health, start erythromycin or penicillin, monitor the ECG for myocarditis, notify public health and give contacts prophylaxis and vaccination.

frontHtml: Stridor in children, sinusitis, pertussis and rhinitis: management: Single dose of oral […]; home with advice on return signs
backHtml: Single dose of oral dexamethasone; home with advice on return signs

frontHtml: Stridor in children, sinusitis, pertussis and rhinitis: management: persistent symptoms for […] without improvement;
backHtml: persistent symptoms for 10 days or more without improvement;

frontHtml: Stridor in children, sinusitis, pertussis and rhinitis: management: In a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia, transplant immunosuppression or high-dose glucocorticoids, facial pain or numbness, nasal congestion and a […] on the turbinate or palate signal mucormycosis until proven otherwise.
backHtml: In a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia, transplant immunosuppression or high-dose glucocorticoids, facial pain or numbness, nasal congestion and a black eschar on the turbinate or palate signal mucormycosis until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Stridor in children, sinusitis, pertussis and rhinitis: management: Treat with a macrolide; […] is preferred, and is the drug of choice in infants under 1 month (erythromycin is linked to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis).
backHtml: Treat with a macrolide; azithromycin is preferred, and is the drug of choice in infants under 1 month (erythromycin is linked to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis).

frontHtml: Stridor in children, sinusitis, pertussis and rhinitis: management: […] is the most effective first-line drug for persistent or moderate–severe symptoms, especially congestion; a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine is an alternative for mild or intermittent symptoms.
backHtml: Intranasal glucocorticoid is the most effective first-line drug for persistent or moderate–severe symptoms, especially congestion; a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine is an alternative for mild or intermittent symptoms.

frontHtml: Pneumonia: community, hospital and aspiration: Pneumonia is a clinical syndrome (fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, crackles or bronchial breathing) confirmed by a […].
backHtml: Pneumonia is a clinical syndrome (fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, crackles or bronchial breathing) confirmed by a new infiltrate on chest x-ray.

frontHtml: Pneumonia: community, hospital and aspiration: Systemic glucocorticoids are suggested by current guidance for […] CAP requiring ICU care, not for non-severe pneumonia, and are avoided in influenza pneumonia.
backHtml: Systemic glucocorticoids are suggested by current guidance for severe CAP requiring ICU care, not for non-severe pneumonia, and are avoided in influenza pneumonia.

frontHtml: Pneumonia: community, hospital and aspiration: Obtain respiratory cultures (endotracheal aspirate in VAP), then start an […] (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem), adding vancomycin or linezolid when MRSA risk is present (IV antibiotics within 90 days, high local MRSA rates, septic shock) and a second antipseudomonal drug of a different class for the highest-risk patients.
backHtml: Obtain respiratory cultures (endotracheal aspirate in VAP), then start an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem), adding vancomycin or linezolid when MRSA risk is present (IV antibiotics within 90 days, high local MRSA rates, septic shock) and a second antipseudomonal drug of a different class for the highest-risk patients.

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, fungal, viral and opportunistic pneumonia: management: If TB is possible, […] (single negative-pressure room, N95 respirators for staff) and collect three sputum samples (at least one early morning) for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a NAAT on at least one, which also screens for rifampin resistance.
backHtml: If TB is possible, place the patient in airborne isolation (single negative-pressure room, N95 respirators for staff) and collect three sputum samples (at least one early morning) for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a NAAT on at least one, which also screens for rifampin resistance.

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, fungal, viral and opportunistic pneumonia: management: Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is treated with an […] of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by a continuation phase of 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin (6 months in all); longer courses are used for some sites and for cavitary disease with positive cultures at 2 months.
backHtml: Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is treated with an intensive phase of 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by a continuation phase of 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin (6 months in all); longer courses are used for some sites and for cavitary disease with positive cultures at 2 months.

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, fungal, viral and opportunistic pneumonia: management: Shorter rifamycin-based regimens are preferred for their completion rates: […], 4 months of daily rifampin , or 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin; 6–9 months of isoniazid is an alternative.
backHtml: Shorter rifamycin-based regimens are preferred for their completion rates: 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, 4 months of daily rifampin , or 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin; 6–9 months of isoniazid is an alternative.

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, fungal, viral and opportunistic pneumonia: management: Treat with […].
backHtml: Treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days.

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, fungal, viral and opportunistic pneumonia: management: Treat with an antiviral (oseltamivir) every patient who is […] of complications (age 65 or older, pregnancy, chronic disease, immunosuppression, nursing-home residents, children under 2), whatever the time since symptom onset .
backHtml: Treat with an antiviral (oseltamivir) every patient who is hospitalized, severely ill or at high risk of complications (age 65 or older, pregnancy, chronic disease, immunosuppression, nursing-home residents, children under 2), whatever the time since symptom onset .

frontHtml: Pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis and deep neck infections: The bacterial cause that matters most is […] ( Streptococcus pyogenes ), responsible for about 20–30% of pharyngitis in school-age children and a much smaller share in adults.
backHtml: The bacterial cause that matters most is group A Streptococcus ( Streptococcus pyogenes ), responsible for about 20–30% of pharyngitis in school-age children and a much smaller share in adults.

frontHtml: Pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis and deep neck infections: Identified in the lab by […] and a positive PYR test; group B streptococci are bacitracin-resistant.
backHtml: Identified in the lab by bacitracin sensitivity and a positive PYR test; group B streptococci are bacitracin-resistant.

frontHtml: Pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis and deep neck infections: Epstein–Barr virus (a herpesvirus) spreads in saliva, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B cells , entering through […] (complement receptor 2).
backHtml: Epstein–Barr virus (a herpesvirus) spreads in saliva, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B cells , entering through CD21 (complement receptor 2).

frontHtml: Pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis and deep neck infections: Pharyngeal infection forms a […] that bleeds when scraped, with marked neck swelling ("bull neck").
backHtml: Pharyngeal infection forms a gray, adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped, with marked neck swelling ("bull neck").

frontHtml: Pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis and deep neck infections: Infection that tracks down it causes […], which is why deep neck abscesses are treated urgently.
backHtml: Infection that tracks down it causes mediastinitis, which is why deep neck abscesses are treated urgently.

frontHtml: Croup, epiglottitis, pertussis, sinusitis and rhinitis: Usual cause: […] (a paramyxovirus with hemagglutinin-neuraminidase); others include RSV, influenza, human metapneumovirus and SARS-CoV-2.
backHtml: Usual cause: parainfluenza virus (a paramyxovirus with hemagglutinin-neuraminidase); others include RSV, influenza, human metapneumovirus and SARS-CoV-2.

frontHtml: Croup, epiglottitis, pertussis, sinusitis and rhinitis: If a film is taken, the anteroposterior neck view shows a tapered subglottic air column, the […].
backHtml: If a film is taken, the anteroposterior neck view shows a tapered subglottic air column, the steeple sign.

frontHtml: Croup, epiglottitis, pertussis, sinusitis and rhinitis: The lateral neck film (only if the child is stable and accompanied by someone who can manage the airway) shows a swollen epiglottis, the […].
backHtml: The lateral neck film (only if the child is stable and accompanied by someone who can manage the airway) shows a swollen epiglottis, the thumb sign.

frontHtml: Croup, epiglottitis, pertussis, sinusitis and rhinitis: Young infants often do not whoop; they present with […], cyanosis or gagging, and they carry most of the deaths.
backHtml: Young infants often do not whoop; they present with apnea, cyanosis or gagging, and they carry most of the deaths.

frontHtml: Croup, epiglottitis, pertussis, sinusitis and rhinitis: Broad, ribbon-like, […] hyphae branching at wide (near right) angles invade vessels and cause infarction and black necrotic tissue on the turbinates or palate, with spread to the orbit, cavernous sinus and brain.
backHtml: Broad, ribbon-like, non-septate hyphae branching at wide (near right) angles invade vessels and cause infarction and black necrotic tissue on the turbinates or palate, with spread to the orbit, cavernous sinus and brain.

frontHtml: Pneumonia and lung abscess: mechanisms, pathology and organisms: […] (days 2–3): alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin; the lobe is red, airless and liver-like.
backHtml: Red hepatization (days 2–3): alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin; the lobe is red, airless and liver-like.

frontHtml: Pneumonia and lung abscess: mechanisms, pathology and organisms: Aspiration of gastric contents causes a chemical […] within hours (acid injury, often in a witnessed event during sedation).
backHtml: Aspiration of gastric contents causes a chemical pneumonitis within hours (acid injury, often in a witnessed event during sedation).

frontHtml: Pneumonia and lung abscess: mechanisms, pathology and organisms: Lying on the back, material runs into the […] and the superior segment of the lower lobes ; upright, it falls to the basal segments of the lower lobes .
backHtml: Lying on the back, material runs into the posterior segment of the upper lobes and the superior segment of the lower lobes ; upright, it falls to the basal segments of the lower lobes .

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, endemic mycoses and opportunistic lung infections: After 3–8 weeks, macrophages present antigen with IL-12, CD4 Th1 cells release interferon-gamma , and activated macrophages form […] (epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, a rim of lymphocytes, central cheese-like necrosis).
backHtml: After 3–8 weeks, macrophages present antigen with IL-12, CD4 Th1 cells release interferon-gamma , and activated macrophages form caseating granulomas (epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, a rim of lymphocytes, central cheese-like necrosis).

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, endemic mycoses and opportunistic lung infections: The subpleural focus is the Ghon focus ; with the involved hilar node it is the […], which may later calcify (Ranke complex).
backHtml: The subpleural focus is the Ghon focus ; with the involved hilar node it is the Ghon complex, which may later calcify (Ranke complex).

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, endemic mycoses and opportunistic lung infections: In adults most active disease is reactivation , seeded in the well-oxygenated […]: cough for weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, fever and weight loss, with fibrocavitary upper-lobe disease on x-ray.
backHtml: In adults most active disease is reactivation , seeded in the well-oxygenated apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes: cough for weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, fever and weight loss, with fibrocavitary upper-lobe disease on x-ray.

frontHtml: Tuberculosis, endemic mycoses and opportunistic lung infections: Orange-red urine, tears and sweat; hepatitis; strong […] (lowers levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, many antiretrovirals)
backHtml: Orange-red urine, tears and sweat; hepatitis; strong CYP450 induction (lowers levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, many antiretrovirals)

frontHtml: The solitary pulmonary nodule and benign airway masses: The cheapest and most powerful test is a […].
backHtml: The cheapest and most powerful test is a prior chest radiograph or CT.

frontHtml: The solitary pulmonary nodule and benign airway masses: Benign calcification (diffuse, central, laminated or popcorn) or […] (hamartoma): no further workup.
backHtml: Benign calcification (diffuse, central, laminated or popcorn) or macroscopic fat (hamartoma): no further workup.

frontHtml: The solitary pulmonary nodule and benign airway masses: […] helps for solid nodules over about 8 mm.
backHtml: PET-CT helps for solid nodules over about 8 mm.

frontHtml: The solitary pulmonary nodule and benign airway masses: Hoarseness that lasts beyond about 4 weeks, or sooner in a smoker or with red flags (stridor, hemoptysis, dysphagia, neck mass, weight loss), needs […] before any empiric treatment such as a proton pump inhibitor.
backHtml: Hoarseness that lasts beyond about 4 weeks, or sooner in a smoker or with red flags (stridor, hemoptysis, dysphagia, neck mass, weight loss), needs laryngoscopy before any empiric treatment such as a proton pump inhibitor.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: screening, diagnosis, staging and treatment: Screening with […] lowers lung cancer mortality in high-risk adults.
backHtml: Screening with annual low-dose CT (LDCT) lowers lung cancer mortality in high-risk adults.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: screening, diagnosis, staging and treatment: Under the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation, screen adults 50–80 years old with a […] history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years ; stop once a person has not smoked for 15 years or has a health problem that limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative surgery.
backHtml: Under the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation, screen adults 50–80 years old with a ≥ 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years ; stop once a person has not smoked for 15 years or has a health problem that limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative surgery.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: screening, diagnosis, staging and treatment: PET-CT for apparently curable disease, to find nodal and distant spread; […] for stage II and above, any neurologic symptoms, and in small cell carcinoma.
backHtml: PET-CT for apparently curable disease, to find nodal and distant spread; brain MRI for stage II and above, any neurologic symptoms, and in small cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: screening, diagnosis, staging and treatment: […], so one procedure both diagnoses and stages: endobronchial ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (EBUS) of enlarged or PET-positive mediastinal nodes; bronchoscopy for central tumors; CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral ones; thoracentesis for an effusion (a malignant effusion is M1 disease).
backHtml: Tissue from the site that gives the highest stage, so one procedure both diagnoses and stages: endobronchial ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (EBUS) of enlarged or PET-positive mediastinal nodes; bronchoscopy for central tumors; CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral ones; thoracentesis for an effusion (a malignant effusion is M1 disease).

frontHtml: Lung cancer: screening, diagnosis, staging and treatment: For nonsquamous NSCLC (and many squamous), […] for targetable alterations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS G12C, MET, RET, NTRK and others) and PD-L1 expression before first-line systemic therapy.
backHtml: For nonsquamous NSCLC (and many squamous), molecular testing for targetable alterations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS G12C, MET, RET, NTRK and others) and PD-L1 expression before first-line systemic therapy.

frontHtml: Hoarseness and neck masses: finding head and neck cancer: Most hoarseness follows a viral laryngitis and settles within 2–3 weeks. backHtml: Most hoarseness follows a viral laryngitis and settles within 2–3 weeks. Visualize the larynx (flexible laryngoscopy, usually by an otolaryngologist) when hoarseness persists beyond about 4 weeks or sooner when there is a concerning feature: tobacco or heavy alcohol use, recent neck or chest surgery or intubation, a neck mass, hemoptysis, dysphagia, odynophagia, stridor or weight loss.

frontHtml: Hoarseness and neck masses: finding head and neck cancer: […] of the node (with HPV/p16 testing in the oropharyngeal pattern, EBV testing when nasopharyngeal carcinoma is possible).
backHtml: Fine-needle aspiration of the node (with HPV/p16 testing in the oropharyngeal pattern, EBV testing when nasopharyngeal carcinoma is possible).

frontHtml: Managing lung metastases, malignant effusion and SVC obstruction: […] can be curative in selected patients: the primary is controlled, there is no disease outside the lung, every nodule can be removed, and enough lung will remain.
backHtml: Pulmonary metastasectomy can be curative in selected patients: the primary is controlled, there is no disease outside the lung, every nodule can be removed, and enough lung will remain.

frontHtml: Managing lung metastases, malignant effusion and SVC obstruction: […] for any new, unexplained effusion large enough to tap: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, Gram stain and culture, and cytology.
backHtml: Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis for any new, unexplained effusion large enough to tap: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, Gram stain and culture, and cytology.

frontHtml: Managing lung metastases, malignant effusion and SVC obstruction: If fluid returns and the lung re-expands : an […] (drained at home) or talc pleurodesis (through a chest tube or at thoracoscopy).
backHtml: If fluid returns and the lung re-expands : an indwelling tunneled pleural catheter (drained at home) or talc pleurodesis (through a chest tube or at thoracoscopy).

frontHtml: Managing lung metastases, malignant effusion and SVC obstruction: Stable patient (most cases): obtain a […] (bronchoscopy, endobronchial ultrasound, mediastinoscopy, CT-guided biopsy, or a peripheral node), because treatment depends on histology: chemotherapy for small cell carcinoma, lymphoma and germ cell tumors; radiation for many non-small cell cancers.
backHtml: Stable patient (most cases): obtain a tissue diagnosis first (bronchoscopy, endobronchial ultrasound, mediastinoscopy, CT-guided biopsy, or a peripheral node), because treatment depends on histology: chemotherapy for small cell carcinoma, lymphoma and germ cell tumors; radiation for many non-small cell cancers.

frontHtml: Managing lung metastases, malignant effusion and SVC obstruction: Life-threatening features (stridor or laryngeal edema, confusion or obtundation from cerebral edema, hemodynamic compromise): urgent […] relieves obstruction within hours; radiation is an alternative; protect the airway.
backHtml: Life-threatening features (stridor or laryngeal edema, confusion or obtundation from cerebral edema, hemodynamic compromise): urgent endovascular stenting relieves obstruction within hours; radiation is an alternative; protect the airway.

frontHtml: Benign tumors of the airways and lung: Both come from […]: repeated forceful vibration of the vocal folds injures the superficial lamina propria (Reinke space), which responds with edema, then fibrosis.
backHtml: Both come from phonotrauma: repeated forceful vibration of the vocal folds injures the superficial lamina propria (Reinke space), which responds with edema, then fibrosis.

frontHtml: Benign tumors of the airways and lung: Exophytic, wart-like squamous papillomas of the larynx caused by […], the low-risk types that also cause anogenital warts.
backHtml: Exophytic, wart-like squamous papillomas of the larynx caused by HPV types 6 and 11, the low-risk types that also cause anogenital warts.

frontHtml: Benign tumors of the airways and lung: A benign but locally destructive, highly vascular tumor that arises near the sphenopalatine foramen in the posterior nasal cavity and occurs almost only in […]; hormonal influence is suspected.
backHtml: A benign but locally destructive, highly vascular tumor that arises near the sphenopalatine foramen in the posterior nasal cavity and occurs almost only in adolescent boys; hormonal influence is suspected.

frontHtml: Benign tumors of the airways and lung: On CT, fat within the nodule or […] (clumped calcified cartilage) is essentially diagnostic.
backHtml: On CT, fat within the nodule or popcorn calcification (clumped calcified cartilage) is essentially diagnostic.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: histologic types and paraneoplastic syndromes: […]: PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma (low PTH, high calcium, low or normal phosphate).
backHtml: Hypercalcemia: PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma (low PTH, high calcium, low or normal phosphate).

frontHtml: Lung cancer: histologic types and paraneoplastic syndromes: […]: ADH from small cell carcinoma; euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine.
backHtml: SIADH: ADH from small cell carcinoma; euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: histologic types and paraneoplastic syndromes: […]: antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release; proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms (dry mouth); incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.
backHtml: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release; proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms (dry mouth); incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.

frontHtml: Lung cancer: histologic types and paraneoplastic syndromes: Superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumors arise at the lung apex and invade the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1: shoulder and medial arm pain, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles) and the cervical sympathetic chain (ipsilateral […]: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). backHtml: Superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumors arise at the lung apex and invade the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1: shoulder and medial arm pain, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles) and the cervical sympathetic chain (ipsilateral Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Superior vena cava syndrome follows compression or invasion of the SVC by a central tumor (most often small cell carcinoma) or mediastinal lymphoma: facial and arm swelling, plethora and distended neck and chest-wall veins, worse when lying down.

frontHtml: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: High-risk human papillomavirus, mostly type 16, causes a growing share of […] cancers (tonsil and base of tongue).
backHtml: High-risk human papillomavirus, mostly type 16, causes a growing share of oropharyngeal cancers (tonsil and base of tongue).

frontHtml: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: The viral oncoprotein […] promotes degradation of p53 and E7 binds and inactivates Rb; the loss of Rb function raises p16 expression, so strong p16 staining is used as a surrogate marker.
backHtml: The viral oncoprotein E6 promotes degradation of p53 and E7 binds and inactivates Rb; the loss of Rb function raises p16 expression, so strong p16 staining is used as a surrogate marker.

frontHtml: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: Laryngeal cancer is strongly tobacco-related. […] (vocal cord) tumors cause hoarseness early and, because the true cords have few lymphatics, rarely spread to nodes at first; this is the most common site and has the best prognosis. Supraglottic tumors present later (sore throat, odynophagia, referred ear pain) and spread to neck nodes early.
backHtml: Laryngeal cancer is strongly tobacco-related. Glottic (vocal cord) tumors cause hoarseness early and, because the true cords have few lymphatics, rarely spread to nodes at first; this is the most common site and has the best prognosis. Supraglottic tumors present later (sore throat, odynophagia, referred ear pain) and spread to neck nodes early.

frontHtml: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: Strongly linked to […], with high incidence in southern China, Southeast Asia, North Africa and Arctic populations; diet (salt-preserved fish) and genetic factors contribute.
backHtml: Strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus, with high incidence in southern China, Southeast Asia, North Africa and Arctic populations; diet (salt-preserved fish) and genetic factors contribute.

frontHtml: Metastases to the lung and pleura; mesothelioma: Two metastases worth special mention: […] (after a molar pregnancy, or from a testicular germ cell tumor) spreads early through the blood and produces hemorrhagic lung nodules with a very high hCG; histology shows sheets of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with no chorionic villi. backHtml: Two metastases worth special mention: choriocarcinoma (after a molar pregnancy, or from a testicular germ cell tumor) spreads early through the blood and produces hemorrhagic lung nodules with a very high hCG; histology shows sheets of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with no chorionic villi. Osteosarcoma of the metaphysis in adolescents most often metastasizes to the lung, and its metastases can calcify because they make osteoid.

frontHtml: Metastases to the lung and pleura; mesothelioma: Tumor on the pleura makes capillaries leaky and blocks lymphatic outflow through the parietal pleura, so fluid accumulates and is an […].
backHtml: Tumor on the pleura makes capillaries leaky and blocks lymphatic outflow through the parietal pleura, so fluid accumulates and is an exudate.

frontHtml: Metastases to the lung and pleura; mesothelioma: Germline […] variants predispose to mesothelioma, uveal and cutaneous melanoma and renal cell carcinoma.
backHtml: Germline BAP1 variants predispose to mesothelioma, uveal and cutaneous melanoma and renal cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Metastases to the lung and pleura; mesothelioma: Most cases are caused by cancer, above all […] and non-Hodgkin lymphoma ; indwelling catheters and pacemaker leads are the main benign causes.
backHtml: Most cases are caused by cancer, above all small cell lung carcinoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma ; indwelling catheters and pacemaker leads are the main benign causes.

frontHtml: Asthma: diagnosis, stepwise care and exacerbations: Current strategy (GINA-style) places an […] in every step, because SABA-only treatment is associated with more severe exacerbations and asthma deaths.
backHtml: Current strategy (GINA-style) places an inhaled corticosteroid in every step, because SABA-only treatment is associated with more severe exacerbations and asthma deaths.

frontHtml: Asthma: diagnosis, stepwise care and exacerbations: […] (one inhaler as the reliever).
backHtml: As-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (one inhaler as the reliever).

frontHtml: Asthma: diagnosis, stepwise care and exacerbations: Severe or poorly responding attacks: […].
backHtml: Severe or poorly responding attacks: IV magnesium sulfate.

frontHtml: Asthma: diagnosis, stepwise care and exacerbations: A […] means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
backHtml: A normal or rising PaCO2 means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

frontHtml: COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis: management: Suspect COPD in an adult with chronic dyspnea, cough or sputum and exposure to smoke or dust. […] confirms persistent airflow limitation.
backHtml: Suspect COPD in an adult with chronic dyspnea, cough or sputum and exposure to smoke or dust. Post-bronchodilator spirometry with FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation.

frontHtml: COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis: management: Test every patient with COPD once for […] (serum level, then phenotype or genotype if low), especially when young, a light smoker, or with basal emphysema or liver disease.
backHtml: Test every patient with COPD once for α1-antitrypsin deficiency (serum level, then phenotype or genotype if low), especially when young, a light smoker, or with basal emphysema or liver disease.

frontHtml: COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis: management: Long-term oxygen therapy (at least 15 hours a day) prolongs survival in stable patients with severe resting hypoxemia: […], or PaO2 56–59 mm Hg with cor pulmonale, edema or hematocrit above 55%.
backHtml: Long-term oxygen therapy (at least 15 hours a day) prolongs survival in stable patients with severe resting hypoxemia: PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg or SaO2 ≤ 88%, or PaO2 56–59 mm Hg with cor pulmonale, edema or hematocrit above 55%.

frontHtml: COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis: management: Controlled oxygen to […].
backHtml: Controlled oxygen to SpO2 88–92%.

frontHtml: COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis: management: […] for acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH ≤ 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg) in a patient who can protect the airway.
backHtml: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation for acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH ≤ 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg) in a patient who can protect the airway.

frontHtml: Asthma: immunology, pathology and pharmacology: In the common allergic (type 2-high) form, inhaled allergens are presented by dendritic cells to naive CD4 T cells, which become […].
backHtml: In the common allergic (type 2-high) form, inhaled allergens are presented by dendritic cells to naive CD4 T cells, which become Th2 cells.

frontHtml: Asthma: immunology, pathology and pharmacology: […]: eosinophil maturation, recruitment and survival.
backHtml: IL-5: eosinophil maturation, recruitment and survival.

frontHtml: Asthma: immunology, pathology and pharmacology: Mucus plugs containing […] (Curschmann spirals) and needle-shaped crystals formed from an eosinophil protein, galectin-10 (Charcot-Leyden crystals).
backHtml: Mucus plugs containing spiral casts of shed epithelium and mucus (Curschmann spirals) and needle-shaped crystals formed from an eosinophil protein, galectin-10 (Charcot-Leyden crystals).

frontHtml: Asthma: immunology, pathology and pharmacology: When spirometry is normal between episodes, a […] shows hyperresponsiveness; a negative challenge makes current asthma unlikely.
backHtml: When spirometry is normal between episodes, a methacholine (or mannitol) challenge shows hyperresponsiveness; a negative challenge makes current asthma unlikely.

frontHtml: COPD, α1-antitrypsin deficiency and bronchiectasis: The central mechanism is a […]: smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase and matrix metalloproteinases, while oxidants in smoke inactivate α1-antitrypsin.
backHtml: The central mechanism is a protease–antiprotease imbalance: smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase and matrix metalloproteinases, while oxidants in smoke inactivate α1-antitrypsin.

frontHtml: COPD, α1-antitrypsin deficiency and bronchiectasis: In the common severe genotype (PiZZ, a single amino-acid substitution), the protein misfolds and polymerizes inside the […].
backHtml: In the common severe genotype (PiZZ, a single amino-acid substitution), the protein misfolds and polymerizes inside the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes.

frontHtml: COPD, α1-antitrypsin deficiency and bronchiectasis: Pathology: […] (a larger gland layer relative to wall thickness, the Reid index, normally below about 0.4), goblet-cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia and small-airway inflammation and fibrosis.
backHtml: Pathology: hypertrophy and hyperplasia of submucosal mucous glands (a larger gland layer relative to wall thickness, the Reid index, normally below about 0.4), goblet-cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia and small-airway inflammation and fibrosis.

frontHtml: COPD, α1-antitrypsin deficiency and bronchiectasis: Primary ciliary dyskinesia: autosomal recessive defects in axonemal […] (or other ciliary proteins).
backHtml: Primary ciliary dyskinesia: autosomal recessive defects in axonemal dynein arms (or other ciliary proteins).

frontHtml: Interstitial lung disease: evaluation and treatment: […]: the key test.
backHtml: High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest: the key test.

frontHtml: Interstitial lung disease: evaluation and treatment: […]: nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor; diarrhea and raised aminotransferases) or pirfenidone (photosensitivity rash, nausea, raised aminotransferases).
backHtml: Antifibrotic therapy: nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor; diarrhea and raised aminotransferases) or pirfenidone (photosensitivity rash, nausea, raised aminotransferases).

frontHtml: Interstitial lung disease: evaluation and treatment: The most important intervention in hypersensitivity pneumonitis is […] (rehoming birds, replacing feather bedding, remediating mold, changing work duties).
backHtml: The most important intervention in hypersensitivity pneumonitis is identifying and removing the antigen (rehoming birds, replacing feather bedding, remediating mold, changing work duties).

frontHtml: Interstitial lung disease: evaluation and treatment: RB-ILD and DIP improve chiefly with […].
backHtml: RB-ILD and DIP improve chiefly with smoking cessation.

frontHtml: Occupational lung disease, sarcoidosis and eosinophilic pneumonias: management: The most effective way to lower lung cancer risk is […], because asbestos and tobacco multiply each other's risk.
backHtml: The most effective way to lower lung cancer risk is smoking cessation, because asbestos and tobacco multiply each other's risk.

frontHtml: Occupational lung disease, sarcoidosis and eosinophilic pneumonias: management: Silicosis : remove from exposure; screen for […] (interferon-γ release assay or tuberculin skin test) and treat latent infection if positive, because silicosis raises the risk of active TB substantially.
backHtml: Silicosis : remove from exposure; screen for latent tuberculosis (interferon-γ release assay or tuberculin skin test) and treat latent infection if positive, because silicosis raises the risk of active TB substantially.

frontHtml: Occupational lung disease, sarcoidosis and eosinophilic pneumonias: management: The least invasive accessible tissue is sampled first: a skin lesion, peripheral node, or mediastinal nodes by […].
backHtml: The least invasive accessible tissue is sampled first: a skin lesion, peripheral node, or mediastinal nodes by endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA).

frontHtml: Restrictive physiology, pneumoconioses and hypersensitivity pneumonitis: A useful anatomic rule: dusts that are cleared poorly by the lymphatics of the upper zones (silica, coal) favor the […]; asbestos fibers, which are long and thin and settle by interception, favor the lower lobes and the pleura.
backHtml: A useful anatomic rule: dusts that are cleared poorly by the lymphatics of the upper zones (silica, coal) favor the upper lobes; asbestos fibers, which are long and thin and settle by interception, favor the lower lobes and the pleura.

frontHtml: Restrictive physiology, pneumoconioses and hypersensitivity pneumonitis: […]: cotton, flax or hemp dust.
backHtml: Byssinosis: cotton, flax or hemp dust.

frontHtml: Restrictive physiology, pneumoconioses and hypersensitivity pneumonitis: […]: nitrogen dioxide accumulates above fresh silage in the first days to weeks after filling.
backHtml: Silo-filler's disease: nitrogen dioxide accumulates above fresh silage in the first days to weeks after filling.

frontHtml: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, sarcoidosis and eosinophilic lung disease: The histologic pattern is […]: patchy, subpleural and basal fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity (old dense collagen next to active fibroblastic foci and normal lung) and honeycomb cysts lined by bronchiolar epithelium.
backHtml: The histologic pattern is usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP): patchy, subpleural and basal fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity (old dense collagen next to active fibroblastic foci and normal lung) and honeycomb cysts lined by bronchiolar epithelium.

frontHtml: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, sarcoidosis and eosinophilic lung disease: A multisystem disease of […] from an exaggerated Th1 (and Th17) response to an unknown antigen.
backHtml: A multisystem disease of noncaseating granulomas from an exaggerated Th1 (and Th17) response to an unknown antigen.

frontHtml: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, sarcoidosis and eosinophilic lung disease: […]: adult-onset asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, eosinophilia, then necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis (mononeuritis multiplex, purpura, cardiomyopathy); p-ANCA (anti-MPO) in under half.
backHtml: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: adult-onset asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, eosinophilia, then necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis (mononeuritis multiplex, purpura, cardiomyopathy); p-ANCA (anti-MPO) in under half.

frontHtml: Acute respiratory failure and ARDS: management: Low tidal volume ventilation : […] of predicted body weight (from height and sex, not actual weight), within a range of 4–8 mL/kg.
backHtml: Low tidal volume ventilation : about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight (from height and sex, not actual weight), within a range of 4–8 mL/kg.

frontHtml: Acute respiratory failure and ARDS: management: Accept a modest rise in PaCO 2 and fall in pH ( […] ) unless contraindicated, for example by raised intracranial pressure.
backHtml: Accept a modest rise in PaCO 2 and fall in pH ( permissive hypercapnia ) unless contraindicated, for example by raised intracranial pressure.

frontHtml: Acute respiratory failure and ARDS: management: […] for severe ARDS (PaO 2 /F I O 2 < 150) for long sessions (at least 12–16 h a day) improves survival by recruiting dorsal lung and evening out ventilation.
backHtml: Prone positioning for severe ARDS (PaO 2 /F I O 2 < 150) for long sessions (at least 12–16 h a day) improves survival by recruiting dorsal lung and evening out ventilation.

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension: management: Anticoagulant choice. […] (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran; the last two after a short course of parenteral heparin) is first line for most patients.
backHtml: Anticoagulant choice. A direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran; the last two after a short course of parenteral heparin) is first line for most patients.

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension: management: Duration. […] for every PE.
backHtml: Duration. At least 3 months for every PE.

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension: management: Always obtain a […] to screen for CTEPH; it is more sensitive than CT angiography for chronic thromboembolic disease.
backHtml: Always obtain a V/Q scan to screen for CTEPH; it is more sensitive than CT angiography for chronic thromboembolic disease.

frontHtml: Respiratory failure, hypoxemia and ARDS: Right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0: alveoli filled with fluid, pus or collapsed; intracardiac shunts; pulmonary arteriovenous malformations): raised gradient and […] , because shunted blood never meets the added oxygen.
backHtml: Right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0: alveoli filled with fluid, pus or collapsed; intracardiac shunts; pulmonary arteriovenous malformations): raised gradient and poor response to 100% oxygen , because shunted blood never meets the added oxygen.

frontHtml: Respiratory failure, hypoxemia and ARDS: Indirect injury: […] (the commonest extrapulmonary cause), severe trauma with shock, multiple transfusions (transfusion-related acute lung injury), acute pancreatitis, burns, drug overdose.
backHtml: Indirect injury: sepsis (the commonest extrapulmonary cause), severe trauma with shock, multiple transfusions (transfusion-related acute lung injury), acute pancreatitis, burns, drug overdose.

frontHtml: Respiratory failure, hypoxemia and ARDS: Diffuse alveolar damage: interstitial and alveolar edema, necrosis of type I pneumocytes, eosinophilic […] (fibrin plus cell debris) lining alveolar ducts
backHtml: Diffuse alveolar damage: interstitial and alveolar edema, necrosis of type I pneumocytes, eosinophilic hyaline membranes (fibrin plus cell debris) lining alveolar ducts

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism, other emboli and pulmonary hypertension: Hypoxemia drives hyperventilation, so the typical gas is […] with a raised A–a gradient; PaO 2 can be normal in a young patient.
backHtml: Hypoxemia drives hyperventilation, so the typical gas is respiratory alkalosis with a raised A–a gradient; PaO 2 can be normal in a young patient.

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism, other emboli and pulmonary hypertension: The commonest ECG finding is […]; signs of RV strain (right axis deviation, new right bundle branch block, T-wave inversion in V1–V4, the S1Q3T3 pattern) are less frequent and insensitive.
backHtml: The commonest ECG finding is sinus tachycardia; signs of RV strain (right axis deviation, new right bundle branch block, T-wave inversion in V1–V4, the S1Q3T3 pattern) are less frequent and insensitive.

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism, other emboli and pulmonary hypertension: Pulmonary hypertension is now defined at right heart catheterization by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) […] at rest (the older threshold was 25). Precapillary disease adds a PCWP ≤ 15 mm Hg and raised pulmonary vascular resistance; postcapillary disease has PCWP > 15 mm Hg (left heart disease).
backHtml: Pulmonary hypertension is now defined at right heart catheterization by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) above 20 mm Hg at rest (the older threshold was 25). Precapillary disease adds a PCWP ≤ 15 mm Hg and raised pulmonary vascular resistance; postcapillary disease has PCWP > 15 mm Hg (left heart disease).

frontHtml: Pulmonary embolism, other emboli and pulmonary hypertension: Mechanism in PAH. Loss-of-function variants in […] (a receptor of the TGF-β superfamily, autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance) remove a brake on smooth muscle proliferation.
backHtml: Mechanism in PAH. Loss-of-function variants in BMPR2 (a receptor of the TGF-β superfamily, autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance) remove a brake on smooth muscle proliferation.

frontHtml: Hypoxemia, hypoventilation and sleep-disordered breathing: Risk factors: obesity, male sex, older age, large neck circumference, retrognathia, […] (the main cause in children), hypothyroidism and acromegaly.
backHtml: Risk factors: obesity, male sex, older age, large neck circumference, retrognathia, tonsillar hypertrophy (the main cause in children), hypothyroidism and acromegaly.

frontHtml: Hypoxemia, hypoventilation and sleep-disordered breathing: Treatment: […] is first-line for moderate–severe or symptomatic disease and improves sleepiness and blood pressure.
backHtml: Treatment: CPAP is first-line for moderate–severe or symptomatic disease and improves sleepiness and blood pressure.

frontHtml: Hypoxemia, hypoventilation and sleep-disordered breathing: A raised […] (≥ 27 mEq/L) is a useful screening clue, and the blood gas typically shows compensated respiratory acidosis.
backHtml: A raised serum bicarbonate (≥ 27 mEq/L) is a useful screening clue, and the blood gas typically shows compensated respiratory acidosis.

frontHtml: Hypoxemia, hypoventilation and sleep-disordered breathing: Exam trap: a post-operative patient on an opioid with SpO2 92% on nasal oxygen and a respiratory rate of 7 is hypoventilating; give […] and support ventilation, not more oxygen.
backHtml: Exam trap: a post-operative patient on an opioid with SpO2 92% on nasal oxygen and a respiratory rate of 7 is hypoventilating; give naloxone and support ventilation, not more oxygen.

frontHtml: Carbon monoxide, methemoglobinemia and altitude illness: Diagnosis: carboxyhemoglobin by […] on an arterial or venous sample.
backHtml: Diagnosis: carboxyhemoglobin by co-oximetry on an arterial or venous sample.

frontHtml: Carbon monoxide, methemoglobinemia and altitude illness: Suspect it in cyanosis with a normal PaO2, SpO2 around 85% that does not improve with oxygen, and […], often minutes to hours after a topical anesthetic spray (endoscopy, transesophageal echocardiography), dapsone or a nitrite.
backHtml: Suspect it in cyanosis with a normal PaO2, SpO2 around 85% that does not improve with oxygen, and chocolate-colored blood, often minutes to hours after a topical anesthetic spray (endoscopy, transesophageal echocardiography), dapsone or a nitrite.

frontHtml: Carbon monoxide, methemoglobinemia and altitude illness: Descent and supplemental oxygen ; […] when descent or oxygen is unavailable
backHtml: Descent and supplemental oxygen ; nifedipine when descent or oxygen is unavailable

frontHtml: Carbon monoxide, methemoglobinemia and altitude illness: Pearl: for every altitude syndrome, […] is the definitive treatment; drugs buy time.
backHtml: Pearl: for every altitude syndrome, descent is the definitive treatment; drugs buy time.

frontHtml: Gas exchange, hypoxemia and control of breathing: In young adults it is about 5–15 mm Hg; it widens with age (a rough upper limit is […]) and with higher FiO2.
backHtml: In young adults it is about 5–15 mm Hg; it widens with age (a rough upper limit is age/4 + 4) and with higher FiO2.

frontHtml: Gas exchange, hypoxemia and control of breathing: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to the […], which follows arterial PCO2 (CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier; H+ does not).
backHtml: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to the pH of cerebrospinal fluid, which follows arterial PCO2 (CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier; H+ does not).

frontHtml: Gas exchange, hypoxemia and control of breathing: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies via the […], aortic bodies via the vagus) respond mainly to a low PaO2 (strongly below about 60 mm Hg), and also to high PaCO2 and low pH.
backHtml: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies via the glossopharyngeal nerve, aortic bodies via the vagus) respond mainly to a low PaO2 (strongly below about 60 mm Hg), and also to high PaCO2 and low pH.

frontHtml: Oxygen transport: hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, methemoglobin and altitude: Right shift (higher P50, more unloading): ↑ H+ and ↑ CO2 (the […]), ↑ temperature, ↑ 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, exercise, high altitude (through 2,3-BPG).
backHtml: Right shift (higher P50, more unloading): ↑ H+ and ↑ CO2 (the Bohr effect), ↑ temperature, ↑ 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, exercise, high altitude (through 2,3-BPG).

frontHtml: Oxygen transport: hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, methemoglobin and altitude: CO binds hemoglobin with an affinity […] that of oxygen.

frontHtml: Oxygen transport: hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, methemoglobin and altitude: Acetazolamide inhibits […] in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonate diuresis and a metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation and speeds acclimatization.

backHtml: Exam trap: CO poisoning and methemoglobinemia both lower oxygen content with a normal PaO2, but pulse oximetry reads near-normal in CO poisoning and about 85% in methemoglobinemia.

frontHtml: Pleural, mediastinal and chest wall disorders: management: Tuberculous effusion : lymphocytic exudate with high […]; pleural biopsy has the highest yield (fluid culture is often negative).

backHtml: Proceed to urgent thoracotomy if the initial drainage is about 1,500 mL or more, if bleeding continues at about 200 mL per hour for 2–4 hours, or if the patient remains unstable despite resuscitation.

backHtml: Open ("sucking") chest wound: cover with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides, then a chest tube away from the wound.

frontHtml: Pleura, mediastinum and chest wall: Light's criteria : an effusion is an exudate if any one is met: pleural/serum protein […]; pleural/serum LDH > 0.6; pleural LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum.
backHtml: Light's criteria : an effusion is an exudate if any one is met: pleural/serum protein > 0.5; pleural/serum LDH > 0.6; pleural LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum.

frontHtml: Pleura, mediastinum and chest wall: Complicated parapneumonic effusion and empyema. Bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space consume glucose and produce lactic acid and CO 2 , so pleural pH falls […] and glucose below 60 mg/dL ; LDH climbs.
backHtml: Complicated parapneumonic effusion and empyema. Bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space consume glucose and produce lactic acid and CO 2 , so pleural pH falls below 7.2 and glucose below 60 mg/dL ; LDH climbs.

frontHtml: Pleura, mediastinum and chest wall: Chylothorax. Milky fluid with triglycerides […] (chylomicrons).
backHtml: Chylothorax. Milky fluid with triglycerides > 110 mg/dL (chylomicrons).

backHtml: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis (antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor), pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia.

frontHtml: Upper airway emergencies: management: Severe obstruction in a conscious infant (younger than 1 year): cycles of […], with the head held lower than the chest.
backHtml: Severe obstruction in a conscious infant (younger than 1 year): cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts, with the head held lower than the chest.

frontHtml: Upper airway emergencies: management: Anaphylaxis (urticaria, wheeze, hypotension, often a trigger such as food, sting or drug): […] into the anterolateral thigh first, repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed; then fluids, oxygen, and adjuncts (antihistamines, glucocorticoids, inhaled β 2 -agonist).
backHtml: Anaphylaxis (urticaria, wheeze, hypotension, often a trigger such as food, sting or drug): intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh first, repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed; then fluids, oxygen, and adjuncts (antihistamines, glucocorticoids, inhaled β 2 -agonist).

frontHtml: Upper airway emergencies: management: Small streaks of blood are common soon after the procedure, but bright red bleeding from 3 days to several weeks after a tracheostomy suggests a […].
backHtml: Small streaks of blood are common soon after the procedure, but bright red bleeding from 3 days to several weeks after a tracheostomy suggests a tracheoinnominate fistula.

backHtml: Exam trap. In laryngeal fracture, the instinct to perform a cricothyrotomy is wrong: the surgical airway should be placed below the injury (tracheostomy).

frontHtml: Chest trauma: primary survey and management: Large-bore IV access and blood products, chest tube; thoracotomy if the initial drainage is […] or more, or if drainage continues at roughly 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or if the patient remains unstable
backHtml: Large-bore IV access and blood products, chest tube; thoracotomy if the initial drainage is about 1,500 mL or more, or if drainage continues at roughly 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or if the patient remains unstable

frontHtml: Chest trauma: primary survey and management: The main danger of rib fractures is […] from poor cough and splinting.
backHtml: The main danger of rib fractures is pneumonia from poor cough and splinting.

frontHtml: Chest trauma: primary survey and management: Blunt rupture is most often […].

backHtml: High yield. A large persistent air leak with a lung that will not re-expand after a chest tube means a tracheobronchial injury: arrange bronchoscopy.

frontHtml: Upper airway injury: anatomy and mechanisms: From above down in the midline: the hyoid bone, the thyrohyoid membrane, the thyroid cartilage (laryngeal prominence), the cricothyroid membrane , the […] (the only complete ring of the airway), then the tracheal rings with the thyroid isthmus usually over rings 2–4.
backHtml: From above down in the midline: the hyoid bone, the thyrohyoid membrane, the thyroid cartilage (laryngeal prominence), the cricothyroid membrane , the cricoid cartilage (the only complete ring of the airway), then the tracheal rings with the thyroid isthmus usually over rings 2–4.

frontHtml: Upper airway injury: anatomy and mechanisms: The […] is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds.
backHtml: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds.

frontHtml: Upper airway injury: anatomy and mechanisms: An aspirated object in an older child or adult usually enters the […], which is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
backHtml: An aspirated object in an older child or adult usually enters the right main bronchus, which is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

frontHtml: Upper airway injury: anatomy and mechanisms: Without it, kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen into […], which increases vascular permeability.
backHtml: Without it, kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen into bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability.

frontHtml: Upper airway injury: anatomy and mechanisms: About 90% of nosebleeds are anterior , from the […] on the anterior septum, where branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries meet. backHtml: About 90% of nosebleeds are anterior , from the Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum, where branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries meet. Posterior bleeds come mostly from the sphenopalatine artery (a branch of the maxillary artery) and are heavier and harder to control.

frontHtml: Chest trauma: pleural, airway and chest wall mechanics: The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal esophageal mesentery and the body wall, and is supplied by the […], which explains pain referred to the shoulder after diaphragmatic irritation.
backHtml: The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal esophageal mesentery and the body wall, and is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), which explains pain referred to the shoulder after diaphragmatic irritation.

frontHtml: Chest trauma: pleural, airway and chest wall mechanics: Primary blast injury : the pressure wave damages air-containing organs at air–tissue interfaces: the […] (most often), the lungs (blast lung: alveolar hemorrhage and edema, the commonest fatal primary injury) and the bowel.
backHtml: Primary blast injury : the pressure wave damages air-containing organs at air–tissue interfaces: the tympanic membrane (most often), the lungs (blast lung: alveolar hemorrhage and edema, the commonest fatal primary injury) and the bowel.

frontHtml: Chest trauma: pleural, airway and chest wall mechanics: Aspirated water, fresh or salt, washes out and inactivates […] and causes alveolar edema, so alveoli collapse and shunt rises, sometimes progressing to ARDS within hours.
backHtml: Aspirated water, fresh or salt, washes out and inactivates surfactant and causes alveolar edema, so alveoli collapse and shunt rises, sometimes progressing to ARDS within hours.

frontHtml: Respiratory distress in the newborn: Low volumes, […] with air bronchograms
backHtml: Low volumes, diffuse fine granular (ground-glass) opacity with air bronchograms

frontHtml: Respiratory distress in the newborn: A single course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) given to a pregnant person at risk of preterm delivery […], generally between 24 and 34 weeks, lowers neonatal death, RDS and intraventricular hemorrhage; it is also considered at the limit of viability and in selected late-preterm cases.
backHtml: A single course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) given to a pregnant person at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days, generally between 24 and 34 weeks, lowers neonatal death, RDS and intraventricular hemorrhage; it is also considered at the limit of viability and in selected late-preterm cases.

frontHtml: Respiratory distress in the newborn: Known or suspected diaphragmatic hernia : avoid […], which inflates the bowel in the chest and further compresses the lungs.
backHtml: Known or suspected diaphragmatic hernia : avoid bag-mask ventilation, which inflates the bowel in the chest and further compresses the lungs.

frontHtml: Respiratory distress in the newborn: Every US state screens newborns for cystic fibrosis, starting with blood […] (raised because pancreatic ducts are obstructed), often followed by a CFTR variant panel.
backHtml: Every US state screens newborns for cystic fibrosis, starting with blood immunoreactive trypsinogen (raised because pancreatic ducts are obstructed), often followed by a CFTR variant panel.

frontHtml: Noisy breathing and congenital airway obstruction in infants: […]; inspiratory, starts in the first weeks, louder supine, with feeding, crying and colds; better prone; growing well
backHtml: Most common cause of infant stridor; inspiratory, starts in the first weeks, louder supine, with feeding, crying and colds; better prone; growing well

frontHtml: Noisy breathing and congenital airway obstruction in infants: Neonate cyanotic at rest and during feeding, […] (mouth open); a catheter will not pass through either nostril; may be part of CHARGE
backHtml: Neonate cyanotic at rest and during feeding, pinker when crying (mouth open); a catheter will not pass through either nostril; may be part of CHARGE

frontHtml: Noisy breathing and congenital airway obstruction in infants: Biphasic stridor that worsens over the first months, often with a […]
backHtml: Biphasic stridor that worsens over the first months, often with a facial hemangioma in a beard distribution

frontHtml: Noisy breathing and congenital airway obstruction in infants: After birth, obtain chest CT with contrast ([…]) to define the lesion and any systemic arterial supply.
backHtml: After birth, obtain chest CT with contrast (CT angiography) to define the lesion and any systemic arterial supply.

frontHtml: Lung development and surfactant: The respiratory tract starts in the fourth week as the […], an outgrowth of the ventral wall of the foregut.
backHtml: The respiratory tract starts in the fourth week as the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud), an outgrowth of the ventral wall of the foregut.

frontHtml: Lung development and surfactant: Surfactant is made by […], stored in lamellar bodies and secreted onto the alveolar surface.
backHtml: Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes, stored in lamellar bodies and secreted onto the alveolar surface.

frontHtml: Lung development and surfactant: The pressure needed to keep an alveolus open follows the […]: P = 2T / r.
backHtml: The pressure needed to keep an alveolus open follows the law of Laplace: P = 2T / r.

frontHtml: Lung development and surfactant: Delays maturation : […] in maternal diabetes (insulin opposes the glucocorticoid effect), male sex, prematurity, cesarean birth without labor.
backHtml: Delays maturation : fetal hyperinsulinemia in maternal diabetes (insulin opposes the glucocorticoid effect), male sex, prematurity, cesarean birth without labor.

frontHtml: Congenital malformations of the lung, airway and diaphragm: Failure of the […] to close lets abdominal organs enter the chest.
backHtml: Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membranes to close lets abdominal organs enter the chest.

frontHtml: Congenital malformations of the lung, airway and diaphragm: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive, caused by defects in axonemal structures, most often the […] that power ciliary bending.
backHtml: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive, caused by defects in axonemal structures, most often the dynein arms that power ciliary bending.

frontHtml: Congenital malformations of the lung, airway and diaphragm: A […] (both fourth arches persist because the distal right dorsal aorta fails to regress) is the most common symptomatic ring; a right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and left ligamentum is next.
backHtml: A double aortic arch (both fourth arches persist because the distal right dorsal aorta fails to regress) is the most common symptomatic ring; a right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and left ligamentum is next.

frontHtml: Drug- and toxin-induced respiratory disease: recognition and management: Prevention and monitoring : baseline chest radiograph and PFTs with DLCO before long-term amiodarone, and evaluation of new respiratory symptoms; […] during bleomycin therapy, with the drug stopped if DLCO falls significantly or symptoms appear; minimize FiO 2 in patients who have received bleomycin; avoid nitrofurantoin as long-term prophylaxis in older adults with reduced kidney function (it is on the Beers list).
backHtml: Prevention and monitoring : baseline chest radiograph and PFTs with DLCO before long-term amiodarone, and evaluation of new respiratory symptoms; serial DLCO during bleomycin therapy, with the drug stopped if DLCO falls significantly or symptoms appear; minimize FiO 2 in patients who have received bleomycin; avoid nitrofurantoin as long-term prophylaxis in older adults with reduced kidney function (it is on the Beers list).

frontHtml: Drug- and toxin-induced respiratory disease: recognition and management: ACE inhibitor cough : stop the drug; cough resolves within days to a few weeks. […] is an appropriate substitute because it rarely causes cough.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor cough : stop the drug; cough resolves within days to a few weeks. An ARB is an appropriate substitute because it rarely causes cough.

frontHtml: Drug- and toxin-induced respiratory disease: recognition and management: COPD with CO 2 retention : titrate oxygen to […] (controlled-delivery devices such as a Venturi mask help); check a blood gas after starting oxygen.
backHtml: COPD with CO 2 retention : titrate oxygen to SpO 2 88–92% (controlled-delivery devices such as a Venturi mask help); check a blood gas after starting oxygen.

frontHtml: Drug- and toxin-induced respiratory disease: recognition and management: Methemoglobinemia : stop the oxidant; give methylene blue for symptoms or high levels; in […], use exchange transfusion or high-dose ascorbic acid instead.
backHtml: Methemoglobinemia : stop the oxidant; give methylene blue for symptoms or high levels; in G6PD deficiency, use exchange transfusion or high-dose ascorbic acid instead.

frontHtml: Drug- and toxin-induced respiratory disease: recognition and management: A patient with "pneumonia that does not respond to antibiotics" who takes amiodarone, nitrofurantoin or methotrexate, or who has recently started immunotherapy, has […] until proven otherwise.
backHtml: A patient with "pneumonia that does not respond to antibiotics" who takes amiodarone, nitrofurantoin or methotrexate, or who has recently started immunotherapy, has drug-induced pneumonitis until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Drug-induced lung injury, airway reactions and respiratory depression: Lung and skin have little […] , the enzyme that inactivates the drug, so they bear the brunt.
backHtml: Lung and skin have little bleomycin hydrolase , the enzyme that inactivates the drug, so they bear the brunt.

frontHtml: Drug-induced lung injury, airway reactions and respiratory depression: An iodinated, highly lipophilic amphiphilic drug that accumulates in tissue and inhibits lysosomal phospholipases, causing phospholipidosis: […] .
backHtml: An iodinated, highly lipophilic amphiphilic drug that accumulates in tissue and inhibits lysosomal phospholipases, causing phospholipidosis: foamy, lipid-laden alveolar macrophages .

frontHtml: Drug-induced lung injury, airway reactions and respiratory depression: Classic patient: older woman on long-term prophylaxis for […].
backHtml: Classic patient: older woman on long-term prophylaxis for recurrent urinary infections.

frontHtml: Drug-induced lung injury, airway reactions and respiratory depression: ACE inhibitors : ACE (kininase II) normally degrades […] and substance P.
backHtml: ACE inhibitors : ACE (kininase II) normally degrades bradykinin and substance P.

frontHtml: Drug-induced lung injury, airway reactions and respiratory depression: Aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs : in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity), […] lowers protective prostaglandin E 2 and shunts arachidonic acid toward the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, raising cysteinyl leukotrienes that constrict airways.
backHtml: Aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs : in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity), COX-1 inhibition lowers protective prostaglandin E 2 and shunts arachidonic acid toward the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, raising cysteinyl leukotrienes that constrict airways.

frontHtml: Oxygen toxicity, hemoglobin poisons, nicotine, vaping and inhaled drugs: Absorption atelectasis : […] normally splints alveoli open; breathing pure oxygen behind a partly obstructed airway lets the oxygen be absorbed completely, and the alveoli collapse.
backHtml: Absorption atelectasis : nitrogen normally splints alveoli open; breathing pure oxygen behind a partly obstructed airway lets the oxygen be absorbed completely, and the alveoli collapse.

frontHtml: Oxygen toxicity, hemoglobin poisons, nicotine, vaping and inhaled drugs: Retinopathy of prematurity : high oxygen in preterm infants […] and halts retinal vessel growth; when the infant returns to room air, the avascular retina becomes hypoxic, VEGF surges and abnormal neovascularization follows.
backHtml: Retinopathy of prematurity : high oxygen in preterm infants suppresses VEGF and halts retinal vessel growth; when the infant returns to room air, the avascular retina becomes hypoxic, VEGF surges and abnormal neovascularization follows.

frontHtml: Oxygen toxicity, hemoglobin poisons, nicotine, vaping and inhaled drugs: Volatile inhalants (solvents, aerosol propellants, butane): sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines and can cause […] ("sudden sniffing death"); toluene causes renal tubular acidosis and neurotoxicity; nitrite inhalants cause methemoglobinemia.
backHtml: Volatile inhalants (solvents, aerosol propellants, butane): sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines and can cause fatal ventricular arrhythmia ("sudden sniffing death"); toluene causes renal tubular acidosis and neurotoxicity; nitrite inhalants cause methemoglobinemia.

frontHtml: Oxygen toxicity, hemoglobin poisons, nicotine, vaping and inhaled drugs: Drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid) commonly produces pleuritis and pleural effusion, with […] and usually without renal or CNS disease.
backHtml: Drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid) commonly produces pleuritis and pleural effusion, with anti-histone antibodies and usually without renal or CNS disease.

frontHtml: Oxygen toxicity, hemoglobin poisons, nicotine, vaping and inhaled drugs: Cyanide (smoke from burning plastics, nitroprusside in excess) blocks cytochrome oxidase: lactic acidosis with a normal PaO 2 and high venous oxygen; […] is the antidote in smoke inhalation.
backHtml: Cyanide (smoke from burning plastics, nitroprusside in excess) blocks cytochrome oxidase: lactic acidosis with a normal PaO 2 and high venous oxygen; hydroxocobalamin is the antidote in smoke inhalation.

frontHtml: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics in a stable patient with suspected endocarditis.
backHtml: suspected IE in a stable patient → blood cultures first, then echo, then antibiotics.

frontHtml: Choose TEE when TTE is negative or limited in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis.
backHtml: a negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis on a prosthetic valve: get a TEE.

frontHtml: Select empiric antibiotics that cover MRSA for suspected endocarditis in a person who injects drugs.
backHtml: empiric therapy for native valve endocarditis in a person who injects drugs must cover MRSA: vancomycin.

frontHtml: Recognize heart failure from valve destruction as an indication for urgent surgery in endocarditis.
backHtml: endocarditis + heart failure from valve dysfunction → urgent surgery.

frontHtml: Identify which patients need endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures.
backHtml: prophylaxis = prosthetic valve, prior IE, specific congenital disease, transplant valvulopathy; not native valve disease.

frontHtml: Order colonoscopy after Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis.
backHtml: S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy, whatever the screening history.

frontHtml: Manage Lyme carditis with high-grade AV block.
backHtml: Lyme carditis with high-grade block → admit, monitor, IV ceftriaxone; a permanent pacemaker is rarely needed.

frontHtml: Recognize perivalvular abscess from persistent bacteremia and new AV block in aortic valve endocarditis.
backHtml: aortic valve endocarditis + persistent bacteremia + new AV block = root abscess → TEE and surgery.

frontHtml: Use cardiac MRI to confirm suspected acute myocarditis.
backHtml: suspected myocarditis with normal coronaries → cardiac MRI.

frontHtml: Diagnose tricuspid endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.
backHtml: multiple cavitating lung nodules + inspiratory-increasing murmur in a person who injects drugs = tricuspid endocarditis.

frontHtml: Narrow therapy to an antistaphylococcal β-lactam for MSSA endocarditis.
backHtml: MSSA → switch from vancomycin to cefazolin or nafcillin.

frontHtml: Identify Staphylococcus aureus as the leading cause of tricuspid endocarditis in people who inject drugs, and its laboratory features.
backHtml: injection drug use + tricuspid murmur + cavitary lung nodules = S. aureus tricuspid endocarditis.

frontHtml: Explain how viridans streptococci adhere to damaged heart valves.
backHtml: viridans streptococci need a damaged valve and use dextran to adhere to its fibrin–platelet deposit.

frontHtml: Associate Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteremia with colonic neoplasia.
backHtml: S. gallolyticus in the blood → colonoscopy.

frontHtml: Distinguish the immunologic and embolic mechanisms of the peripheral signs of endocarditis.
backHtml: painful nodules (Osler) are immunologic; painless macules on palms and soles (Janeway) are embolic.

frontHtml: Recognize Coxiella burnetii as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis and describe its transmission.
