backHtml: livestock + culture-negative endocarditis = Coxiella , acquired by inhalation.

frontHtml: Associate Bartonella quintana with louse exposure and culture-negative endocarditis.
backHtml: body lice + culture-negative endocarditis → B. quintana .

frontHtml: Identify the transmission and organ involvement of chronic Chagas disease.
backHtml: cardiomyopathy + megaesophagus/megacolon + Latin America = Chagas, spread by triatomine feces.

frontHtml: Explain the pathogenesis of syphilitic aortitis.
backHtml: ascending aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation + positive treponemal test → vasa vasorum endarteritis.

frontHtml: Recognize Lyme carditis as AV block after erythema migrans.
backHtml: erythema migrans followed by heart block = Lyme carditis.

frontHtml: Describe the virus most associated with viral myocarditis.
backHtml: coxsackievirus B (picornavirus: naked, + ssRNA) is the classic cause of viral myocarditis.

frontHtml: Explain biofilm production by coagulase-negative staphylococci in prosthetic valve endocarditis.
backHtml: S. epidermidis + prosthetic material = biofilm infection.

frontHtml: Choose secondary prophylaxis and its duration after rheumatic fever with carditis.
backHtml: rheumatic fever with valve disease → monthly benzathine penicillin for at least 10 years (or until 40).

frontHtml: Treat group A streptococcal pharyngitis to prevent rheumatic fever.
backHtml: strep throat → 10 days of amoxicillin or penicillin (primary prevention of rheumatic fever).

frontHtml: Order echocardiography to detect subclinical carditis in Sydenham chorea.
backHtml: Sydenham chorea → echocardiogram for silent carditis, then secondary prophylaxis.

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic rheumatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy with a β-blocker.
backHtml: symptomatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy → β-blocker (plus a diuretic).

frontHtml: Choose warfarin for secondary prevention in antiphospholipid syndrome with Libman–Sacks endocarditis.
backHtml: antiphospholipid syndrome with arterial thrombosis → warfarin, not a DOAC.

frontHtml: Treat nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis with heparin.
backHtml: NBTE with emboli → full-dose heparin.

frontHtml: Start glucocorticoids immediately in suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms.
backHtml: suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms → steroids now, biopsy later.

frontHtml: Diagnose Takayasu arteritis with vascular imaging.
backHtml: suspected Takayasu arteritis → MR or CT angiography.

frontHtml: Confirm carcinoid syndrome with 5-HIAA testing.
backHtml: flushing + diarrhea + right-sided valve disease → urine 5-HIAA.

frontHtml: Diagnose complete Kawasaki disease from the clinical criteria.
backHtml: 5+ days of fever + conjunctiva, mouth, rash, hands and feet, neck node = Kawasaki disease.

frontHtml: Treat Kawasaki disease with IVIG and aspirin.
backHtml: Kawasaki disease → IVIG + aspirin, then serial echocardiography.

frontHtml: Defer live vaccines after IVIG for Kawasaki disease.
backHtml: after Kawasaki IVIG, delay live vaccines about 11 months; give inactivated flu vaccine during aspirin therapy.

frontHtml: Explain molecular mimicry between the streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue in rheumatic fever.
backHtml: rheumatic fever = anti–M protein immunity cross-reacting with heart (molecular mimicry).

frontHtml: Identify Anitschkow cells within Aschoff bodies in rheumatic carditis.
backHtml: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells = rheumatic carditis.

frontHtml: Describe the valve pathology of chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis.
backHtml: rheumatic heart disease → commissural fusion → mitral stenosis.

frontHtml: Identify group A streptococcal pharyngitis as the trigger of rheumatic fever.
backHtml: throat → rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis; skin → glomerulonephritis only.

frontHtml: Associate Libman–Sacks endocarditis with antiphospholipid antibodies.
backHtml: Libman–Sacks = lupus/antiphospholipid, vegetations on both sides of the leaflet.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis in advanced cancer.
backHtml: cancer + sterile vegetations + multiple emboli = NBTE from hypercoagulability.

frontHtml: Explain why carcinoid heart disease affects mainly right-sided valves.
backHtml: carcinoid heart disease is right-sided because the lung inactivates serotonin.

frontHtml: Recognize coronary aneurysm as the major complication of Kawasaki disease.
backHtml: Kawasaki disease → coronary artery aneurysm, the reason for IVIG and serial echocardiography.

frontHtml: Identify the histology of Takayasu arteritis.
backHtml: granulomatous aortitis in a woman under 40 = Takayasu; over 50 = giant cell arteritis.

frontHtml: Identify tocilizumab as an IL-6 receptor antagonist used in giant cell arteritis.
backHtml: giant cell arteritis steroid-sparing therapy = tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor).

frontHtml: Explain the autoimmune mechanism of post-myocardial infarction pericarditis.
backHtml: pericarditis 1–6 weeks after MI = autoimmune Dressler syndrome; pericarditis in the first few days = direct extension of necrosis.

frontHtml: Choose prompt surgical excision for cardiac myxoma.
backHtml: diagnose myxoma, then remove it; there is no medical treatment.

frontHtml: Manage asymptomatic cardiac rhabdomyomas in infancy with observation.
backHtml: asymptomatic infant rhabdomyomas are watched, not removed.

frontHtml: Diagnose left atrial myxoma from constitutional, embolic and positional auscultatory findings.
backHtml: a culture-negative endocarditis picture with positional mitral findings is a myxoma until echocardiography says otherwise.

frontHtml: Recommend genetic evaluation and family screening for suspected Carney complex.
backHtml: familial myxoma syndromes require surveillance of the patient and screening of the family.

frontHtml: Choose excision for an embolizing papillary fibroelastoma.
backHtml: excise a papillary fibroelastoma that is symptomatic or mobile.

frontHtml: Recognize malignant pericardial tamponade.
backHtml: cancer + hypotension + JVD + pulsus paradoxus + electrical alternans = malignant tamponade; drain it.

frontHtml: Choose a pericardial window for recurrent malignant pericardial effusion.
backHtml: recurrent malignant effusion → definitive drainage (window or prolonged catheter), not repeated taps.

frontHtml: Order echocardiography for a suspected cardioembolic stroke in a young patient.
backHtml: embolic stroke in a young patient → echocardiography.

frontHtml: Distinguish atrial myxoma from other left atrial masses on echocardiography.
backHtml: septal stalk + left atrium + mobility = myxoma.

frontHtml: Plan echocardiographic surveillance after excision of a sporadic myxoma.
backHtml: after myxoma excision, follow with echocardiography; no adjuvant therapy is needed.

frontHtml: Identify the histology of a cardiac myxoma.
backHtml: myxoma = myxoma cells in a myxoid matrix, most often on the left atrial side of the septum.

frontHtml: Link the constitutional symptoms of cardiac myxoma to tumor secretion of interleukin-6.
backHtml: fever, weight loss and inflammatory labs with a left atrial mass point to IL-6 from a myxoma.

frontHtml: Connect cardiac rhabdomyoma with tuberous sclerosis and loss of mTOR inhibition.
backHtml: cardiac rhabdomyoma in an infant suggests tuberous sclerosis, a disorder of unchecked mTOR signalling.

frontHtml: Recognize Carney complex and its PRKAR1A protein kinase A defect.
backHtml: familial, multiple or recurrent myxomas with lentigines and endocrine tumors suggest Carney complex ( PRKAR1A ).

frontHtml: Recognize that metastases are the most common tumors of the heart.
backHtml: the most common tumor of the heart is a metastasis; the pericardium is the layer most often involved.

frontHtml: Identify melanoma as the cancer with the highest rate of cardiac metastasis.
backHtml: melanoma has the highest propensity for cardiac metastasis; lung and breast cancer give the most cases in absolute terms.

frontHtml: Explain the positional obstructive symptoms of a left atrial myxoma.
backHtml: positional symptoms of mitral obstruction in sinus rhythm suggest a mobile left atrial myxoma.

frontHtml: Predict the embolic destination of a right atrial tumor.
backHtml: right-sided tumors embolize to the lungs; left-sided tumors embolize to systemic organs such as the brain.

frontHtml: Recognize papillary fibroelastoma as an embolizing valve tumor.
backHtml: papillary fibroelastoma is a valve tumor of older adults that can cause stroke.

frontHtml: Identify cardiac angiosarcoma by site, behavior and endothelial markers.
backHtml: an invasive right atrial mass with hemorrhagic effusion and endothelial markers is angiosarcoma.

frontHtml: Choose a DOAC for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score.
backHtml: Nonvalvular AF with a high CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score: start a DOAC.

frontHtml: Select warfarin for atrial fibrillation associated with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
backHtml: AF with a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis requires warfarin, not a DOAC.

frontHtml: Treat unstable tachycardia with a pulse by synchronized cardioversion.
backHtml: Any tachycardia with a pulse that causes instability is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

frontHtml: Choose adenosine after failed vagal maneuvers for stable paroxysmal SVT.
backHtml: Stable paroxysmal SVT: vagal maneuvers first, then IV adenosine.

frontHtml: Recognize Mobitz type II AV block and its indication for permanent pacing.
backHtml: Mobitz II without a reversible cause is an indication for a permanent pacemaker.

frontHtml: Escalate from atropine to pacing in unstable complete heart block.
backHtml: Unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine: transcutaneous pacing, then transvenous pacing.

frontHtml: Treat drug-induced torsades de pointes with IV magnesium.
backHtml: Torsades de pointes with a pulse: IV magnesium, stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes.

frontHtml: Manage stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation without AV nodal blocking drugs.
backHtml: Pre-excited AF: procainamide or cardioversion; never AV nodal blockers.

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic tachy–brady syndrome with a permanent pacemaker before rate control.
backHtml: Tachy–brady syndrome with symptomatic pauses: pace first, then control the tachycardia.

frontHtml: Distinguish failure to capture from other pacemaker malfunctions.
backHtml: Spikes without capture soon after implantation suggest lead dislodgement.

frontHtml: Prioritize immediate defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation.
backHtml: Witnessed VF: defibrillate immediately, then resume compressions.

frontHtml: Give amiodarone for refractory ventricular fibrillation after the third shock.
backHtml: Refractory VF/pulseless VT after the third shock: amiodarone (or lidocaine).

frontHtml: Refer a resuscitated patient with ST elevation for emergent coronary angiography.
backHtml: ROSC with ST elevation: emergent coronary angiography, whether or not the patient is awake.

frontHtml: Localize Mobitz type I second-degree AV block to the AV node from its rhythm strip.
backHtml: Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat localizes block to the AV node, which is usually benign.

frontHtml: Explain the ECG triad of ventricular pre-excitation by an accessory pathway.
backHtml: Short PR + delta wave + slightly wide QRS = an accessory pathway pre-exciting the ventricle.

frontHtml: Identify use-dependent Na⁺ channel blockade by class IC antiarrhythmics.
backHtml: Rate-dependent QRS widening with little QT change is the hallmark of class IC sodium channel blockers.

frontHtml: Relate congenital long QT with deafness to loss of the slow delayed-rectifier potassium current.
backHtml: Long QT + congenital deafness = recessive loss of I Ks potassium current (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen).

frontHtml: Identify the funny current as the target of ivabradine and its effect on SA node automaticity.
backHtml: Ivabradine slows the sinus rate by blocking I f (HCN channels) without negative inotropy.

frontHtml: Link I Kr blockade by class III antiarrhythmics to phase 3 prolongation and QT lengthening.
backHtml: Class III drugs block K⁺ efflux in phase 3, prolonging repolarization and the QT interval.

frontHtml: Explain how adenosine terminates paroxysmal SVT.
backHtml: Adenosine causes seconds-long AV nodal block via A 1 -receptor-mediated K⁺ efflux, terminating AV node–dependent SVT.

frontHtml: Locate the circuit and curative ablation target of typical atrial flutter.
backHtml: Typical atrial flutter circles the tricuspid annulus; ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus cures it.

frontHtml: Trace the afferent and efferent limbs of the carotid sinus reflex.
backHtml: Carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents run in CN IX; the efferent bradycardia runs in CN X.

frontHtml: Add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist to complete guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF.
backHtml: HFrEF needs all four pillars (ARNI/ACEi/ARB, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) unless contraindicated.

frontHtml: Recognize non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as harmful in HFrEF.
backHtml: in HFrEF, swap diltiazem or verapamil for an evidence-based beta-blocker.

frontHtml: Use noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation for hypoxemic acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema in an alert patient.
backHtml: hypoxemic cardiogenic pulmonary edema in an awake patient → noninvasive ventilation plus nitrates and diuretic.

frontHtml: Treat low-output ('cold and wet') decompensated heart failure with an inotrope.
backHtml: cold and wet heart failure with borderline blood pressure → inotropic support (dobutamine or milrinone).

frontHtml: Recognize thyrotoxicosis as a cause of high-output heart failure.
backHtml: new atrial fibrillation with high-output failure and wide pulse pressure in a young adult → check thyroid function.

frontHtml: Apply the criteria for a primary-prevention ICD in HFrEF.
backHtml: EF ≤ 35%, NYHA II–III, ≥ 3 months of GDMT → primary-prevention ICD; add CRT only for wide QRS (especially LBBB ≥ 150 ms).

frontHtml: Manage hyperkalemia after starting a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist in HFrEF.
backHtml: potassium above 5.5 mEq/L on an MRA → hold or reduce the MRA and recheck soon.

frontHtml: Predict recovery of ventricular function in tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is largely reversible once the rate is controlled.

frontHtml: Choose an SGLT2 inhibitor to reduce hospitalization in HFpEF.
backHtml: SGLT2 inhibitors are a first-line drug class across the whole ejection-fraction range.

frontHtml: Describe how systolic dysfunction changes the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship and ventricular volumes.
backHtml: systolic dysfunction = flatter ESPVR, larger end-systolic volume, right-shifted loop.

frontHtml: Identify ventricular wall stretch as the stimulus for BNP secretion.
backHtml: BNP is a stretch signal from the ventricle; a normal level argues against heart failure.

frontHtml: Explain why an ACE inhibitor must be stopped 36 hours before a neprilysin inhibitor is started.
backHtml: never combine a neprilysin inhibitor with an ACE inhibitor; stop the ACE inhibitor 36 hours before starting sacubitril–valsartan.

frontHtml: Choose eplerenone when spironolactone causes antiandrogenic adverse effects in HFrEF.
backHtml: spironolactone-related gynecomastia → switch to eplerenone to keep the MRA benefit.

frontHtml: Link wet beriberi (high-output heart failure) to thiamine-dependent enzymes.
backHtml: warm, bounding high-output failure in a malnourished drinker = wet beriberi; give thiamine.

frontHtml: Explain how chronic alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
backHtml: chronic hypoxemic lung disease causes pulmonary hypertension through hypoxic vasoconstriction, leading to cor pulmonale; correcting hypoxemia with oxygen is the key therapy.

frontHtml: Recognize the giant v wave of acute mitral regurgitation from chordal rupture.
backHtml: acute MR = small stiff left atrium, giant v waves, sudden pulmonary edema, and a deceptively soft murmur.

frontHtml: Choose fibrinolysis followed by transfer when primary PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes.
backHtml: STEMI with expected PCI delay over 120 minutes → fibrinolysis within 30 minutes, then transfer.

frontHtml: Manage a hemodynamically stable NSTEMI with antithrombotic therapy and an early invasive strategy.
backHtml: stable NSTEMI → DAPT + anticoagulation + early (≤ 24 h) invasive strategy; no fibrinolysis.

frontHtml: Give fluids, not nitrates, for hypotension from right ventricular infarction.
backHtml: right ventricular infarction is preload-dependent: give fluids, avoid nitrates and diuretics.

frontHtml: Select vasodilator stress perfusion imaging for suspected ischemia in a patient with LBBB.
backHtml: LBBB or paced rhythm → vasodilator (not exercise) perfusion imaging.

frontHtml: Avoid nitrates after recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use.
backHtml: ask about PDE-5 inhibitors before giving any nitrate.

frontHtml: Intensify lipid-lowering therapy with ezetimibe when LDL remains high on a maximal statin after ACS.
backHtml: LDL still ≥ 70 mg/dL on maximal statin after ACS → add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor.

frontHtml: Choose primary PCI for STEMI presenting to a PCI-capable hospital.
backHtml: STEMI at a PCI-capable center → primary PCI, door-to-device ≤ 90 minutes.

frontHtml: Prescribe 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS treated with a stent.
backHtml: ACS + stent → DAPT for 12 months by default, then lifelong single antiplatelet therapy.

frontHtml: Localize an inferior STEMI on the ECG to the right coronary artery.
backHtml: inferior leads (II, III, aVF) → usually the right coronary artery; look for bradycardia, AV block and right ventricular involvement.

frontHtml: Relate the timing of free wall rupture to the macrophage phase of infarct healing.
backHtml: rupture of the free wall, septum or papillary muscle occurs while macrophages are clearing the infarct, roughly days 3–14.

frontHtml: Explain contraction band necrosis as a feature of reperfusion injury.
backHtml: contraction bands = calcium-driven hypercontraction of lethally injured myocytes after reperfusion.

frontHtml: Explain how nitrates relieve exertional angina by reducing preload.
backHtml: nitrates relieve stable angina mainly by venodilation → lower preload → lower wall stress and oxygen demand.

frontHtml: Explain clopidogrel resistance in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.
backHtml: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers cannot activate clopidogrel well.

frontHtml: Choose a calcium channel blocker for vasospastic angina based on its mechanism.
backHtml: vasospastic angina → calcium channel blocker (± nitrate); avoid non-selective beta-blockers.

frontHtml: Explain coronary steal during vasodilator stress perfusion imaging.
backHtml: vasodilator stress reveals stenoses by heterogeneity of flow, not by raising oxygen demand.

frontHtml: Use serial troponin kinetics to recognize reinfarction a few days after a myocardial infarction.
backHtml: Reinfarction is recognized by a new rise (> 20%) on serial troponin, not by a single elevated value.

frontHtml: Identify the features of a rupture-prone (vulnerable) atherosclerotic plaque.
backHtml: plaque vulnerability depends on cap thinness and inflammation more than on the degree of stenosis.

frontHtml: Select ICD placement for primary prevention of sudden death in high-risk hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: in HCM, an ICD (not antiarrhythmic drugs) prevents sudden death in patients with high-risk features such as unexplained syncope, family history of sudden death or wall thickness ≥30 mm.

frontHtml: Choose first-line pharmacotherapy for symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: obstructive HCM → β-blocker first; avoid vasodilators and diuretics that shrink the ventricle.

frontHtml: Counsel a patient with peripartum cardiomyopathy and persistent LV dysfunction about future pregnancy.
backHtml: peripartum cardiomyopathy with persistent LV dysfunction → advise against further pregnancy; relapse risk is highest when the EF has not recovered.

frontHtml: Identify abstinence as the key disease-modifying step in alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: in alcoholic cardiomyopathy, total abstinence plus standard HFrEF therapy is the intervention most likely to restore function.

frontHtml: Use urgent echocardiography to evaluate a new murmur with deterioration after myocardial infarction.
backHtml: new murmur + sudden deterioration after MI → urgent echocardiography.

frontHtml: Manage post-infarction papillary muscle rupture with emergency surgery and bridging support.
backHtml: acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture → mechanical support as a bridge to emergency surgery.

frontHtml: Interpret a right-heart oxygen step-up to diagnose post-infarction ventricular septal rupture.
backHtml: post-MI septal rupture = harsh LLSB murmur with thrill + O 2 step-up in the RV; confirm with echocardiography and arrange closure.

frontHtml: Treat hypotension in right ventricular infarction with volume rather than preload-lowering drugs.
backHtml: RV infarction is preload-dependent: give IV fluids and avoid nitrates, diuretics and morphine.

frontHtml: Manage left ventricular thrombus in a post-infarction aneurysm with oral anticoagulation.
backHtml: post-MI LV thrombus → oral anticoagulation; persistent ST elevation weeks after MI suggests an aneurysm.

frontHtml: Advise on return to competitive sport after acute myocarditis.
backHtml: myocarditis → no competitive sport for 3–6 months, then return only after normal reassessment.

frontHtml: Select disease-modifying therapy for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: ATTR cardiomyopathy (positive bone scan, no monoclonal protein) → transthyretin stabilizer plus diuretics.

frontHtml: Identify the sarcomere protein defect underlying hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: HCM = autosomal dominant sarcomere gene variant → myocyte disarray, asymmetric septal hypertrophy and risk of exertional sudden death.

frontHtml: Predict how manoeuvres that change ventricular volume alter the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: anything that enlarges the LV (handgrip, squatting, leg raise) softens the HCM murmur; anything that shrinks it (Valsalva, standing, vasodilators) makes it louder.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism and course of takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: takotsubo = stress-triggered catecholamine surge → transient apical ballooning with normal coronaries; recovery in weeks.

frontHtml: Recognize chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy and its causative organism.
backHtml: heart failure + RBBB + apical aneurysm + dysphagia in someone from rural Latin America = chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy.

frontHtml: Identify the precursor protein in senile (wild-type transthyretin) cardiac amyloidosis.
backHtml: thick walls + low voltage + carpal tunnel history in an older man with no monoclonal protein = ATTR amyloid cardiomyopathy.

frontHtml: Relate post-infarction papillary muscle rupture to coronary anatomy.
backHtml: inferior MI → posteromedial papillary muscle (single supply from the PDA) → rupture with acute MR at days 2–7.

frontHtml: Match the histology of a healing infarct to the timing of free wall rupture.
backHtml: rupture peaks when macrophages have cleared necrotic muscle but collagen has not yet formed (roughly days 3–14).

frontHtml: Recognize the histologic hallmark of viral myocarditis.
backHtml: viral myocarditis = lymphocytes plus myocyte necrosis; MRI enhancement is subepicardial or mid-wall rather than subendocardial.

frontHtml: Explain concentric hypertrophy as the myocyte response to pressure overload.
backHtml: pressure overload → sarcomeres in parallel → concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction; volume overload → sarcomeres in series → eccentric hypertrophy.

frontHtml: Treat uncomplicated acute pericarditis with an NSAID plus colchicine as an outpatient.
backHtml: uncomplicated acute pericarditis → NSAID + colchicine at home; reserve steroids for second line.

frontHtml: Choose aspirin for pericarditis early after myocardial infarction.
backHtml: pericarditis after MI → aspirin, not other NSAIDs or steroids.

frontHtml: Use bedside echocardiography to confirm suspected cardiac tamponade.
backHtml: suspected tamponade → immediate bedside echocardiography.

frontHtml: Treat cardiac tamponade with urgent pericardiocentesis.
backHtml: tamponade → drain the pericardium now; avoid diuretics, vasodilators and, when possible, positive-pressure ventilation before drainage.

frontHtml: Manage a recurrent malignant pericardial effusion with a pericardial window.
backHtml: recurrent malignant effusion → pericardial window (or extended drainage), not repeated taps.

frontHtml: Select pericardiectomy for chronic symptomatic constrictive pericarditis.
backHtml: chronic calcific constriction with symptoms despite diuretics → pericardiectomy.

frontHtml: Treat uremic pericarditis by intensifying dialysis.
backHtml: uremic pericarditis without tamponade → more dialysis.

frontHtml: Treat a hypothyroid pericardial effusion with thyroid hormone replacement.
backHtml: hypothyroid pericardial effusion without tamponade → treat the hypothyroidism, not the fluid.

frontHtml: Recognize the ECG pattern of acute pericarditis.
backHtml: diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression (with PR elevation in aVR) + pleuritic positional pain + rub = acute pericarditis.

frontHtml: Explain referred pericardial pain through phrenic nerve innervation.
backHtml: pericardial (and diaphragmatic) pain refers to the trapezius ridge via the phrenic nerve, C3–C5.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in cardiac tamponade.
backHtml: pulsus paradoxus in tamponade comes from inspiratory septal shift that steals left ventricular filling.

frontHtml: Relate the jugular venous waveform to the hemodynamics of cardiac tamponade.
backHtml: tamponade = equalized diastolic pressures + lost y descent; constriction = prominent y descent.

frontHtml: Explain the pericardial knock of constrictive pericarditis.
backHtml: constrictive pericarditis = Kussmaul sign + pericardial knock + calcified pericardium; radiation and cardiac surgery are common causes in high-income countries.

frontHtml: Identify fibrinous pericarditis as the typical lesion of uremia.
backHtml: uremic and post-infarction pericarditis are fibrinous; the rough fibrin surfaces produce the friction rub.

frontHtml: Explain the immune mechanism of post-infarction (Dressler) pericarditis.
backHtml: pericarditis 1–3 days after MI = local inflammation over the infarct; weeks after MI = autoimmune post-cardiac injury syndrome.

frontHtml: Interpret electrical alternans as a sign of a large pericardial effusion.
backHtml: electrical alternans + low voltage + tachycardia = large effusion, often with tamponade.

frontHtml: Recognize drug-induced lupus pericarditis and its antibody marker.
backHtml: pericarditis in a patient on hydralazine, procainamide or isoniazid with positive ANA and anti-histone antibodies = drug-induced lupus.

frontHtml: Choose TAVR for an older, higher-risk patient with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
backHtml: symptomatic severe AS → valve replacement; older or higher-risk patients with suitable anatomy → TAVR.

frontHtml: Evaluate a diastolic murmur with echocardiography.
backHtml: any diastolic murmur → echocardiography, even without symptoms.

frontHtml: Recognize an innocent Still murmur and reassure.
backHtml: soft, musical, position-dependent systolic murmur with normal S2 and pulses in a well child → innocent murmur, reassure.

frontHtml: Maintain warfarin, not a DOAC, for anticoagulation of a mechanical heart valve.
backHtml: mechanical valve → warfarin for life; never a DOAC.

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy with a β1-selective blocker.
backHtml: symptomatic MS in pregnancy → β 1 -selective blocker + careful diuretic; slow the heart to lengthen diastole.

frontHtml: Manage acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis with urgent surgery.
backHtml: acute severe AR with heart failure → urgent valve surgery; no balloon pump, no β-blockade.

frontHtml: Recommend valve replacement for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis with reduced ejection fraction.
backHtml: asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF <50% → valve replacement.

frontHtml: Refer asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation with early LV dysfunction for mitral valve repair.
backHtml: asymptomatic severe primary MR with LVEF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm → surgery; repair over replacement.

frontHtml: Apply endocarditis prophylaxis rules to a patient with an annuloplasty ring.
backHtml: annuloplasty rings, prosthetic valves and prior endocarditis → amoxicillin before gingival dental procedures.

frontHtml: Choose warfarin for atrial fibrillation in rheumatic mitral stenosis.
backHtml: AF + moderate/severe rheumatic MS → warfarin, regardless of risk score.

frontHtml: Identify dystrophic calcification as the mechanism of age-related aortic stenosis.
backHtml: calcific AS in older adults = dystrophic calcification (normal serum calcium) driven by the same risk factors as atherosclerosis.

frontHtml: Associate Turner syndrome with bicuspid aortic valve.
backHtml: Turner syndrome → bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation; an ejection click suggests a mobile bicuspid valve.

frontHtml: Predict the effect of ventricular volume on the click of mitral valve prolapse.
backHtml: less LV volume (standing, Valsalva) → earlier click and longer murmur in MVP; more volume (squatting, handgrip, leg raise) → later click.

frontHtml: Explain why a shorter S2–opening snap interval indicates more severe mitral stenosis.
backHtml: in MS, a shorter S2–OS interval = higher left atrial pressure = more severe stenosis.

frontHtml: Explain the wide pulse pressure of chronic aortic regurgitation.
backHtml: chronic AR = big stroke volume + diastolic runoff into the LV → wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses.

frontHtml: Explain molecular mimicry in rheumatic heart disease.
backHtml: rheumatic heart disease = molecular mimicry (type II) after group A strep pharyngitis; the mitral valve is affected most.

frontHtml: Explain right-sided valve involvement in carcinoid heart disease.
backHtml: carcinoid heart disease affects right-sided valves because the lungs inactivate serotonin.

frontHtml: Recognize mechanical hemolysis with schistocytes as a prosthetic valve complication.
backHtml: anemia with schistocytes and a negative Coombs test after valve surgery → mechanical hemolysis from a leak or prosthesis.

frontHtml: Explain acquired von Willebrand syndrome in severe aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome).
backHtml: AS + GI angiodysplasia bleeding → shear-induced loss of large vWF multimers; valve replacement helps.

frontHtml: Manage drug-induced orthostatic hypotension in an older adult by deprescribing.
backHtml: in an older adult with new orthostatic hypotension, stop the offending drug before adding treatment.

frontHtml: Diagnose neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from the heart-rate response.
backHtml: a large standing pressure fall with little heart-rate rise points to neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

frontHtml: Begin non-pharmacologic management of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: non-drug measures are the first treatment of symptomatic orthostatic hypotension once culprit drugs are removed.

frontHtml: Select pharmacotherapy for orthostatic hypotension refractory to non-drug measures.
backHtml: midodrine is a standard pressor for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension refractory to non-drug measures.

frontHtml: Manage supine hypertension in a patient treated for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: manage supine hypertension by avoiding late pressor doses and lying flat, not with daytime long-acting antihypertensives.

frontHtml: Order the initial evaluation for a patient with syncope.
backHtml: start syncope evaluation with history, examination including orthostatic vital signs, and a 12-lead ECG.

frontHtml: Interpret orthostatic vital signs and laboratory results to identify hypovolemic orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: orthostatic hypotension with a brisk heart-rate rise and prerenal laboratory findings indicates volume depletion.

frontHtml: Identify the clinical consequences of orthostatic hypotension in older adults.
backHtml: orthostatic hypotension in older adults predicts falls and fractures.

frontHtml: Diagnose multiple system atrophy as a cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with cerebellar signs and levodopa-unresponsive parkinsonism suggests multiple system atrophy.

frontHtml: Recommend dietary measures for postprandial hypotension in autonomic failure.
backHtml: postprandial hypotension is managed with small, low-refined-carbohydrate meals and avoiding alcohol.

frontHtml: Describe the baroreceptor reflex response to standing.
backHtml: a fall in arterial pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which triggers sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal.

frontHtml: Recognize multiple system atrophy as a cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and identify its histopathology.
backHtml: multiple system atrophy is an oligodendroglial α-synucleinopathy with early autonomic failure and poor levodopa response.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of orthostatic hypotension caused by α 1 antagonists.
backHtml: α 1 antagonists cause first-dose orthostatic hypotension through venous and arteriolar dilation.

frontHtml: Relate the flat heart-rate response in orthostatic hypotension to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
backHtml: orthostatic hypotension with almost no heart-rate rise in long-standing diabetes indicates autonomic neuropathy.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism and principal adverse effect of midodrine.
backHtml: midodrine is a peripheral α 1 agonist whose dose-limiting effect is supine hypertension.

frontHtml: Predict the electrolyte effect of fludrocortisone from its mechanism.
backHtml: fludrocortisone expands volume through mineralocorticoid action and causes hypokalemia.

frontHtml: Describe how droxidopa is converted to norepinephrine.
backHtml: droxidopa is decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to norepinephrine.

frontHtml: Recognize primary adrenal insufficiency as a cause of orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: primary adrenal insufficiency causes non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation.

frontHtml: Predict neurohormonal changes in hypovolemic orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: hypovolemic orthostatic hypotension activates renin with a brisk compensatory tachycardia.

frontHtml: Explain why aging increases susceptibility to orthostatic hypotension.
backHtml: older adults are prone to orthostatic hypotension because baroreflex sensitivity and other compensations decline with age.

frontHtml: Manage low-risk stage 1 hypertension.
backHtml: low-risk stage 1 hypertension starts with lifestyle modification and reassessment in 3–6 months.

frontHtml: Confirm the diagnosis of hypertension with out-of-office blood pressure measurement.
backHtml: confirm office hypertension with home or ambulatory readings, which also detect white-coat hypertension.

frontHtml: Choose an ACE inhibitor or ARB for hypertension with diabetic albuminuria.
backHtml: use an ACE inhibitor or ARB in hypertension with albuminuria.

frontHtml: Select an initial antihypertensive for a Black adult without compelling indications.
backHtml: for Black adults without CKD or heart failure, start with a thiazide-type diuretic or a calcium channel blocker.

frontHtml: Screen for primary aldosteronism in resistant hypertension with hypokalemia.
backHtml: resistant hypertension, especially with hypokalemia, calls for an aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

frontHtml: Manage hypertensive emergency with controlled IV pressure reduction.
backHtml: hypertensive emergency: titratable IV drug, reduce mean pressure by ≤ 25% in the first hour.

frontHtml: Manage severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage.
backHtml: severe hypertension without acute organ damage is treated with oral therapy and close follow-up, not rapid IV lowering.

frontHtml: Calculate the number needed to treat from a trial's event rates.
backHtml: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction.

frontHtml: Identify limits of external validity in a randomized trial.
backHtml: exclusion criteria limit the generalizability (external validity) of trial results.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of ACE inhibitor-induced cough.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema come from bradykinin accumulation.

frontHtml: Predict electrolyte and metabolic effects of thiazide diuretics.
backHtml: thiazides lower urinary calcium and can raise serum calcium, a useful effect in calcium stone formers.

frontHtml: Distinguish primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism using renin and aldosterone.
backHtml: primary aldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin.

frontHtml: Identify the arteriolar pathology of malignant hypertension.
backHtml: malignant hypertension produces hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis.

frontHtml: Recognize fibromuscular dysplasia as a cause of renovascular hypertension.
backHtml: fibromuscular dysplasia is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic arteriopathy that causes renovascular hypertension in young women.

frontHtml: Explain why α blockade must precede β blockade in pheochromocytoma.
backHtml: in pheochromocytoma, give α blockade before β blockade to avoid unopposed α 1 vasoconstriction.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker-induced edema.
backHtml: dihydropyridine CCB edema results from arteriolar-dominant dilation raising capillary hydrostatic pressure.

frontHtml: Prescribe high-intensity statin therapy after an acute coronary syndrome.
backHtml: after acute coronary syndrome, start a high-intensity statin.

frontHtml: Recommend cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia.
backHtml: suspected familial hypercholesterolemia calls for cascade testing of first-degree relatives.

frontHtml: Apply statin therapy to adults aged 40–75 with diabetes.
backHtml: adults aged 40–75 with diabetes should take at least a moderate-intensity statin.

frontHtml: Manage statin-associated muscle symptoms with a normal creatine kinase.
backHtml: for mild statin muscle symptoms with normal CK, pause and rechallenge rather than abandon statin therapy.

frontHtml: Treat severe hypertriglyceridemia to prevent pancreatitis.
backHtml: severe hypertriglyceridemia (about ≥ 1,000 mg/dL) is treated with a fibrate plus removal of secondary causes to prevent pancreatitis.

frontHtml: Identify hypothyroidism as a secondary cause of hypercholesterolemia.
backHtml: exclude hypothyroidism (TSH) in new hypercholesterolemia.

frontHtml: Add ezetimibe for LDL above goal on maximal statin therapy.
backHtml: add ezetimibe when LDL is above goal on a maximally tolerated statin.

frontHtml: Escalate to a PCSK9 inhibitor for persistent LDL elevation after MI.
backHtml: add a PCSK9 inhibitor when LDL remains above goal on statin plus ezetimibe in very-high-risk ASCVD.

frontHtml: Choose dietary management for familial chylomicronemia syndrome.
backHtml: familial chylomicronemia is managed with a very-low-fat diet, using medium-chain triglycerides for calories.

frontHtml: Explain how statins lower plasma LDL cholesterol.
backHtml: statins lower plasma LDL mainly by up-regulating hepatic LDL receptors.

frontHtml: Identify the genetic defect in familial hypercholesterolemia.
backHtml: familial hypercholesterolemia: autosomal dominant LDL-receptor defect with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease.

frontHtml: Recognize familial chylomicronemia from lipoprotein lipase deficiency.
backHtml: LPL (or apoC-II) deficiency causes chylomicronemia with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.

frontHtml: Identify dysbetalipoproteinemia and its apolipoprotein E genotype.
backHtml: dysbetalipoproteinemia: apoE2/E2 plus a second hit, remnant accumulation and palmar xanthomas.

frontHtml: Link abetalipoproteinemia to fat-soluble vitamin E deficiency.
backHtml: abetalipoproteinemia (MTP deficiency) causes fat malabsorption, acanthocytes and vitamin E-deficiency neurologic disease.

frontHtml: Explain the CYP3A4 interaction that causes statin-induced rhabdomyolysis.
backHtml: CYP3A4 inhibitors raise simvastatin levels and can precipitate rhabdomyolysis.

frontHtml: Identify the mediator of niacin-induced flushing.
backHtml: niacin flushing is prostaglandin-mediated and is reduced by aspirin.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of PCSK9 inhibitors.
backHtml: PCSK9 antibodies increase LDL-receptor recycling.

frontHtml: Choose CT angiography to confirm suspected aortic dissection in a hemodynamically stable patient.
backHtml: Stable patient with suspected dissection → CT angiography; unstable patient → transesophageal echo at the bedside.

frontHtml: Start an intravenous beta-blocker as first-line medical therapy for uncomplicated type B aortic dissection.
backHtml: In aortic dissection, give an intravenous beta-blocker first for rate control, then a vasodilator if pressure stays high.

frontHtml: Recognize complicated type B dissection and choose endovascular repair.
backHtml: Malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion or refractory pain makes a type B dissection 'complicated' and calls for urgent (usually endovascular) repair.

frontHtml: Choose transesophageal echocardiography for an unstable patient with suspected aortic dissection.
backHtml: Unstable suspected aortic dissection → TEE where the patient is (ideally the operating room), not a trip to CT.

frontHtml: Select one-time abdominal ultrasonography for AAA screening in a man aged 65–75 who has smoked.
backHtml: AAA screening: one abdominal ultrasound for men 65–75 who have ever smoked.

frontHtml: Manage a small, slowly growing abdominal aortic aneurysm with surveillance and smoking cessation.
backHtml: Asymptomatic AAA below ~5.5 cm (men) with slow growth → surveillance and smoking cessation, not repair.

frontHtml: Send a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected ruptured AAA directly for operative repair.
backHtml: Hypotension + pain + pulsatile mass in an older smoker = ruptured AAA → straight to repair.

frontHtml: Identify superior vena cava obstruction from facial plethora and upper-body venous distension.
backHtml: SVC obstruction raises venous pressure in the head, neck and both arms, producing facial plethora and chest-wall collaterals.

frontHtml: Recognize tamponade from hemopericardium as the fatal complication of type A aortic dissection.
backHtml: Ascending aortic dissection most often kills by rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade.

frontHtml: Link Marfan syndrome to fibrillin-1 and cystic medial degeneration of the aorta.
backHtml: Marfan syndrome = fibrillin-1 defect → cystic medial degeneration of the aortic root → aneurysm and dissection.

frontHtml: Identify cystic medial degeneration as the histology of hypertensive or age-related ascending aortic aneurysm.
backHtml: Ascending aortic aneurysm with hypertension or aging = cystic medial degeneration.

frontHtml: Relate the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve under the aortic arch to hoarseness from an arch aneurysm.
backHtml: Hoarseness from a left vocal fold palsy can be the presenting sign of an aortic arch aneurysm.

frontHtml: Describe the vasa vasorum endarteritis of tertiary syphilitic aortitis and its link to aortic regurgitation.
backHtml: Syphilitic aortitis = endarteritis of the vasa vasorum → ascending aortic aneurysm with aortic regurgitation.

frontHtml: Recognize vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and its type III collagen defect.
backHtml: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1, type III collagen) causes spontaneous arterial rupture in young adults.

frontHtml: Explain the proteolytic, inflammatory mechanism of abdominal aortic aneurysm.
backHtml: AAA = inflammation-driven proteolysis of medial elastin and collagen, promoted by smoking.

frontHtml: Apply the law of Laplace to explain rising wall tension in an enlarging aneurysm.
backHtml: Laplace: wall tension rises in proportion to radius, so aneurysms beget further dilation.

frontHtml: Explain how a proximal aortic dissection can produce an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
backHtml: Inferior STEMI with back pain and an inter-arm pressure gap suggests a type A dissection involving the right coronary ostium.

frontHtml: Prescribe supervised exercise as first-line therapy for intermittent claudication.
backHtml: Claudication: optimize risk factors, then a supervised exercise program before drugs or revascularization.

frontHtml: Interpret an ABI above 1.40 and choose the toe-brachial index.
backHtml: ABI > 1.40 = noncompressible vessels → measure the toe-brachial index.

frontHtml: Add cilostazol for persistent claudication when there is no heart failure.
backHtml: Persistent claudication after exercise therapy → add cilostazol if there is no heart failure.

frontHtml: Start immediate intravenous heparin for acute limb ischemia before urgent revascularization.
backHtml: Acute limb ischemia: give IV heparin at once, then revascularize urgently according to limb viability.

frontHtml: Recognize chronic limb-threatening ischemia and arrange revascularization.
backHtml: Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulcer, gangrene) → urgent imaging and revascularization.

frontHtml: Diagnose atheroembolic disease after an arterial procedure.
backHtml: Blue toes with good pulses, livedo, eosinophilia and delayed AKI after catheterization = atheroembolism.

frontHtml: Choose early carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic severe carotid stenosis.
backHtml: Symptomatic 70–99% carotid stenosis → endarterectomy within about 2 weeks (plus best medical therapy).

frontHtml: Evaluate suspected secondary Raynaud phenomenon with antinuclear antibody testing.
backHtml: Raynaud with ulcers, sclerodactyly or late onset → test ANA (and nailfold capillaries) for a connective-tissue disease.

frontHtml: Diagnose chronic mesenteric ischemia with CT angiography.
backHtml: Postprandial pain + food fear + weight loss in a vasculopath = chronic mesenteric ischemia → CT angiography.

frontHtml: Identify the fatty streak as intimal foam cells, the earliest lesion of atherosclerosis.
backHtml: The fatty streak = intimal foam cells; it is the earliest lesion of atherosclerosis.

frontHtml: Explain the role of migrated smooth muscle cells in forming the fibrous cap of an atheroma.
backHtml: Intimal smooth muscle cells build the fibrous cap; macrophage proteases weaken it.

frontHtml: Describe the pathogenesis of hyaline arteriolosclerosis in hypertension and diabetes.
backHtml: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis = plasma-protein leakage plus excess matrix, from chronic hypertension and diabetes.

frontHtml: Distinguish Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis from atherosclerosis.
backHtml: Pipe-stem medial calcification (Mönckeberg) does not obstruct flow but makes arteries noncompressible.

frontHtml: Recognize atheroembolic disease after vascular procedures and its biopsy finding.
backHtml: Blue toes + livedo + AKI after catheterization, with pulses present → cholesterol emboli (needle-shaped clefts).

frontHtml: Identify tobacco as the driver of thromboangiitis obliterans.
backHtml: Buerger disease is driven by tobacco; complete cessation is the only effective treatment.

frontHtml: Choose a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for primary Raynaud phenomenon and explain its vascular selectivity.
backHtml: Raynaud phenomenon: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (vascular-selective) are first-line drugs.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of cilostazol and its contraindication in heart failure.
backHtml: Cilostazol (PDE3 inhibitor) improves claudication but is contraindicated in heart failure.

frontHtml: Explain how CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles reduce the effect of clopidogrel.
backHtml: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers cannot activate clopidogrel well, so platelet inhibition and protection fall.

frontHtml: Predict the renin–aldosterone pattern of renovascular hypertension from fibromuscular dysplasia.
backHtml: Renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia) → high renin and high aldosterone.

frontHtml: Use compression ultrasonography directly when pretest probability of DVT is high.
backHtml: DVT likely → compression ultrasound; DVT unlikely → D-dimer first.

frontHtml: Choose a direct oral anticoagulant for uncomplicated proximal DVT.
backHtml: Uncomplicated proximal DVT → a DOAC for most patients.

frontHtml: Set a 3-month duration of anticoagulation for VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor.
backHtml: First VTE provoked by surgery or another major transient factor → 3 months of anticoagulation.

frontHtml: Use D-dimer testing to exclude DVT when pretest probability is low.
backHtml: Low pretest probability of DVT → D-dimer; a negative result rules DVT out.

frontHtml: Recognize when an inferior vena cava filter is indicated for DVT.
backHtml: Acute proximal DVT + contraindication to anticoagulation → IVC filter; anticoagulate later when safe.

frontHtml: Manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia by stopping heparin and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant.
backHtml: Suspected HIT: stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant before results return.

frontHtml: Manage limited superficial thrombophlebitis conservatively.
backHtml: Small catheter-related superficial thrombophlebitis → warm compresses and NSAIDs.

frontHtml: Recognize phlegmasia cerulea dolens.
backHtml: Massive, blue, painful swollen leg = phlegmasia cerulea dolens (iliofemoral DVT) → urgent clot removal.

frontHtml: Choose pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a high-risk medical inpatient.
backHtml: Medical inpatient at increased VTE risk and low bleeding risk → prophylactic LMWH or UFH.

frontHtml: Treat a venous leg ulcer with compression after confirming adequate arterial supply.
backHtml: Venous ulcer with normal ABI → compression therapy (check the ABI first).

frontHtml: Choose LMWH for venous thromboembolism during pregnancy.
backHtml: VTE in pregnancy → LMWH; avoid warfarin (teratogenic) and DOACs.

frontHtml: Select anticoagulation for cancer-associated deep vein thrombosis.
backHtml: Cancer-associated VTE → LMWH or a DOAC, continued while the cancer is active.

frontHtml: Identify venous stasis as the main mechanism of travel-related deep vein thrombosis.
backHtml: Long-haul travel or immobility = stasis, one limb of the Virchow triad.

frontHtml: Explain the molecular basis of factor V Leiden.
backHtml: Factor V Leiden: factor Va resists activated protein C → venous thrombosis.

frontHtml: Describe how the prothrombin G20210A variant increases thrombotic risk.
backHtml: Prothrombin G20210A (3′ UTR) → more prothrombin → venous thrombosis.

frontHtml: Explain warfarin-induced skin necrosis through differential half-lives of vitamin K-dependent proteins.
backHtml: Warfarin skin necrosis: protein C falls before the long-lived procoagulant factors → transient hypercoagulability.

frontHtml: Link heparin resistance to antithrombin deficiency.
backHtml: Heparin needs antithrombin; inherited antithrombin deficiency causes thrombosis with heparin resistance.

frontHtml: Explain why low-molecular-weight heparin acts mainly against factor Xa.
backHtml: LMWH = mostly anti-Xa because short chains cannot bridge antithrombin to thrombin.

frontHtml: Describe the immune mechanism of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
backHtml: HIT: IgG to heparin–PF4 → platelet activation → thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, 5–10 days after starting heparin.

frontHtml: Match idarucizumab to dabigatran reversal.
backHtml: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors.

frontHtml: Describe the decoy mechanism of andexanet alfa.
backHtml: Andexanet alfa is a decoy Xa that soaks up direct factor Xa inhibitors.

frontHtml: Explain the hemosiderin pigmentation of chronic venous insufficiency.
backHtml: Brown skin of chronic venous insufficiency = hemosiderin from extravasated red cells.

frontHtml: Recognize Trousseau syndrome as a sign of occult visceral adenocarcinoma.
backHtml: Migratory thrombophlebitis + weight loss (± new diabetes) → look for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

frontHtml: Diagnose cardiac tamponade after penetrating chest trauma.
backHtml: stab wound in the cardiac box + hypotension + distended neck veins + equal breath sounds → tamponade.

frontHtml: Manage penetrating cardiac injury with tamponade by immediate surgical repair.
backHtml: penetrating cardiac injury with tamponade → operating room, not a needle.

frontHtml: Identify the indication for resuscitative thoracotomy in penetrating chest trauma.
backHtml: penetrating chest trauma with recent loss of pulses → resuscitative thoracotomy.

frontHtml: Screen for blunt cardiac injury with an ECG and troponin.
backHtml: screen blunt chest trauma with ECG + troponin; normal both → BCI excluded.

frontHtml: Admit stable patients with blunt cardiac injury and ECG changes for continuous monitoring.
backHtml: blunt cardiac injury with ECG changes, stable → monitored bed, not angiography or antiarrhythmics.

frontHtml: Choose CT angiography to diagnose blunt thoracic aortic injury in a stable patient.
backHtml: suspected blunt aortic injury in a stable patient → CT angiography of the chest.

frontHtml: Begin anti-impulse therapy with an IV beta-blocker in contained blunt aortic injury.
backHtml: contained blunt aortic injury → IV beta-blocker first (esmolol), then a vasodilator if needed, then TEVAR.

frontHtml: Prioritize control of active hemorrhage over repair of a contained blunt aortic injury.
backHtml: with multiple injuries, treat active hemorrhage first; repair a contained aortic tear once the patient is stable, and never beta-block a patient in hemorrhagic shock.

frontHtml: Treat suspected commotio cordis with immediate CPR and defibrillation.
backHtml: collapse after a chest blow in sport → CPR and AED immediately.

frontHtml: Recognize and confirm tamponade from iatrogenic ventricular puncture.
backHtml: new shock after a pacing lead or catheter procedure → echocardiography for perforation and tamponade.

frontHtml: Identify the right ventricle as the anterior-most cardiac chamber.
backHtml: anterior chest wounds most often injure the right ventricle.

frontHtml: Link the site of blunt aortic injury to the embryology of the ligamentum arteriosum.
backHtml: isthmus tears occur at the ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the ductus arteriosus (left sixth arch).

frontHtml: Explain why deceleration injures the aorta at the isthmus.
backHtml: blunt aortic injury happens where a mobile segment meets a fixed one.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in cardiac tamponade.
backHtml: pulsus paradoxus reflects exaggerated ventricular interdependence when the pericardium cannot expand.

frontHtml: Relate commotio cordis to the vulnerable period of ventricular repolarization.
backHtml: commotio cordis = chest blow during the vulnerable period of repolarization → VF; treat with immediate defibrillation.

frontHtml: Recognize equalization of diastolic pressures in cardiac tamponade.
backHtml: equalized, raised diastolic pressures across all chambers = tamponade (constriction can look similar).

frontHtml: Explain obstructive shock in tamponade as a failure of diastolic filling.
backHtml: tamponade lowers output by restricting diastolic filling, not by weakening the heart.

frontHtml: Describe the layers crossed during subxiphoid pericardiocentesis.
backHtml: pericardial fluid lies between the parietal (fused to fibrous) and visceral serous layers; the right ventricle is the structure at risk beyond it.

frontHtml: Recognize radiographic signs of blunt thoracic aortic injury.
backHtml: after deceleration injury, a widened mediastinum or obscured aortic knob → CT angiography.

frontHtml: Start prostaglandin E1 in a newborn with suspected duct-dependent cyanotic heart disease.
backHtml: suspected duct-dependent cyanotic heart disease → start alprostadil now.

frontHtml: Diagnose coarctation of the aorta from an arm–leg pressure gradient and radiofemoral delay.
backHtml: in young hypertensive patients, always compare arm and leg pulses and pressures.

frontHtml: Manage a hypercyanotic spell in tetralogy of Fallot.
backHtml: tet spell → knee-chest and oxygen first; avoid inotropes.

frontHtml: Manage a small asymptomatic ventricular septal defect with observation.
backHtml: the loudness of a VSD murmur does not track its size; small, asymptomatic VSDs are observed.

frontHtml: Select transcatheter closure for a hemodynamically significant secundum ASD.
backHtml: secundum ASD + RV enlargement + normal PVR → device closure.

frontHtml: Choose PFO closure after a cryptogenic stroke in a younger adult with a high-risk PFO.
backHtml: young cryptogenic stroke + high-risk PFO → PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy.

frontHtml: Confirm a suspected PDA in a preterm infant with echocardiography.
backHtml: suspect PDA in a preterm infant → echocardiography before treatment.

frontHtml: Choose a COX inhibitor to close a hemodynamically significant PDA in a preterm infant.
backHtml: preterm PDA needing closure → ibuprofen or indomethacin if no contraindication.

frontHtml: Recognize a fixed split second heart sound as the sign of an atrial septal defect.
backHtml: fixed split S 2 = ASD.

frontHtml: Relate tetralogy of Fallot to anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.
backHtml: tetralogy of Fallot = malaligned outlet septum (neural crest/conotruncal defect).

frontHtml: Explain transposition of the great arteries as failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral.
backHtml: a non-spiralling aorticopulmonary septum gives transposition; maternal diabetes is a classic association.

frontHtml: Link Down syndrome to endocardial cushion (AV septal) defects.
backHtml: Down syndrome → AV septal defect → endocardial cushions.

frontHtml: Explain how COX inhibitors close a patent ductus arteriosus.
backHtml: COX inhibitors close a PDA; PGE 1 (alprostadil) keeps it open.

frontHtml: Explain shunt reversal in Eisenmenger syndrome.
backHtml: late cyanosis with a softening murmur and loud P 2 in an unrepaired shunt = Eisenmenger syndrome.

frontHtml: Recognize anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery as a cause of infant myocardial ischemia.
backHtml: infant + feeding-related distress + Q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6 = anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery.

frontHtml: Use benzodiazepines first in cocaine-associated chest pain.
backHtml: Cocaine chest pain: aspirin plus benzodiazepines first; avoid β-blockers during acute intoxication.

frontHtml: Order baseline LV function assessment before anthracycline chemotherapy.
backHtml: Obtain a baseline echocardiogram before anthracycline therapy.

frontHtml: Manage a significant LVEF decline during trastuzumab therapy.
backHtml: A significant asymptomatic EF drop on trastuzumab: hold the drug, treat, reimage in weeks, and consider restarting.

frontHtml: Choose safe antihypertensive therapy after ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema.
backHtml: After ACE inhibitor angioedema, never use any ACE inhibitor or sacubitril-valsartan; choose another class.

frontHtml: Switch from an ACE inhibitor to an ARB for ACE inhibitor–induced cough.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB, especially when RAS blockade is needed (albuminuria, HFrEF).

frontHtml: Recognize chronic digoxin toxicity and its indications for digoxin-specific antibody fragments.
backHtml: Life-threatening digoxin toxicity (bradyarrhythmia, hypotension, hyperkalemia): give digoxin Fab.

frontHtml: Manage dose-related dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker edema.
backHtml: Treat amlodipine edema by lowering the dose and adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB, not by adding a diuretic.

frontHtml: Choose a non–QT-prolonging antibiotic in a patient with methadone-associated QT prolongation.
backHtml: When the QTc is already prolonged, choose non–QT-prolonging alternatives; for chlamydia that is doxycycline.

frontHtml: Identify dexrazoxane as the cardioprotective agent for anthracycline therapy.
backHtml: Dexrazoxane protects against anthracycline cardiomyopathy.

frontHtml: Contrast the mechanism and reversibility of trastuzumab cardiotoxicity with anthracycline toxicity.
backHtml: Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is HER2-mediated dysfunction that usually reverses after the drug is held.

frontHtml: Recognize cocaine-associated myocardial ischemia and the drug's mechanism.
backHtml: Cocaine blocks catecholamine reuptake, causing coronary vasoconstriction and increased myocardial oxygen demand.

frontHtml: Explain the bradykinin mechanism of ACE inhibitor angioedema.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated.

frontHtml: Explain hyperkalemia from renin–angiotensin–aldosterone blockade at the level of the principal cell.
backHtml: RAAS blockers and aldosterone antagonists cause hyperkalemia by reducing principal-cell K⁺ secretion.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of dihydropyridine-induced peripheral edema.
backHtml: Dihydropyridine edema comes from precapillary arteriolar dilation, so it responds poorly to diuretics.

frontHtml: Identify minoxidil's mechanism from its characteristic adverse effects.
backHtml: Minoxidil opens K ATP channels; expect hypertrichosis, fluid retention and reflex tachycardia.

frontHtml: Explain the P-glycoprotein interaction between amiodarone and digoxin.
backHtml: Amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine and clarithromycin raise digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein.

frontHtml: Recognize first-dose orthostatic hypotension from α1-adrenergic blockade.
backHtml: First-dose orthostatic syncope is the classic adverse effect of α 1 blockers.

frontHtml: Recognize 5-fluorouracil–induced coronary vasospasm.
backHtml: Fluoropyrimidines cause coronary vasospasm with transient ST elevation and normal coronaries.

frontHtml: Choose rapid antigen testing for a child with features suggesting streptococcal pharyngitis.
backHtml: With features suggesting streptococcal pharyngitis, test first (rapid antigen test, culture back-up in children) and treat only a positive result.

frontHtml: Select treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis in a patient with penicillin anaphylaxis.
backHtml: GAS pharyngitis with penicillin anaphylaxis: clindamycin or a macrolide; cephalexin only for non-anaphylactic allergy.

frontHtml: Manage a peritonsillar abscess with drainage and antibiotics.
backHtml: Peritonsillar abscess needs drainage plus antibiotics covering streptococci and anaerobes.

frontHtml: Prioritize controlled airway management in suspected epiglottitis.
backHtml: Suspected epiglottitis: do nothing that upsets the child; secure the airway in a controlled setting first.

frontHtml: Advise activity restriction to prevent splenic rupture in infectious mononucleosis.
backHtml: Mononucleosis: no contact sports for at least 3–4 weeks and until the spleen is normal.

frontHtml: Manage acute viral rhinosinusitis without antibiotics or imaging.
backHtml: Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral; antibiotics only for persistent (10+ days), severe-onset or double-worsening illness.

frontHtml: Treat rhino-orbital mucormycosis with urgent debridement and amphotericin B.
backHtml: Mucormycosis: debride urgently, start amphotericin B at once, reverse the predisposing condition.

frontHtml: Recommend Tdap during each pregnancy to prevent infant pertussis.
backHtml: Give Tdap in every pregnancy, ideally at 27–36 weeks, to protect the newborn.

frontHtml: Identify group A Streptococcus by its hemolysis pattern and bacitracin sensitivity.
backHtml: Group A Streptococcus is beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative and bacitracin-sensitive.

frontHtml: Explain the immune-complex mechanism of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
backHtml: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex (type III) disease with low C3 that appears 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis.

frontHtml: Identify the cell type behind atypical lymphocytosis in infectious mononucleosis.
backHtml: Atypical lymphocytes in mononucleosis are reactive CD8+ T cells, not infected B cells.

frontHtml: Name the receptor Epstein–Barr virus uses to enter B cells.
backHtml: EBV binds CD21 on B cells.

frontHtml: Relate the Hib conjugate vaccine antigen to prevention of epiglottitis.
backHtml: The Hib vaccine is a PRP capsule conjugated to protein, which lets infants respond.

frontHtml: Localize the airway narrowing responsible for the signs of croup.
backHtml: Croup narrows the subglottic airway, giving a barking cough and inspiratory stridor (steeple sign).

frontHtml: Recognize the histology of rhinocerebral mucormycosis in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis.
backHtml: Mucormycosis: DKA plus black necrotic sinus tissue; broad non-septate hyphae that invade vessels.

frontHtml: Recognize the lymphocytosis of pertussis in an adolescent with waning immunity.
backHtml: Pertussis causes lymphocytosis; adolescents lose vaccine immunity and need a Tdap booster.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of the immediate phase of allergic rhinitis.
backHtml: Allergic rhinitis begins with allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells (type I hypersensitivity).

frontHtml: Recognize myocarditis as the major toxin-mediated complication of pharyngeal diphtheria.
backHtml: Diphtheria: gray adherent pseudomembrane, and its toxin causes myocarditis and neuropathy.

frontHtml: Trace the fascial pathway by which retropharyngeal infection reaches the mediastinum.
backHtml: The danger space links retropharyngeal infection to the posterior mediastinum.

frontHtml: Choose outpatient empiric therapy for low-risk community-acquired pneumonia.
backHtml: Healthy outpatient with CAP and no risk factors: oral amoxicillin (or doxycycline); keep fluoroquinolones for patients with comorbidities.

frontHtml: Choose empiric antibiotics for severe community-acquired pneumonia without resistance risk factors.
backHtml: Severe CAP: beta-lactam plus macrolide (or plus fluoroquinolone); add MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage only for specific risk factors.

frontHtml: Select empiric therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia with risk factors for resistant organisms.
backHtml: VAP with resistance risk: MRSA coverage plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, then de-escalate by cultures.

frontHtml: Order the rapid confirmatory test for suspected Legionella pneumonia.
backHtml: Severe pneumonia with hyponatremia, diarrhea and water exposure: send a Legionella urine antigen.

frontHtml: Manage suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis with isolation and sputum testing.
backHtml: Suspected active TB: isolate first, then three sputum samples for smear, culture and NAAT before therapy.

frontHtml: Treat latent tuberculosis infection with a preferred short rifamycin-based regimen.
backHtml: Positive IGRA + no symptoms + normal x-ray = latent TB; treat with a short rifamycin-based regimen.

frontHtml: Treat moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia with TMP-SMX and adjunctive glucocorticoids.
backHtml: PJP with PaO2 < 70 mm Hg or A–a gradient ≥ 35: TMP-SMX plus prednisone.

frontHtml: Treat influenza in high-risk patients with a neuraminidase inhibitor regardless of symptom duration.
backHtml: High-risk patients with influenza get oseltamivir even after 48 hours of symptoms.

frontHtml: Manage mild bronchiolitis in an infant with supportive care.
backHtml: Bronchiolitis is diagnosed clinically and treated supportively; no routine x-ray, bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics.

frontHtml: Start standard four-drug therapy for drug-susceptible active pulmonary tuberculosis.
backHtml: Active drug-susceptible TB: 2 months of four drugs, then 4 months of isoniazid plus rifampin, with pyridoxine.

frontHtml: Manage hepatotoxicity during tuberculosis treatment.
backHtml: TB drug hepatitis: stop the hepatotoxic drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide), then rechallenge one at a time.

frontHtml: Explain why beta-lactams fail against Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
backHtml: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so beta-lactams cannot work and Gram stain shows nothing.

frontHtml: Identify Legionella pneumonia and its culture requirements.
backHtml: Legionella: water source, hyponatremia, diarrhea; few organisms on Gram stain; grows on charcoal yeast extract with cysteine and iron.

frontHtml: Recognize the histological stages of lobar pneumonia.
backHtml: Red hepatization = neutrophils + red cells + fibrin filling alveoli at about days 2–3 of lobar pneumonia.

frontHtml: Explain the cell-mediated immune response that contains primary tuberculosis.
backHtml: Containment of TB depends on the IL-12 → Th1 → interferon-gamma → activated macrophage axis, with TNF holding granulomas together.

frontHtml: Link isoniazid neuropathy to pyridoxine depletion and its prevention.
backHtml: Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in malnourished or alcohol-using patients.

frontHtml: Match ethambutol optic neuritis to the drug's mechanism.
backHtml: Ethambutol: arabinosyltransferase inhibitor; watch for optic neuritis with red-green color loss.

frontHtml: Identify coccidioidomycosis by geography and tissue form.
backHtml: Spherules with endospores + southwestern US dust + erythema nodosum = Coccidioides.

frontHtml: Recognize invasive aspergillosis in neutropenia and its tissue morphology.
backHtml: Invasive aspergillosis: neutropenia + halo sign; septate hyphae branching at acute angles that invade vessels.

frontHtml: Identify Pneumocystis pneumonia and the mechanism of its first-line drug.
backHtml: Pneumocystis is treated with TMP-SMX (two sequential folate-synthesis steps); its membrane lacks ergosterol.

frontHtml: Predict the site of aspiration lung abscess from the patient's position.
backHtml: Supine aspiration lands in the posterior upper-lobe or superior lower-lobe segments, usually on the right.

frontHtml: Obtain prior imaging as the first step in evaluating an incidental pulmonary nodule.
backHtml: old images first: they are cheap, safe and often settle the question.

frontHtml: Recognize benign CT features of a pulmonary nodule that end the workup.
backHtml: benign calcification or fat in a nodule = reassure; no follow-up is needed.

frontHtml: Apply size and risk to decide that a tiny incidental nodule needs no follow-up.
backHtml: tiny solid nodule + low-risk patient = no follow-up.

frontHtml: Choose PET-CT for a new solid nodule with intermediate probability of malignancy.
backHtml: new solid nodule over 8 mm, intermediate risk: PET-CT and/or biopsy, not watchful waiting alone.

frontHtml: Refer a fit patient with a high-probability, negatively staged nodule for surgical resection.
backHtml: high-probability nodule + negative staging + fit patient = surgery.

frontHtml: Order laryngoscopy for persistent hoarseness in a smoker before empiric therapy.
backHtml: persistent hoarseness in a smoker: look at the vocal folds first.

frontHtml: Treat vocal fold nodules first with voice therapy.
backHtml: vocal fold nodules: voice therapy first.

frontHtml: Image, rather than biopsy, a suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.
backHtml: suspected angiofibroma: image, do not biopsy.

frontHtml: Start intranasal glucocorticoids as first-line treatment for nasal polyps.
backHtml: nasal polyps: intranasal steroid first; escalate to surgery or biologics when it fails.

frontHtml: Image and biopsy a unilateral nasal mass in an adult to exclude neoplasm.
backHtml: unilateral nasal polyp in an adult: image and biopsy.

frontHtml: Manage a persistent pure ground-glass nodule with prolonged CT surveillance.
backHtml: persistent pure ground-glass nodule: long CT follow-up, not PET and not immediate surgery.

frontHtml: Identify the histologic composition of a pulmonary hamartoma from its CT features.
backHtml: fat plus popcorn calcification in a lung nodule means hamartoma: cartilage, fat and epithelial clefts.

frontHtml: Identify HPV 6 and 11 as the cause of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.
backHtml: wart-like laryngeal masses in a young child mean HPV 6/11 papillomatosis.

frontHtml: Diagnose juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma from age, sex and recurrent unilateral epistaxis.
backHtml: teenage boy + recurrent unilateral epistaxis + posterior nasal mass = angiofibroma; image it, do not biopsy it in the office.

frontHtml: Explain the leukotriene mechanism of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
backHtml: asthma + nasal polyps + NSAID reaction = leukotriene overproduction after COX-1 inhibition.

frontHtml: Link pediatric nasal polyps to cystic fibrosis and its CFTR defect.
backHtml: a child with nasal polyps needs a sweat chloride test.

frontHtml: Explain the phonotrauma pathogenesis and location of vocal fold nodules.
backHtml: nodules = bilateral, anterior-middle third junction, phonotrauma.

frontHtml: Recognize a calcified granuloma from histoplasmosis as a benign solitary nodule.
backHtml: dense or central calcification in a nodule usually means an old granuloma; in the Ohio/Mississippi valleys think histoplasmosis.

frontHtml: Recognize inverted papilloma and its association with squamous cell carcinoma.
backHtml: unilateral nasal polyp in an adult = rule out inverted papilloma or carcinoma; inverted papilloma is removed completely because of its link to carcinoma.

frontHtml: Apply lung cancer screening eligibility criteria.
backHtml: 50–80 years, ≥ 20 pack-years, quit < 15 years ago → annual low-dose CT.

frontHtml: Manage superior vena cava syndrome in a stable patient.
backHtml: stable SVC syndrome → biopsy before treatment; stridor or cerebral edema → urgent stent.

frontHtml: Treat severe hypercalcemia of malignancy.
backHtml: hypercalcemia of malignancy: IV saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate.

frontHtml: Choose the diagnostic procedure that both diagnoses and stages suspected lung cancer.
backHtml: in suspected lung cancer, biopsy the lesion that establishes the highest stage, often a mediastinal node by EBUS.

frontHtml: Choose curative treatment for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer.
backHtml: early-stage NSCLC in a fit patient → surgical resection; SBRT if inoperable.

frontHtml: Choose first-line treatment for extensive-stage small cell lung carcinoma.
backHtml: SCLC is a systemic disease: chemoimmunotherapy (extensive) or chemoradiation (limited), not surgery.

frontHtml: Evaluate persistent hoarseness in an adult at risk of laryngeal cancer.
backHtml: persistent hoarseness in a smoker → laryngoscopy.

frontHtml: Evaluate a persistent neck mass in an adult at risk for head and neck cancer.
backHtml: adult neck mass that persists → FNA, not open excision.

frontHtml: Manage malignant spinal cord compression.
backHtml: suspected cord compression: steroids now, whole-spine MRI now, then radiation or surgery.

frontHtml: Explain the role of early concurrent palliative care in metastatic lung cancer.
backHtml: palliative care is for symptoms and goals at any stage, concurrent with cancer treatment; hospice is different.

frontHtml: Select first-line therapy for metastatic EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer.
backHtml: driver mutation present → targeted therapy first, even with high PD-L1.

frontHtml: Identify squamous cell lung carcinoma from location, cavitation and PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.
backHtml: central + cavitation + PTHrP hypercalcemia = squamous cell carcinoma, recognized by keratin pearls.

frontHtml: Link an activating EGFR mutation in lung adenocarcinoma to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.
backHtml: never-smoker adenocarcinoma with an EGFR mutation is treated with an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome and its association with small cell carcinoma.
backHtml: proximal weakness that improves with use, areflexia and dry mouth in a smoker = Lambert-Eaton, from small cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Localize a superior sulcus tumor from brachial plexus and sympathetic chain findings.
backHtml: shoulder pain + hand wasting + Horner syndrome = superior sulcus tumor.

frontHtml: Connect SIADH to small cell lung carcinoma and its neuroendocrine immunoprofile.
backHtml: SIADH with a central mass = small cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor (chromogranin, synaptophysin).

frontHtml: Describe how HPV E6 and E7 cause oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
backHtml: p16-positive tonsil cancer is HPV-driven: E7 inactivates Rb, E6 degrades p53.

frontHtml: Associate nasopharyngeal carcinoma with Epstein-Barr virus and its presenting signs.
backHtml: adult unilateral serous otitis + neck node + East Asian background = EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

frontHtml: Recognize ectopic ACTH secretion by small cell lung carcinoma.
backHtml: rapid ectopic ACTH syndrome with severe hypokalemia = small cell lung carcinoma.

frontHtml: Explain immune-related adverse events of PD-1 checkpoint blockade.
backHtml: checkpoint inhibitor toxicity is autoimmune (loss of T-cell tolerance), treated with steroids.

frontHtml: Distinguish the prognosis of bronchial carcinoid from small cell carcinoma.
backHtml: bronchial typical carcinoid: young nonsmoker, endobronchial polyp, cured by resection.

frontHtml: Associate hypertrophic osteoarthropathy with non-small cell lung cancer.
backHtml: clubbing plus periostitis in a smoker suggests NSCLC, especially adenocarcinoma.

frontHtml: Perform diagnostic thoracentesis for a new unexplained pleural effusion.
backHtml: new effusion in a cancer survivor: diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis first.

frontHtml: Interpret malignant pleural fluid cytology as metastatic disease needing systemic therapy.
backHtml: a malignant effusion means advanced disease, treated systemically.

frontHtml: Choose an indwelling pleural catheter for a recurrent malignant effusion with trapped lung.
backHtml: recurrent malignant effusion: catheter or talc if the lung re-expands; catheter if it is trapped.

frontHtml: Apply Light criteria and fluid features to identify a malignant effusion.
backHtml: bloody lymphocytic exudate + weight loss = malignant effusion until proved otherwise.

frontHtml: Obtain tissue before treating a stable patient with malignant SVC syndrome.
backHtml: stable SVC syndrome: biopsy before treatment.

frontHtml: Treat life-threatening SVC syndrome with urgent endovascular stenting.
backHtml: SVC syndrome with stridor or confusion: stent now.

frontHtml: Recognize candidates for pulmonary metastasectomy.
backHtml: controlled primary + few resectable lung metastases + adequate reserve = consider metastasectomy (colorectal, sarcoma, renal cell).

frontHtml: Choose thoracoscopic biopsy to diagnose suspected mesothelioma.
backHtml: suspected mesothelioma or persistently cytology-negative exudate: thoracoscopic pleural biopsy.

frontHtml: Obtain tissue for a solitary new lung nodule in a patient with a history of cancer.
backHtml: solitary new nodule in a cancer survivor: obtain tissue before treating.

frontHtml: Recognize re-expansion pulmonary edema after large-volume thoracentesis.
backHtml: new opacities in the drained lung after a large-volume tap = re-expansion edema.

frontHtml: Counsel that metastatic germ cell tumors are usually curable with chemotherapy.
