backHtml: lung metastases from a germ cell tumor are usually curable with chemotherapy.

frontHtml: Recognize the hematogenous pattern of pulmonary metastases.
backHtml: multiple round basal-peripheral nodules = hematogenous metastases.

frontHtml: Explain the lymphatic mechanism and CT pattern of lymphangitic carcinomatosis.
backHtml: septal and peribronchovascular thickening plus severe dyspnea in a cancer patient = lymphangitic spread.

frontHtml: Use immunohistochemistry to identify renal cell carcinoma metastatic to the lung.
backHtml: PAX8 = kidney (also ovary, thyroid); TTF-1 = lung (and thyroid).

frontHtml: Distinguish mesothelioma from adenocarcinoma by immunohistochemistry.
backHtml: calretinin/WT1 positive, CEA/TTF-1 negative = mesothelioma.

frontHtml: Interpret pleural plaques as a benign marker of asbestos exposure.
backHtml: pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure; they are not premalignant.

frontHtml: Identify BAP1 tumor predisposition as a cause of familial mesothelioma.
backHtml: mesothelioma without asbestos + family uveal melanoma/RCC = germline BAP1.

frontHtml: Identify small cell carcinoma as the leading cause of SVC syndrome.
backHtml: SVC syndrome + central mass + SIADH in a smoker = small cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Identify the histology of choriocarcinoma metastatic to the lung.
backHtml: choriocarcinoma = trophoblast without villi, very high hCG, hemorrhagic lung metastases.

frontHtml: Explain why osteosarcoma lung metastases may calcify.
backHtml: calcified lung metastases in a teenager suggest osteosarcoma.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of a malignant pleural exudate.
backHtml: malignant effusion = exudate from leaky capillaries plus blocked lymphatic outflow.

frontHtml: Recognize the ultrastructural signature of mesothelioma.
backHtml: long, slender microvilli on electron microscopy = mesothelioma.

frontHtml: Choose the initial diagnostic test for suspected asthma.
backHtml: Confirm suspected asthma with pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry first.

frontHtml: Select reliever therapy that includes an inhaled corticosteroid for mild asthma.
backHtml: Mild asthma: as-needed ICS–formoterol, not SABA alone.

frontHtml: Recognize impending respiratory failure in acute asthma and intubate.
backHtml: Drowsiness and a rising PaCO2 in acute asthma mean intubation.

frontHtml: Identify smoking cessation as the disease-modifying intervention in COPD.
backHtml: Stopping smoking is what slows COPD progression.

frontHtml: Escalate COPD maintenance therapy using exacerbation history and eosinophils.
backHtml: In COPD, add an ICS for exacerbations when eosinophils are high.

frontHtml: Apply the criteria for survival-improving long-term oxygen in COPD.
backHtml: PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg at rest in stable COPD → long-term oxygen ≥ 15 h/day.

frontHtml: Choose noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory acidosis in a COPD exacerbation.
backHtml: COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic acidosis in an alert patient → NIV.

frontHtml: Interpret a flow–volume loop showing fixed upper airway obstruction.
backHtml: Plateaus on both limbs of the flow–volume loop = fixed upper airway obstruction, e.g. post-intubation tracheal stenosis.

frontHtml: Choose the diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis presenting in adulthood.
backHtml: Adult bronchiectasis plus pancreatitis or obstructive azoospermia → sweat chloride.

frontHtml: Identify when to test for α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
backHtml: Test every COPD patient once for α1-antitrypsin deficiency, especially young patients with basal emphysema.

frontHtml: Identify the eosinophil as the source of Charcot-Leyden crystals in asthmatic sputum.
backHtml: Crystals in asthmatic sputum come from eosinophils; the coiled casts come from mucus and shed epithelium.

frontHtml: Explain the different mechanisms of lung and liver injury in α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
backHtml: α1-antitrypsin deficiency hurts the lung by loss of function and the liver by retention of misfolded protein.

frontHtml: Predict the pulmonary function pattern of emphysema.
backHtml: Emphysema: obstruction, hyperinflation and a low DLCO.

frontHtml: Relate the mechanism and adverse effects of long-acting muscarinic antagonists.
backHtml: LAMAs relax airway smooth muscle by blocking M3 receptors; watch for dry mouth and urinary retention.

frontHtml: Distinguish the targets of asthma biologics.
backHtml: Anti-IL-5 drugs starve eosinophils; anti-IL-5Rα kills them by ADCC.

frontHtml: Recognize the histologic hallmark of chronic bronchitis.
backHtml: Chronic bronchitis = mucous gland hypertrophy (high Reid index).

frontHtml: Explain the basis of the sweat chloride test in cystic fibrosis.
backHtml: Cystic fibrosis raises sweat chloride by failure of ductal reabsorption.

frontHtml: Identify the structural defect in primary ciliary dyskinesia.
backHtml: Bronchiectasis + sinusitis + immotile sperm ± situs inversus = dynein arm defect.

frontHtml: Classify the hypersensitivity mechanisms of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.
backHtml: ABPA is type I plus type III hypersensitivity to airway-colonizing Aspergillus.

frontHtml: Explain effort-independent expiratory flow limitation in emphysema.
backHtml: Loss of recoil and tethering makes expiratory flow in emphysema effort-independent through dynamic airway compression.

frontHtml: Choose high-resolution CT as the initial imaging test for suspected interstitial lung disease.
backHtml: Suspected ILD: HRCT is the key next test; biopsy only when HRCT is indeterminate.

frontHtml: Select antifibrotic therapy for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
backHtml: IPF is treated with an antifibrotic (nintedanib or pirfenidone), not immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Manage Löfgren syndrome without biopsy or systemic glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Löfgren syndrome is treated symptomatically with NSAIDs; it usually resolves without steroids or biopsy.

frontHtml: Choose EBUS-guided needle aspiration to confirm suspected sarcoidosis.
backHtml: Suspected sarcoidosis: biopsy the least invasive involved site; for mediastinal nodes, EBUS-TBNA.

frontHtml: Prioritize antigen avoidance in hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
backHtml: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: antigen avoidance first; steroids only if severe or progressive.

frontHtml: Interpret pulmonary function tests showing extraparenchymal restriction from obesity.
backHtml: Restriction with normal DLCO and a very low ERV suggests obesity.

frontHtml: Counsel smoking cessation as the key preventive measure after asbestos exposure.
backHtml: After asbestos exposure, smoking cessation gives the largest reduction in lung cancer risk.

frontHtml: Screen patients with silicosis for latent tuberculosis infection.
backHtml: Diagnose silicosis → test for latent tuberculosis and treat if positive.

frontHtml: Treat chronic eosinophilic pneumonia with systemic glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia responds dramatically to systemic glucocorticoids after infection is excluded.

frontHtml: Diagnose eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
backHtml: Asthma + eosinophilia + mononeuritis multiplex = EGPA; ANCA is often negative.

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic sarcoidosis-related hypercalcemia with glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Sarcoid hypercalcemia (low PTH, high calcitriol) is treated with glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Identify bronchogenic carcinoma as the most common malignancy after asbestos exposure.
backHtml: Asbestos is most specific for mesothelioma but most often causes lung carcinoma, especially in smokers.

frontHtml: Relate silica-induced macrophage dysfunction to an increased risk of tuberculosis.
backHtml: Silicosis means upper-lobe nodules, eggshell nodes and a high risk of tuberculosis.

frontHtml: Explain the cell-mediated mechanism of chronic beryllium disease.
backHtml: Berylliosis is a type IV (Th1) hypersensitivity that mimics sarcoidosis; the lymphocyte proliferation test separates them.

frontHtml: Distinguish extraparenchymal from parenchymal restriction using DLCO.
backHtml: Restriction with a normal DLCO points outside the lung parenchyma: muscles, chest wall or obesity.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis.
backHtml: Granulomatous hypercalcemia is PTH-independent calcitriol made by macrophages.

frontHtml: Recognize usual interstitial pneumonia as the histologic pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
backHtml: UIP = patchy, temporally heterogeneous subpleural fibrosis with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism and main adverse effects of nintedanib.
backHtml: Nintedanib slows IPF by blocking PDGF, FGF and VEGF receptor tyrosine kinases; expect diarrhea.

frontHtml: Identify the hypersensitivity mechanisms of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
backHtml: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis combines type III and type IV reactions to an inhaled organic antigen.

frontHtml: Identify helminths whose larvae migrate through the lungs and cause Loeffler syndrome.
backHtml: Migrating infiltrates plus eosinophilia = larval lung migration (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides).

frontHtml: Recognize silo-filler's disease and its biphasic course.
backHtml: Silo-filler's disease is NO 2 injury: delayed pulmonary edema, then bronchiolitis obliterans.

frontHtml: Recognize rheumatoid pneumoconiosis in a dust-exposed patient with rheumatoid arthritis.
backHtml: Rheumatoid arthritis + mineral dust + multiple peripheral nodules = rheumatoid pneumoconiosis.

frontHtml: Set lung-protective tidal volume from predicted body weight in ARDS.
backHtml: ARDS: tidal volume ~6 mL/kg predicted body weight and plateau pressure ≤ 30 cm H 2 O.

frontHtml: Choose prone positioning for severe ARDS that persists despite lung-protective ventilation.
backHtml: severe ARDS (P/F < 150) despite low tidal volume and PEEP → prone ventilation; ECMO is the next rescue.

frontHtml: Select noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory failure in a COPD exacerbation.
backHtml: hypercapnic acidosis in COPD with an alert patient → bilevel NIV; intubate if it fails or contraindications appear.

frontHtml: Choose CT pulmonary angiography for a stable patient with high clinical probability of PE.
backHtml: high pretest probability → CTPA (no D-dimer); low/intermediate → D-dimer first; contrast contraindicated → V/Q.

frontHtml: Select a DOAC as initial therapy for low-risk pulmonary embolism.
backHtml: stable PE without RV strain → DOAC; thrombolysis only for hypotension; filter only if anticoagulation is impossible.

frontHtml: Treat high-risk pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock using systemic thrombolysis.
backHtml: PE with sustained hypotension → systemic thrombolysis (embolectomy if contraindicated); RV failure tolerates fluid poorly.

frontHtml: Order compression ultrasonography first for suspected PE in a pregnant patient with DVT symptoms.
backHtml: suspected PE in pregnancy with leg symptoms → leg compression ultrasound first; treat VTE in pregnancy with LMWH.

frontHtml: Use V/Q scanning to screen for CTEPH in pulmonary hypertension after pulmonary embolism.
backHtml: pulmonary hypertension after PE → V/Q scan for CTEPH; treat with lifelong anticoagulation and evaluate for endarterectomy.

frontHtml: Apply radiographic confirmation of feeding tube position to prevent respiratory failure from misplaced enteral feeding.
backHtml: confirm blind feeding-tube placement with a radiograph before feeding; auscultation is not reliable.

frontHtml: Identify hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage) as the histologic hallmark of early ARDS.
backHtml: early ARDS = diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes; type II pneumocytes proliferate later as the epithelium repairs.

frontHtml: Explain why shunt causes hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen in ARDS.
backHtml: hypoxemia that hardly improves on 100% oxygen means shunt; ARDS hypoxemia is mainly shunt.

frontHtml: Calculate the A–a gradient and use it to identify hypoventilation as the cause of hypoxemia.
backHtml: high PaCO 2 + normal A–a gradient = pure hypoventilation (drugs, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall); a raised gradient means lung disease.

frontHtml: Explain the respiratory alkalosis that accompanies acute pulmonary embolism.
backHtml: PE: tachypnea, hypoxemia, raised A–a gradient and low PaCO 2 (respiratory alkalosis); hypercapnia appears only with massive PE or exhaustion.

frontHtml: Associate heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension with BMPR2 loss-of-function variants.
backHtml: familial PAH = BMPR2 (autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance) → medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, plexiform lesions.

frontHtml: Identify endothelin receptor antagonism from the monitoring requirements of bosentan.
backHtml: endothelin receptor antagonists (-sentans): teratogenic; bosentan is hepatotoxic.

frontHtml: Recognize fat embolism syndrome after a long-bone fracture.
backHtml: long-bone fracture + 1–3 days + hypoxemia + confusion + axillary/conjunctival petechiae = fat embolism.

frontHtml: Explain the pressure conditions that allow venous air embolism during central line removal.
backHtml: venous air embolism needs an open vein + venous pressure below atmospheric (upright, inspiring); prevent with head-down position and exhalation/Valsalva.

frontHtml: Recognize hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with pulmonary AVMs and its autosomal dominant inheritance.
backHtml: HHT is autosomal dominant; pulmonary AVMs → hypoxemia, orthodeoxia, paradoxical stroke and brain abscess.

frontHtml: Choose the diagnostic study for suspected sleep apnea with cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
backHtml: Suspected sleep apnea with heart failure or other major comorbidity → in-lab polysomnography.

frontHtml: Select first-line therapy for severe obstructive sleep apnea.
backHtml: Moderate–severe symptomatic OSA → CPAP.

frontHtml: Confirm carbon monoxide poisoning with co-oximetry.
backHtml: Suspected CO poisoning → co-oximetry; ignore a normal pulse oximeter.

frontHtml: Identify indications for hyperbaric oxygen in carbon monoxide poisoning.
backHtml: CO poisoning with syncope or a level above about 25% → consider hyperbaric oxygen.

frontHtml: Treat drug-induced methemoglobinemia with methylene blue.
backHtml: Symptomatic methemoglobinemia → IV methylene blue.

frontHtml: Recommend prophylaxis for acute mountain sickness.
backHtml: Prevent AMS with gradual ascent and acetazolamide for higher-risk travelers.

frontHtml: Manage high-altitude pulmonary edema.
backHtml: HAPE → descend and give oxygen.

frontHtml: Diagnose obesity hypoventilation syndrome from an awake blood gas.
backHtml: Obesity + awake hypercapnia + no other cause = obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

frontHtml: Recognize and reverse opioid-induced hypoventilation masked by supplemental oxygen.
backHtml: Normal SpO2 on oxygen does not exclude opioid hypoventilation; give naloxone.

frontHtml: Manage central sleep apnea in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
backHtml: Central sleep apnea in HFrEF: treat the heart failure first; avoid adaptive servo-ventilation.

frontHtml: Calculate the A–a gradient to identify hypoventilation as the cause of hypoxemia.
backHtml: High PaCO2 + normal A–a gradient = hypoventilation.

frontHtml: Distinguish shunt from V/Q mismatch by the response to supplemental oxygen.
backHtml: Hypoxemia that 100% oxygen cannot fix means shunt.

frontHtml: Describe the effects of carbon monoxide on oxygen content and the dissociation curve.
backHtml: CO: low oxygen content, left shift, normal PaO2 and a falsely normal oximeter.

frontHtml: Link methylene blue's action to NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway.
backHtml: Methylene blue needs NADPH from G6PD to reduce methemoglobin.

frontHtml: Identify the peripheral chemoreceptors as the sensors of hypoxemia at altitude.
backHtml: Hypoxemia is sensed by the carotid bodies; PaCO2 by the central chemoreceptors.

frontHtml: Explain how acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness.
backHtml: Acetazolamide prevents mountain sickness by producing a metabolic acidosis that drives ventilation.

frontHtml: Describe regional V/Q differences in the upright lung.
backHtml: Upright lung: apex has the highest V/Q and PAO2; base has the most ventilation and perfusion.

frontHtml: Explain exercise desaturation in interstitial lung disease by diffusion limitation.
backHtml: Fibrosis + exercise = diffusion-limited oxygen transfer and desaturation.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanisms of oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD.
backHtml: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD is mainly V/Q worsening plus the Haldane effect, not loss of drive.

frontHtml: Choose chest tube drainage for a complicated parapneumonic effusion on the basis of pleural fluid pH and glucose.
backHtml: parapneumonic effusion with pH < 7.2, glucose < 60 mg/dL, loculation, pus or positive Gram stain → chest tube + antibiotics.

frontHtml: Use the serum-pleural albumin gradient to recognize a pseudoexudate after diuresis.
backHtml: diuresed heart-failure effusion that barely meets Light's criteria: albumin gradient > 1.2 g/dL → still a transudate.

frontHtml: Treat tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression before imaging.
backHtml: tension pneumothorax: decompress first, chest tube second, x-ray last.

frontHtml: Manage a small, stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax with observation.
backHtml: small, stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax → observe with oxygen and repeat x-ray; drain if large, symptomatic or secondary.

frontHtml: Recommend VATS with pleurodesis to prevent recurrent primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
backHtml: recurrent (second ipsilateral) or occupational-risk pneumothorax → VATS bleb resection + pleurodesis.

frontHtml: Choose water-soluble contrast esophagography to diagnose spontaneous esophageal rupture.
backHtml: vomiting → chest pain + pneumomediastinum (+ left effusion) = Boerhaave; confirm with water-soluble contrast study, not barium or endoscopy first.

frontHtml: Manage post-sternotomy mediastinitis with surgical debridement and intravenous antibiotics.
backHtml: post-sternotomy fever + drainage + sternal click = mediastinitis → debridement + IV antibiotics.

frontHtml: Recognize the chest-tube output thresholds for thoracotomy in traumatic hemothorax.
backHtml: hemothorax: chest tube first; thoracotomy if ≥ 1,500 mL immediately, ~200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or ongoing instability.

frontHtml: Relate a transudative pleural effusion in heart failure to raised capillary hydrostatic pressure.
backHtml: transudate = pressure problem (heart failure, low albumin); exudate = leaky or blocked pleura (infection, cancer, inflammation).

frontHtml: Identify the thoracic duct as the source of a postoperative chylothorax.
backHtml: chylothorax (TG > 110 mg/dL) = thoracic duct injury (surgery, trauma) or obstruction (lymphoma).

frontHtml: Recognize primary spontaneous pneumothorax and its cause in a tall, thin young smoker.
backHtml: tall, thin young smoker + sudden pleuritic pain + hyperresonance = primary spontaneous pneumothorax from apical blebs.

frontHtml: Explain the hemodynamic mechanism of shock in tension pneumothorax.
backHtml: tension pneumothorax = obstructive shock from reduced venous return; decompress before imaging.

frontHtml: Distinguish a large pleural effusion from consolidation, collapse and pneumothorax by examination.
backHtml: dull + decreased fremitus + trachea away = large effusion; dull + decreased fremitus + trachea toward = collapse.

frontHtml: Associate an anterior mediastinal mass in myasthenia gravis with thymoma.
backHtml: anterior mediastinal mass + myasthenia gravis = thymoma (others in the anterior compartment: teratoma/germ cell, lymphoma, thyroid).

frontHtml: Relate posterior mediastinal neuroblastoma to its neural crest origin.
backHtml: posterior mediastinum = neurogenic tumors; in children, neuroblastoma (neural crest).

frontHtml: Explain the low pH and glucose of a complicated parapneumonic effusion.
backHtml: low pleural pH and glucose in pneumonia = infected (complicated) effusion → drain it.

frontHtml: Differentiate costochondritis from Tietze syndrome and other causes of pleuritic chest pain.
backHtml: costochondritis: reproducible tenderness of several costosternal joints without swelling; Tietze adds swelling.

frontHtml: Manage suspected foreign body aspiration in a toddler with rigid bronchoscopy.
backHtml: suspected airway foreign body in a child is removed by rigid bronchoscopy.

frontHtml: Choose abdominal thrusts for severe foreign-body airway obstruction in a conscious adult.
backHtml: severe choking in a conscious adult: abdominal thrusts; if unresponsive: CPR.

frontHtml: Choose the correct choking maneuver for an infant younger than 1 year.
backHtml: for a choking infant, use back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts.

frontHtml: Decide on early intubation for inhalation injury with signs of airway involvement.
backHtml: smoke inhalation with hoarseness or stridor needs early intubation.

frontHtml: Treat carbon monoxide poisoning after smoke inhalation with 100% oxygen.
backHtml: carbon monoxide poisoning: 100% oxygen; consider hyperbaric oxygen when severe.

frontHtml: Select targeted therapy for a laryngeal attack of hereditary angioedema.
backHtml: acute hereditary angioedema of the airway: C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, not epinephrine or antihistamines.

frontHtml: Manage airway obstruction from a neck hematoma after thyroidectomy.
backHtml: airway compromise from a post-thyroidectomy hematoma: open the wound at the bedside first.

frontHtml: Give emergency management for a tracheoinnominate fistula.
backHtml: massive tracheostomy bleeding: overinflate the cuff, compress the innominate artery, then surgery.

frontHtml: Manage anterior epistaxis that persists after direct pressure.
backHtml: anterior epistaxis: pressure, then vasoconstrictor and cautery, then anterior packing.

frontHtml: Treat a nasal septal hematoma with incision and drainage.
backHtml: always look for a septal hematoma after nasal trauma and drain it promptly.

frontHtml: Choose the safest airway in a patient with laryngeal fracture and stridor.
backHtml: laryngeal fracture with airway compromise is managed by tracheostomy, not cricothyrotomy.

frontHtml: Identify the right main bronchus as the usual site of an aspirated foreign body and explain why.
backHtml: aspirated foreign bodies favor the right main bronchus because of its width and steep angle.

frontHtml: Relate bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury to loss of the posterior cricoarytenoid and airway obstruction.
backHtml: the posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal folds; bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury closes the glottis.

frontHtml: Identify external superior laryngeal nerve injury from loss of vocal pitch after thyroid surgery.
backHtml: loss of high pitch with normal fold movement after thyroid surgery points to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

frontHtml: Recognize hereditary angioedema and predict a low C4 level.
backHtml: hereditary angioedema is screened with a low C4; the swelling is caused by bradykinin.

frontHtml: Explain how ACE inhibitors cause angioedema through bradykinin.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor angioedema is caused by bradykinin, so it lacks hives and responds poorly to antihistamines.

frontHtml: Match epinephrine's receptor effects to its actions in anaphylaxis.
backHtml: in anaphylaxis, epinephrine relieves upper airway edema through α 1 vasoconstriction.

frontHtml: Identify the arterial source of posterior epistaxis.
backHtml: posterior nosebleeds arise from the sphenopalatine branch of the maxillary artery.

frontHtml: Locate the cricothyroid membrane from surface landmarks.
backHtml: cricothyrotomy goes through the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

frontHtml: Describe how carbon monoxide impairs oxygen transport.
backHtml: carbon monoxide lowers oxygen content and shifts the curve left while PaO 2 and pulse oximetry stay normal.

frontHtml: Explain why a nasal septal hematoma threatens the septal cartilage.
backHtml: septal cartilage is avascular, so a septal hematoma must be drained before the cartilage dies.

frontHtml: Identify the brachiocephalic artery as the vessel involved in tracheoinnominate fistula.
backHtml: massive bleeding weeks after a tracheostomy suggests a tracheoinnominate fistula.

frontHtml: Treat a tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression before imaging.
backHtml: tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis treated by immediate decompression.

frontHtml: Give initial treatment for an open pneumothorax.
backHtml: open pneumothorax: three-sided occlusive dressing, then a chest tube away from the wound.

frontHtml: Treat a traumatic hemothorax with tube thoracostomy.
backHtml: hemothorax with shock: resuscitate and place a chest tube to drain and measure the bleeding.

frontHtml: Identify the indications for thoracotomy in traumatic hemothorax.
backHtml: massive hemothorax (≥1,500 mL initially or ongoing brisk bleeding with instability) needs thoracotomy.

frontHtml: Choose regional analgesia for an older adult with multiple rib fractures and poor pain control.
backHtml: rib fractures in older adults: escalate to regional analgesia to protect breathing and cough.

frontHtml: Manage flail chest with pulmonary contusion using analgesia and judicious fluids.
backHtml: pulmonary contusion: avoid fluid overload; ventilate for respiratory failure, not for the flail itself.

frontHtml: Manage an acute traumatic diaphragmatic rupture.
backHtml: acute traumatic diaphragmatic rupture is repaired surgically, usually through the abdomen.

frontHtml: Choose bronchoscopy to diagnose a tracheobronchial injury after blunt chest trauma.
backHtml: suspected tracheobronchial injury is confirmed with bronchoscopy.

frontHtml: Plan observation after a submersion injury in a well-appearing child.
backHtml: asymptomatic drowning victims are observed for several hours before discharge.

frontHtml: Interpret ventilator pressures to recognize tension pneumothorax in a ventilated patient.
backHtml: in a ventilated patient, raised peak and plateau pressures with hypotension and a silent side mean tension pneumothorax.

frontHtml: Explain the hemodynamic mechanism of tension pneumothorax.
backHtml: tension pneumothorax causes shock by obstructing venous return.

frontHtml: Describe the position of the intercostal neurovascular bundle relative to the ribs.
backHtml: chest drains and needles go over the upper border of the rib to avoid the intercostal bundle.

frontHtml: Explain paradoxical chest wall movement in flail chest.
backHtml: a flail segment moves inward on inspiration because it is pulled by falling pleural pressure.

frontHtml: Identify shunt physiology as the cause of hypoxemia in pulmonary contusion.
backHtml: pulmonary contusion causes shunt-type hypoxemia that responds only partly to oxygen.

frontHtml: Explain why traumatic diaphragmatic rupture usually involves the left hemidiaphragm.
backHtml: blunt diaphragmatic rupture is usually left sided because the liver protects the right.

frontHtml: Relate referred shoulder pain to phrenic nerve innervation of the diaphragm.
backHtml: diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of hypoxemia after a submersion injury.
backHtml: drowning causes hypoxemia mainly through surfactant loss, alveolar collapse and shunt.

frontHtml: Apply Boyle's law to pulmonary barotrauma and arterial gas embolism in divers.
backHtml: breath-holding during ascent causes alveolar rupture and arterial gas embolism by Boyle's law.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of traumatic asphyxia.
backHtml: traumatic asphyxia produces craniofacial congestion and petechiae from retrograde venous pressure.

frontHtml: Classify blast injuries and identify blast lung as a primary blast injury.
backHtml: primary blast injury affects air-filled organs: ears, lungs and bowel.

frontHtml: Recognize the signs of a main bronchus rupture after blunt trauma.
backHtml: a persistent large air leak with a lung that will not re-expand means a bronchial tear near the carina.

frontHtml: Recognize congenital diaphragmatic hernia in a newborn.
backHtml: scaphoid abdomen + shifted heart sounds in a distressed newborn = diaphragmatic hernia.

frontHtml: Manage the initial airway in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
backHtml: diaphragmatic hernia: intubate and decompress the stomach; no bag-mask; delayed repair.

frontHtml: State the main prognostic determinants in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
backHtml: CDH prognosis = lung hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension, not the repair itself.

frontHtml: Distinguish transient tachypnea of the newborn from other causes of neonatal distress.
backHtml: term + cesarean without labor + fluid in the fissures = transient tachypnea of the newborn.

frontHtml: Treat neonatal respiratory distress syndrome that is failing CPAP.
backHtml: RDS failing CPAP (rising oxygen need) → give surfactant.

frontHtml: Use antenatal corticosteroids to prevent neonatal RDS in preterm labor.
backHtml: preterm labor before 34 weeks → antenatal corticosteroids.

frontHtml: Manage mild laryngomalacia in an infant.
backHtml: laryngomalacia with good growth and no red flags → reassure and follow.

frontHtml: Give immediate airway management for bilateral choanal atresia.
backHtml: cyanosis relieved by crying + a catheter that will not pass the nose → oral airway.

frontHtml: Diagnose a vascular ring in an infant with stridor and feeding difficulty.
backHtml: biphasic stridor + feeding difficulty + posterior esophageal indentation = vascular ring.

frontHtml: Confirm a positive cystic fibrosis newborn screen with sweat chloride testing.
backHtml: positive CF newborn screen → sweat chloride test; one variant does not mean carrier only.

frontHtml: Apply current neonatal resuscitation steps to a non-vigorous infant with meconium-stained fluid.
backHtml: meconium-exposed and apneic → ventilate; do not delay for routine tracheal suctioning.

frontHtml: Identify type II pneumocytes as the source of surfactant in neonatal RDS.
backHtml: preterm + ground-glass lungs = surfactant deficiency from immature type II pneumocytes.

frontHtml: Apply the law of Laplace to explain alveolar instability without surfactant.
backHtml: without surfactant, small alveoli collapse into large ones (Laplace); surfactant equalizes them.

frontHtml: Explain delayed surfactant maturation in infants of diabetic mothers.
backHtml: infant of a diabetic mother: big but surfactant-immature because insulin delays lung maturation.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism by which antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal RDS.
backHtml: antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by boosting surfactant production.

frontHtml: Relate congenital diaphragmatic hernia to its embryologic origin.
backHtml: posterolateral (Bochdalek) diaphragmatic hernia = failed pleuroperitoneal membrane closure.

frontHtml: Recognize the most common type of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula and its embryology.
backHtml: coiled tube + gas in the abdomen = esophageal atresia with distal TEF (faulty tracheoesophageal septum).

frontHtml: Diagnose pulmonary sequestration from its systemic arterial supply.
backHtml: lower-lobe mass + aortic arterial supply + no bronchial connection = pulmonary sequestration.

frontHtml: Link primary ciliary dyskinesia to axonemal dynein defects and its clinical features.
backHtml: immotile sperm + bronchiectasis + situs inversus = dynein arm defect (primary ciliary dyskinesia).

frontHtml: Identify the histology of a bronchogenic cyst.
backHtml: bronchogenic cyst = foregut bud with an airway-type wall (respiratory epithelium, cartilage).

frontHtml: Explain why extrathoracic dynamic airway obstruction causes inspiratory stridor.
backHtml: extrathoracic dynamic obstruction → inspiratory stridor; intrathoracic → expiratory.

frontHtml: Explain the embryology of a double aortic arch.
backHtml: double aortic arch = persistent distal right dorsal aorta; a ring around trachea and esophagus.

frontHtml: Manage bleomycin pulmonary toxicity during chemotherapy.
backHtml: Bleomycin pneumonitis: stop the drug permanently and give glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Minimize inspired oxygen in patients previously treated with bleomycin.
backHtml: After bleomycin, keep FiO 2 as low as safely possible during anesthesia.

frontHtml: Manage amiodarone pulmonary toxicity.
backHtml: Amiodarone lung toxicity: stop the drug and give steroids; expect slow resolution because of its long half-life.

frontHtml: Identify nitrofurantoin as a cause of chronic interstitial lung disease in an older adult.
backHtml: Chronic nitrofurantoin prophylaxis in older adults can cause pulmonary fibrosis; stop it.

frontHtml: Change antihypertensive therapy after ACE inhibitor–associated angioedema.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor angioedema: stop the entire class permanently and switch to an unrelated antihypertensive.

frontHtml: Treat opioid-induced respiratory depression with naloxone.
backHtml: Opioid toxidrome with hypoventilation: ventilate, then give naloxone titrated to breathing.

frontHtml: Choose supportive care over flumazenil in benzodiazepine overdose in a chronic user.
backHtml: Benzodiazepine overdose: supportive care; avoid flumazenil in chronic users and seizure disorders.

frontHtml: Diagnose e-cigarette or vaping product use–associated lung injury.
backHtml: Vaping THC + GI symptoms + bilateral ground-glass with negative infection workup = EVALI.

frontHtml: Recognize oxygen-induced hypercapnia in a COPD exacerbation.
backHtml: SpO 2 of 99% in a CO 2 retainer is too high; it can worsen hypercapnia.

frontHtml: Start noninvasive ventilation for persistent hypercapnic acidosis in a COPD exacerbation.
backHtml: COPD exacerbation with persistent respiratory acidosis despite controlled oxygen → noninvasive ventilation.

frontHtml: Explain why bleomycin selectively injures the lung.
backHtml: Bleomycin targets lung and skin because they lack bleomycin hydrolase; it spares the marrow.

frontHtml: Recognize the histologic signature of amiodarone pulmonary toxicity.
backHtml: Amiodarone lung: foamy, lipid-laden macrophages (phospholipidosis) and high-attenuation opacities.

frontHtml: Identify bradykinin accumulation as the cause of ACE inhibitor cough.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema come from bradykinin; switch to an ARB for cough.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
backHtml: Aspirin/NSAID-induced asthma is a leukotriene shunt, not IgE allergy.

frontHtml: Explain beta-blocker–induced bronchospasm in asthma.
backHtml: Nonselective beta-blockers can provoke refractory bronchospasm in asthma by blocking β 2 receptors.

frontHtml: Predict the blood gas pattern of opioid-induced hypoventilation.
backHtml: Pure hypoventilation: high PaCO 2 , hypoxemia, normal A–a gradient.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanisms of oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD.
backHtml: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD is mainly worsened V/Q matching plus the Haldane effect.

frontHtml: Describe the action of methylene blue in methemoglobinemia.
backHtml: Nitrite inhalant → methemoglobinemia → methylene blue reduces Fe 3+ back to Fe 2+ .

frontHtml: Classify the nicotinic receptor and relate it to nicotine's acute effects.
backHtml: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors, ligand-gated cation channels in ganglia, adrenal medulla and brain.

frontHtml: Identify methotrexate pneumonitis and the drug's mechanism.
backHtml: Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor) can cause dose-independent hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

frontHtml: Explain the two-phase pathogenesis of retinopathy of prematurity.
backHtml: Retinopathy of prematurity: oxygen suppresses VEGF, then relative hypoxia triggers VEGF-driven neovascularization.
